studies.sample_size: 472 cases analysed (504 patients enrolled; two-of-four partitions = 354 training / 118 test per fold)
studies.ai_purpose: Compare a neural network with logistic regression for diagnosing community-acquired MRSA at admission, to support the decision to give vancomycin
studies.best_model: Neural network (NN)

raw.Title: Diagnosis of MRSA with neural networks and logistic regression approach
raw.Population_Description: 504 patients culture-positive for S. aureus within the first 24 hours of admission to five Pittsburgh-area medical facilities (March 1996-March 1997); UPMC 17.6%, VAMC 17.8%, community teaching hospital 27.7%, two suburban non-teaching hospitals 36.9%
raw.Data_Source_Other: Compiled patient information (demographics, clinical and bacteriologic data) from five Pittsburgh-area medical facilities - not an EHR or registry extraction
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Logistic regression marked eight variables significant at alpha = 0.10: age, decubiti (Decub), diabetes mellitus (Dm), hospital worker (Employ type #1), extended-care worker (Employ type #2), peritoneal dialysis, skin wound/lesion, vancomycin use (Vanco). No ranked importance for the NN (weights not interpretable)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Neural network (feed-forward backpropagation, 38 input / 15 hidden / 1 output neurons, BrainMaker): AUC 0.928 (SD 0.016), overall classification accuracy 89.83% in subsample 1; logistic regression (8 significant variables): AUC 0.869 (SD 0.019), MSSA cases correctly classified 75 (86.21%) to 80 (91.95%), MRSA cases 67.74% to 77.42%
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Neural network (NN)
raw.Accuracy_Value: 89.83% overall classification accuracy (NN)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: NN model, four-fold cross-validation subsample 1 (test set of 118 patients)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: NN model applied to the complete data set of 472 patients (six models built from two-of-four partitions, best chosen)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and evaluated only by four-fold cross-validation with stratified sampling on 472 patients from one metropolitan area; no external or prospective validation reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: All data came from health-care facilities within Pittsburgh, PA and surrounding suburbs; the study may not have general applicability because the population under investigation is unique
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Authors warn that a flexible NN with many hidden-layer parameters carries substantial overfitting risk, and that the NN's inability to explain its output makes justification of results difficult; the motivation cites vancomycin overuse harms (toxicity, resistance, cost)
raw.Reviewer_Notes: PDF text layer carries no table bodies for tables 4 and 5 (the robustness and AUC computation tables), so all per-model figures quoted here come from the narrative text
raw.Unresolved_Items: Full per-subgroup accuracy ranges and the table 5 AUC computation are not readable from the text layer; whether table 3's hit/false-alarm rates belong to the NN is left for the team
raw.Sample_Size: 472 cases analysed (504 patients enrolled; two-of-four partitions = 354 training / 118 test per fold)
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Patients culture-positive for S. aureus within the first 24 hours of admission to one of five Pittsburgh-area facilities, March 1996 to March 1997
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Patients transferred from an acute facility or nursing home excluded (community-acquired MRSA focus); records with conflicting inputs/opposing outputs eliminated; incomplete records handled with an 'unknown' column
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Dataset_Size: 472 cases (504 patients enrolled)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Missing categorical/symbolic data coded with an added 'unknown' column (1 = missing, 0 otherwise); records with unknown facts excluded when few; the one continuous variable (age) had no missing values
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: One metropolitan area only: five facilities in and around Pittsburgh, PA - university hospital 17.6%, VA medical centre 17.8%, community teaching hospital 27.7%, two suburban non-teaching hospitals 36.9%; authors note limited general applicability
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture sites recorded as inputs: urine, respiratory tract, blood, post-op wound, skin wound/lesion, feces, plus 'unknown' site
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus: binary outcome of MRSA (output 1) versus MSSA (output 0) among patients culture-positive for S. aureus on admission
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (penicillin, cephalosporins); glycopeptides (vancomycin); aminoglycosides; quinolones
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Penicillin, vancomycin, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, quinolones (use within 2 weeks before admission)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary classification of patients: output value 1 = positive diagnosis (MRSA), 0 = negative diagnosis (MSSA), from laboratory-confirmed culture results
raw.AI_Purpose: Compare a neural network with logistic regression for diagnosing community-acquired MRSA at admission, to support the decision to give vancomycin
raw.Feature_Engineering: 38 input neurons from table 1: normalised age, sex, employment type (hospital / extended-care worker), admission route, seven culture sites plus 'unknown', diabetes, peritoneal and haemodialysis, IV drug use, seven immunosuppression causes plus 'unknown', wound types, indwelling devices, and five antibiotic classes used in the prior 2 weeks plus 'unknown'
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: All 38 risk factors entered the NN; logistic regression retained 8 variables considered significant at alpha = 0.10
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 8 (logistic regression); no reduction for the NN
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Stratified random sampling within the four-fold cross-validation, so the proportion of MRSA in each subset is approximately the same
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Trial and error over 1-30 hidden neurons (15 chosen: lowest root mean square error); learning rate 0.9 found empirically optimal; training stopped when 95% of training facts were accurately predicted
raw.Software_Libraries: BrainMaker (commercial neural-network package, California Scientific Software); SAS used for the AUC fitting method cited
raw.Other_Metrics: AUC with standard deviations (0.016 NN, 0.019 LR); z-statistic 3.0013 with p = 0.001; overall classification accuracy and its variation range across subsamples; hit and false-alarm rates by cutoff point
raw.Baseline_Method: Logistic regression, fitted on the same cross-validation partitions
raw.Baseline_Performance: AUC 0.869 (SD 0.019); MSSA cases correctly classified 75 (86.21%) to 80 (91.95%), MRSA cases 67.74% to 77.42%
raw.Internal_Validation: Four-fold cross-validation with stratified random sampling (k = 4)
raw.Train_Test_Split: Three of four partitions (354 patients) for model building, the fourth (118 patients) for testing; every partition served as test data in turn
raw.Overfitting_Method: Warning that a flexible NN with many parameters in the hidden layer risks substantial overfitting; hidden neurons limited to 15 selected by lowest root mean square error
raw.Clinical_Insights: Eight variables were significant for community-acquired MRSA - age, decubiti, diabetes mellitus, hospital worker, extended-care worker, peritoneal dialysis, skin wound/lesion and vancomycin use - and LR coefficients can be read as odds ratios
raw.Generalisability_Details: Authors state the study may not have general applicability because the population under investigation is unique to Pittsburgh; the model is argued to suit urban facilities with scarce resources
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Four-fold cross-validation with stratified random sampling on 472 patients; no external or prospective validation reported
raw.Integration_Point: Clinician completes a survey and runs the model before culture results are available, so no laboratory work is needed prior to prediction
raw.End_User_Described: Physicians admitting patients to health care facilities (clinicians)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction before culture results return, so appropriate antibiotics can be prescribed sooner; earlier suspicion enables prompt isolation (cohorting or barrier precautions), cutting lag time and nosocomial spread; an MSSA result lets vancomycin and isolation be avoided
raw.Stewardship_Details: No stewardship impact measured for the model; the paper quantifies overtreatment under a risk-factor-based vancomycin policy (61%, 190/313) and undertreatment of 6% (29/472) to motivate the prediction tool
raw.Barriers_List: NN lacks explanation power and accountability, so results are hard to justify; NN is short of uniqueness and reproducibility; danger of substantial overfitting; requires a large number of training cases and performs well only on data resembling the training set
raw.Facilitators_List: No laboratory work needed before prediction; the clinician simply fills out a survey and runs the model; most beneficial where medical resources are scarce; NN handles many variables and interactions
raw.Future_Directions: Show how prediction models can be developed and used for clinical problems such as MRSA in a specific community; the same approach is proposed for intensive care and nursing-home admissions
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Logistic regression significance testing at alpha = 0.10 (no importance ranking reported for the neural network)
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: No formal interaction testing; the NN is described as possessing flexible nonlinear modelling capabilities and as able to handle complicated factor interactions
raw.Limitation_Categories: Single geographic area (Pittsburgh, PA and suburbs) limiting general applicability; missing data (~10%) and conflicting records removed; NN overfitting risk; neither model exceeded 0.95 accuracy
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: About 10% of patient records were incomplete (symbolically or numerically); records with very similar inputs but opposing outputs were eliminated because NN and LR cannot handle conflicting facts; data shuffled to avoid order effects
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model architecture, training, cutoffs and validation are described in narrative detail; the numeric robustness and AUC computation tables (4 and 5) are not readable in the text layer

studies.title: DeepAMR for predicting co-occurrent resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
countries_all: study isolates come from 16 countries across six continents
studies.sample_size: 8388 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with DST for all four first-line drugs (primary analysis dataset; subset of >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs)
studies.ai_purpose: To develop DeepAMR, an end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder that predicts resistance to four first-line anti-TB drugs simultaneously (capturing resistance co-occurrence and the latent lineage structure), and to benchmark it against a direct-association SNP baseline, random forest, SVM, MLKNN and ensemble classification chains
studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
studies.best_model: DeepAMR (end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder) - decided on AUROC, the best AUROC for all six outcomes (e.g. 98.7% for MDR-TB)

raw.Title: DeepAMR for predicting co-occurrent resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
raw.Country_Countries: United Kingdom (lead author institution); study isolates come from 16 countries across six continents
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
raw.WHO_Region: AFR; AMR; EMR; EUR; SEAR; WPR
raw.Funder_Names: Royal Academy of Engineering; EPSRC; Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; Wellcome Trust; NIHR; Royal Society
raw.Population_Description: 8388 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with phenotypic DST for all four first-line anti-TB drugs (INH, EMB, RIF, PZA) - a subset of >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs; isolates from TB patients in 16 countries across six continents. Lineages: 3000 unknown, 2200 European, 1300 CentralAsian, 1200 EastAsian, fewer WestAfrica1, WestAfrica2 and Animal
raw.Data_Source_Other: Multi-country research cohort of MTB isolates with whole-genome sequences and phenotypic DST (CRyPTIC consortium; sequencing described in Walker et al. 2015)
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by permutation feature importance (Figure 3). INH: katG S315T, fabG1 C-15T, fabG1 G-17T (top three); also lineage-related or uncharacterised hits inhA S94A, katG S315N, embC V981L, rpoB C-61T, fabG1 T-8A. EMB: rpoB S450L, embB M306I, embB M306V, embB Q497R. RIF: nine of the top 11 SNPs are known RIF determinants (incl. rpoB S450L, rpoB H445Y, rpoB H445C, rpoB D435Y). PZA: manB D152N, rpoB C-61T, embC R738Q
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: DeepAMR (end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder) - decided on AUROC, the best AUROC for all six outcomes (e.g. 98.7% for MDR-TB)
raw.Sensitivity_Value: 96.3% (DeepAMR, MDR-TB - highest sensitivity value for DeepAMR)
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
raw.Specificity_Value: 96.7% (DeepAMR, PANS-TB - highest specificity value for DeepAMR in Table 1)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; PANS-TB outcome
raw.F1_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
raw.AUROC_Value: 98.7% (DeepAMR, MDR-TB - highest AUROC reported for DeepAMR)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validation is internal only: a single cohort of 8388 isolates split into training, validation and testing sets, with multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation performed 100 times and average performance reported on the hold-out test data. No external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment is reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Uneven resistance co-occurrence between drugs and equal objective weighting per drug; second-line cross-resistance ignored (inaccurate phenotyping, over-fitting risk with few resistant isolates); dataset too small for optimal multi-class classification; class weights computed on the training set may differ in testing (increased covariance); sensitivity/specificity/AUROC may not be the best evaluation for multi-label learning; t-SNE clusters are parameter-sensitive and may be false findings; permutation feature importance assumes feature independence and can over-rank rare SNPs
raw.Sample_Size: 8388 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with DST for all four first-line drugs (primary analysis dataset; subset of >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: none declared
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: MTB isolates with complete phenotype for the four first-line drugs (n = 8388); isolates were selected from the >13 000 tested with up to 11 drugs because there were few strains with resistance co-occurrence for second-line drugs
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: MTB isolates without complete phenotype for the four first-line drugs (analysis restricted to n = 8388); resistance co-occurrence of second-line drugs excluded from modelling
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
raw.Data_Source_Name: CRyPTIC consortium multi-country TB isolate cohort (no named database; sequencing described in Walker et al. 2015)
raw.Dataset_Size: 8388 isolates in the primary analysis set; >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs in the wider dataset; 13 403 MTB strains in the phenotype overview
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Nucleotide bases that could not be called with confidence denoted 'null calls' and excluded from the analysis; same pre-processing as Yang et al. (2017)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates drawn from 16 countries across six continents via the CRyPTIC consortium; lineage composition reported (3000 unknown, 2200 European, 1300 CentralAsian, 1200 EastAsian, fewer WestAfrica1, WestAfrica2, Animal), so the sample is globally distributed but lineage-imbalanced
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the four first-line anti-TB drugs isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB), rifampicin (RIF) and pyrazinamide (PZA), plus multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB, resistant to at least INH and RIF) and pan-susceptible TB (PANS-TB); predicted from WGS mutations and compared with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing
raw.Drug_Classes: First-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide); second-line drugs referenced in context (fluoroquinolones, injectable second-line drugs)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), ethambutol (EMB), pyrazinamide (PZA); MDR/XDR definitions also name fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) and amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Per-drug resistant/susceptible label predicted from WGS mutations; MDR-TB determined by the joint predicted resistance for INH and RIF, PANS-TB by predicted susceptibility to all four first-line drugs; reference standard is the phenotypic DST
raw.AI_Purpose: To develop DeepAMR, an end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder that predicts resistance to four first-line anti-TB drugs simultaneously (capturing resistance co-occurrence and the latent lineage structure), and to benchmark it against a direct-association SNP baseline, random forest, SVM, MLKNN and ensemble classification chains
raw.Feature_Engineering: Binary input vector per isolate: presence of a SNP variable coded 1, absence 0; every isolate represented by a 5919-dimension binary vector
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: None for the primary analysis (whole feature set F1); a secondary feature set F2 removed all previously identified resistance SNPs; SNP ranking by permutation feature importance
raw.Num_Features_Total: 5919 SNPs
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 5919 (feature set F1, all SNPs); feature subset F2 removes the previously identified SNPs - F2 dimension not reported
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Class weight for individual labels set to the ratio of resistant to susceptible isolates in the training set (SVM and RF)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Internal cross-validation on the training set of every experiment for SVM, RF and MLKNN; ECC and DeepAMR hyperparameters chosen by minimising hamming loss and then fixed across all bootstrap experiments
raw.Software_Libraries: Keras (augmented cluster layer referred to the GitHub project 'Keras_Deep_Clustering')
raw.Other_Metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, F1 score and AUROC (mean and SD across 100 bootstrap samples); hamming loss used for hyperparameter selection; adjusted rand index used to choose the number of clusters; Wilcoxon signed-rank test P-values versus the DA baseline
raw.Baseline_Method: Direct association (DA): any resistance determinant for a drug present in the Walker et al. (2015) catalogue labels the isolate resistant ('OR' rule); at least one determinant for both INH and RIF labels MDR-TB; no resistance determinants for the four first-line drugs labels PANS-TB
raw.Baseline_Performance: DA: best sensitivity 94.9% (RIF) and 94.1% (PANS-TB), best F1 95.1% (RIF) and 94.8% (PANS-TB); much worse for PZA (sensitivity 47.9%, AUROC 73.0%)
raw.Internal_Validation: Single cohort split into training, validation and testing sets; 30% hold-out test data; multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation repeated 100 times (100 bootstrap experiments) with average test performance reported
raw.Train_Test_Split: 30% of data held out for testing in every experiment (70/30 split), average results over 100 bootstrap samples
raw.CV_Folds: Number of folds not stated; multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation performed 100 times
raw.Overfitting_Method: Unsupervised pre-training of the denoising auto-encoders then fine-tuning; batch normalisation and dropout layers used only in training to avoid over-fitting; training stopped when validation loss stopped improving after 5 epochs
raw.Clinical_Insights: INH and RIF resistance determinants dominate sensitivity variation for INH and RIF classification; both RIF and EMB determinants matter for EMB classification; lineage-associated SNPs contribute most to PZA classification, with RIF, EMB and SM determinants also affecting it - consistent with PZA resistance depending on co-occurrence with RIF, EMB and SM
raw.Generalisability_Details: Authors note the dataset is too small for optimal multi-class classification and that t-SNE visual clusters are strongly influenced by parameter choice and may be false findings; kernel t-SNE and UMAP are suggested as alternatives
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Evidence setting the level: internal hold-out validation only - a single cohort (8388 isolates) split into training, validation and testing sets with 30% held out, multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation repeated 100 times and average test performance reported; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment evidence
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing anti-TB treatment: the stated motivation is to speed up prescribing the best drug to individual patients
raw.Barriers_List: Second-line drug phenotyping too inaccurate and too few resistant isolates (over-fitting risk), so cross-resistance beyond first-line drugs was ignored; dataset too small for optimal multi-class classification; class weight computed on the training set may not hold in testing; sensitivity/specificity/AUROC may not be best for multi-label evaluation; t-SNE parameter sensitivity and no out-of-sample extension; permutation importance assumes feature independence
raw.Facilitators_List: End-to-end integration of non-linear dimensionality reduction and multi-label learning, so high-level data abstraction and classification are learned jointly; large multi-country cohort (8388 isolates, 16 countries); source code shared; unsupervised pre-training with fine-tuning
raw.Future_Directions: Kernel t-SNE as a parametric extension giving explicit out-of-sample extension, and UMAP as a faster alternative that preserves more global structure; better SNP ranking by learning variable importance within the model rather than permutation importance
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (genomic mutation features and WGS/DST laboratory measurements; no clinical, demographic, pharmacological, behavioural, environmental or temporal predictors)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation feature importance: the unscaled sensitivity reduction after randomly permuting one feature column at a time
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: inhA S94A and fabG1 T-8A are stated to be previously uncharacterized; other top-ranked SNPs are lineage-related (embC V981L, rpoB C-61T associated with the Central Asian sub-lineage, embC T270I) or belong to other drugs' resistance (rpoB S450L for RIF, rpsL K43R for streptomycin, embB G406S for EMB)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data: uneven resistance co-occurrence, small dataset, second-line drugs excluded. Modelling: equal objective weighting per drug, class-weight shift between training and testing, sensitivity/specificity/AUROC suboptimal for multi-label evaluation, permutation importance assumes independence and over-ranks rare SNPs, t-SNE parameter sensitivity and limitations, possible phenotype/DST errors
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Phenotype errors on the four first-line drugs may mislead classification; class weight computed on the training set may differ in the testing set (increased covariance); inaccurate second-line drug phenotyping; rare SNPs ranked highly by permutation importance despite negligible sensitivity effect
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model development is well described (architecture, objectives, pre-training, thresholds, hyperparameter strategy), with detail deferred to Supplements C and G; however several items are absent (hardware, programming language, dataset identifiers, external validation, data availability) and Table 1's numbers are severely mangled in the pypdf text layer, making metric extraction error-prone
raw.Page_References: Article pp. 3240-3249 (text layer pp. 1-10); abstract p. 1; methods pp. 2-4; Table 1 and its note p. 3; results pp. 5-7; discussion and limitations pp. 7-8; references pp. 8-10

studies.title: Using Natural Language Processing to Improve Accuracy of Automated Notifiable Disease Reporting
studies.sample_size: 64,554 HL7 messages interpreted (categories 1 and 2) from 19,034 unique patients; test set 232,776 messages from 53,338 unique patients; training set 3,957 messages
studies.ai_purpose: To test whether a rule-based NLP system (REX) improves the accuracy and completeness of automated electronic laboratory reporting of notifiable conditions, using MRSA in unstructured free-text culture reports as the test case
studies.pathogens_reported: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); similar phrasing from Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus Epidermidis and Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Hominis caused potential false positives
studies.best_model: REX (Regenstrief EXtraction tool) - highest sensitivity/specificity/PPV/F-measure versus the existing ELR processor

raw.Title: Using Natural Language Processing to Improve Accuracy of Automated Notifiable Disease Reporting
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
raw.Population_Description: HL7 laboratory result messages containing the keywords 'MRSA', 'methicillin' or 'Aureus' from the Indiana Network for Patient Care (INPC): test set 232,776 messages from 131 data sources covering 53,338 unique patients; 64,554 messages (categories 1 and 2) interpreted, from 41 sources and 19,034 unique patients; training set 3,957 messages from 25 sources
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: REX (Regenstrief EXtraction tool, rule-based NLP) - sensitivity 99.96%, specificity 99.71%, PPV 99.81%, F-measure 0.9989 on 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages; existing operational automated ELR notifiable condition processor with limited NLP - interpreted only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages as positive
raw.Best_Performing_Model: REX (Regenstrief EXtraction tool) - highest sensitivity/specificity/PPV/F-measure versus the existing ELR processor
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: REX's rules and knowledge base were adapted on a December 2007 training set and then applied to a separate one-year test set (232,776 messages) with physician manual review as the gold standard; the paper reports no prospective or external multicentre validation of this MRSA module
raw.Reported_Limitations: Developer of the software also acted as the gold standard and evaluator of the data extraction process; negation detection more difficult in these messages; many free-text results disregarded grammatical rules (incomplete sentences, spelling errors, poor punctuation); substantial variation in laboratories' use of the HL7 standard; ambiguous reports
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: 74 false positives (73 caused by improper sentence detection, e.g. 'MRSA DNA....NEGATIVE') and 17 false negatives (a spelling error and 'rule out MRSA' phrasing); false positives add to public health's burden to cull spurious results
raw.Sample_Size: 64,554 HL7 messages interpreted (categories 1 and 2) from 19,034 unique patients; test set 232,776 messages from 53,338 unique patients; training set 3,957 messages
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: All INPC laboratory HL7 messages containing the keywords 'methicillin', 'MRSA' or 'Aureus': training set December 2007 (3,957 messages from 25 unique message sources); test set January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008 inclusive (232,776 messages from 131 data sources, 53,338 unique patients)
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Category 4 messages excluded using business rules: not originating from a known source of laboratory results messages; containing no result (HL7 OBX or NTE) segment; result pending according to the OBX-11 component. Non-laboratory reports (e.g. discharge summaries) and pending results were also excluded; only final results processed
raw.Data_Types_Used: Free text / clinical notes
raw.Data_Source_Name: Indiana Network of Patient Care (INPC)
raw.Dataset_Size: 232,776 HL7 messages containing MRSA keywords over 12 months (test set); 64,554 interpreted; training set 3,957 messages
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single regional health information exchange in Indiana, USA (INPC); 41 laboratory sources within that HIE; 232,776 messages from 131 data sources overall
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture results (approximately 97% of the tests); blood culture result messages used for the comparison with the existing ELR system
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) positive laboratory reports for notifiable disease reporting
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); similar phrasing from Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus Epidermidis and Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Hominis caused potential false positives
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin (the 'methicillin' keyword defines MRSA); clindamycin named only inside an example report phrase
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary message-level classification: category 1 = MRSA positive, category 2 = MRSA keyword present but negated; the final positive or negative determination was made by the physician reviewer and became the gold standard
raw.AI_Purpose: To test whether a rule-based NLP system (REX) improves the accuracy and completeness of automated electronic laboratory reporting of notifiable conditions, using MRSA in unstructured free-text culture reports as the test case
raw.Feature_Engineering: Keyword concepts ('methicillin', 'MRSA', 'Aureus') detected with regular expressions, plus a window of words before and after the keyword to determine context (negated, ambiguous, historical); false-negation pattern database; patterns added to handle variation in HL7 OBX-3, OBX-5 and NTE reporting formats
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Literature search plus training-set frequency analysis to identify frequently occurring words and phrases that express MRSA infection
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Iterative testing-analysis-modification cycle: after initially modifying the software and knowledge base, reports were processed to find false positive and false negative errors and subsequent adjustments were made to REX
raw.Other_Metrics: F-measure 0.9989 for the test data; false positives 74 and false negatives 17 (Table 1: REX/manual review positives 39,491 vs 74, negatives 17 vs 24,972); reporting-rate comparison: existing ELR processor identified only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages
raw.Baseline_Method: Existing operational automated ELR notifiable condition processor with limited NLP capability (longest common string comparator and basic negation detection)
raw.Baseline_Performance: Identified only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages as positive
raw.Internal_Validation: Rules adapted on the December 2007 training set, then applied to a separate one-year test set; REX output compared with physician manual review as the gold standard
raw.Train_Test_Split: Training set December 2007 (3,957 messages from 25 sources); test set January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008 (232,776 messages from 131 data sources, 53,338 unique patients)
raw.Clinical_Insights: Errors traced to sentence delimitation and negation context: a full stop before 'NEGATIVE' caused 73 false positives, and 'rule out MRSA' placed close to a positive MRSA phrase caused 16 false negatives
raw.Maturity_Evidence: REX was adapted on a December 2007 training set and evaluated on a separate one-year test set against physician manual review (internal validation); the paper states REX is currently used to augment notifiable disease reporting to the ISDH but reports no prospective or external validation of this MRSA module
raw.Integration_Point: HL7 message flow of the Indiana Network for Patient Care / automated ELR pipeline feeding the notifiable condition processor that transmits category 1 (positive) messages to public health
raw.End_User_Described: Public health agencies (Indiana State Department of Health) receiving automated notifiable disease reports
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: ELR system identifies potentially reportable candidate tests by LOINC codes and transmits positive results to public health; microbiology culture results arrive as unstructured free text; REX classifies HL7 messages into four categories and only category 1 (positive) messages are transmitted for public health reporting
raw.Barriers_List: Free-text results with poor punctuation, spelling errors and incomplete sentences; substantial variation in how laboratories use the HL7 standard; look-alike organism names (S. epidermidis, S. hominis); ambiguous reports; sentence-level processing limits
raw.Facilitators_List: Conforming HL7 laboratory messages to the HITSP standard (results in OBX-5, one result per segment, abnormal flags in OBX-8), including LOINC codes for test names and SNOMED-CT codes for results, which would reduce variation and improve detection accuracy
raw.Future_Directions: Add other conditions (e.g. Shigella, Salmonella) to REX's database; move healthcare towards national HIT standardisation of HL7 message content

raw.Reported_Limitations: No valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; a random sample from more facilities would have improved the completeness analysis but was logistically infeasible; per-site samples were small so no VA site-specific accuracy estimates could be reported; completeness cannot be confirmed for unsampled VA sites.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Systematic biases can be introduced when data are derived from or processed electronically; microbiology data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA, and report-format variation across sites and years could affect extraction.

raw.Unresolved_Items: The paper reports accuracy against two reference sets (independently derived electronic data and expert-reviewed annotation) and at two levels (S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference); it does not state which is primary, and the values differ. Whether the multi-site, multi-year VA comparison constitutes external validation is also a judgement call.
raw.Sample_Size: 33,024,796 unique microbiology records from 128 VistA sites (152 currently active acute care hospitals; 170 total hospitals over 1990-2009); validation comparisons used 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: None of the authors have received reimbursements, fees, funding, or salary from an organization that may gain or lose financially from this publication; there are no outstanding patents; all authors have affiliations with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Microbiology documents containing the strings “staph”, “coag”, “mrsa”, “orsa”, “oxacillin” or “aureus” (10,000 randomly selected records) queued for expert review; VISN 4 and Salt Lake City microbiology data that had already been annotated; PCS microbiology records collected from all VistA systems, 1990-2009
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: MRSA surveillance screens were removed before information extraction: 4,002 records identified as screens in the expert-reviewed data set were removed, and screening studies were identified by reviewers but removed during evaluation of information extraction accuracy
raw.Data_Types_Used: Free text / clinical notes; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: VA Patient Care Services (PCS) microbiology data extracted from VistA; VISN 4 data warehouse; VA Salt Lake City Health Care System (VA SLC HCS) data warehouse
raw.Dataset_Size: 33,024,796 unique microbiology records from 128 VistA sites; expert-annotation sample of 10,000 records; validation comparisons of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Completeness estimated by matching microbiology accession numbers against independently derived data warehouse records (98.5%, 95% CI 98.5-98.6%) and by analysing gaps in sequentially ordered accession numbers, which yields a lower bound because gaps also arise from non-patient samples
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Nationwide VA microbiology data from 128 VistA sites representing 152 currently active acute care hospitals; comparison data came from eleven VA sites, VISN 4 (ten hospitals) and VA SLC, plus ten randomly sampled hospitals for sequence-gap analysis; no site-specific accuracy estimates could be reported
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: All cultured sample and specimen types appearing in microbiology reports (11,596 unique types reviewed); MRSA surveillance tests from the anterior nares were filtered out before extraction
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance inferred for cultures in which S. aureus was detected (i.e. MRSA), together with identification of S. aureus itself, extracted from free-text microbiology reports and validated against independently derived electronic data and expert annotation
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) and coagulase-positive S. aureus
raw.Drug_Classes: Antimicrobials recorded in susceptibility testing: penicillinase-resistant penicillins (oxacillin, nafcillin, methicillin) and cephalosporins (cefoxitin, cefazolin, cephalothin), plus mecA / penicillin binding protein 2A testing
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: oxacillin; cefoxitin; cefazolin; cephalothin; nafcillin; methicillin (resistance); penicillin binding protein 2A / mecA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: A culture was positive for methicillin resistance when S. aureus was detected and the detected susceptibilities indicated resistance; susceptibility terms were mapped to resistant, susceptible or indeterminate, and resistance could be evidenced by oxacillin, cefoxitin, penicillin binding protein 2A or mecA testing, or by resistance to cefazolin, cephalothin, nafcillin, or a simple statement of methicillin resistance
raw.AI_Purpose: Apply NLP information extraction to nationwide VA free-text microbiology reports to extract organisms and antibiotic susceptibilities and infer MRSA, then validate the extraction against independently derived electronic data and expert annotation
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 0 - no models compared; a single rule-based NLP information extraction system was developed and assessed against two independent reference standards (electronic data warehouse and expert annotation)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Hand-crafted rules exploiting the semi-structured report templates (section identification, organism detection, susceptibility detection, MRSA inference); descriptor terms for quantity, concentration and resistance were stripped to leave the organism name, which was then mapped to SNOMED-CT; susceptibility terms were mapped to resistant/susceptible/indeterminate
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative manual rule and term-list development on training reports with detailed failure analysis after each iteration
raw.Software_Libraries: Apache Unstructured Information Management Architecture (UIMA); MUMPS (VistA database language); SQL relational database
raw.Other_Metrics: MRSA surveillance-screen filter: sensitivity 99.4%, specificity 97.9%; data completeness 98.5% (95% CI 98.5-98.6%); NPV 100% against electronic data and 98.6% (S. aureus) / 99.8% (methicillin resistance) against expert-reviewed data
raw.Internal_Validation: Random split of the expert-annotated sample into training and test sets (half in each; all Salt Lake City data used for training), with a second comparison set of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
raw.Train_Test_Split: Half of the expert-annotated records for training and half for the test set; the validation comparison used a second set of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
raw.Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Decision rules / surrogate tree
raw.Clinical_Insights: Clinical experts were involved in developing the NLP tools and inference algorithms; clinical nurses experienced in reading microbiology reports annotated S. aureus status, methicillin resistance and surveillance-test status, and discordant records were re-reviewed by a domain expert
raw.Generalisability_Details: Authors state the NLP methods are robust and should serve well against other organisms, but caution that report-format variation may be greater when combining data from disparate non-VA health systems, and they could not report VA site-specific accuracy
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Rule-based NLP system developed on VA microbiology data and evaluated against two independent reference standards using a random training/test split; the extraction runs as a background data-collection service on VINCI but has not been evaluated prospectively or in routine clinical decision-making
raw.Integration_Point: Background data-extraction process that pulls microbiology reports from VistA at each medical centre through RPCs/VistaWeb into a secure SQL database, with NLP applied on the VINCI computing environment before use in surveillance analyses
raw.End_User_Described: Infection-control programmes and surveillance analysts / researchers - for example the VA Inpatient Evaluation Center, which gathered the data to evaluate the National MRSA Prevention Initiative
raw.Barriers_List: Differing data models between systems; messaging strategies; security issues; microbiology data siloed at each hospital; loss of standardised structured fields in the free-text format; report-format variation between centres and over years; MUMPS has only one data type so there are no data type checks; data may be entered in the wrong place in VistA
raw.Facilitators_List: Reuse of existing, reliable VA data processes (RPCs and VistaWeb) that require no independent maintenance and can run as a background process; semi-structured report templates that support rule-based extraction; expert annotation and clinical expert involvement; availability of independent reference data sets
raw.Future_Directions: Contribute the dataset and methods to a comprehensive infectious disease surveillance system; validate routine data warehouse pulls for completeness and concordance; extend the NLP methods to other organisms; combine data across non-VA health systems
raw.Limitation_Categories: Reference standard and data access: no valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; only a sample of facilities could be studied; no VA site-specific accuracy estimates; small per-site samples; report-format variation across sites and over time
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: MUMPS has only one data type so there are no data type checks; data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA; microbiology report formats changed over the years and varied between centres; sequence gaps in accession numbers at about half the sites examined

studies.title: Epidemiology and prediction of multidrug-resistant bacteria based on hospital level
studies.sample_size: Monthly hospital-level data for October 2010 to October 2020 (39 indicators per month); the number of patients or isolates is not reported in the text
studies.ai_purpose: Use a random forest model and cross-correlation analysis to explore hospital-level factors affecting MDRB infections and their predictive power, and build a regression tree model to predict the number of hospitalised patients with MDRB infection in order to build an early-warning platform for drug resistance
studies.pathogens_reported: Escherichia coli (E. coli), Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Klebsiella Pneumonia (K. pneumoniae), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Haemophilus influenzae; the five MDRB analysed are ESBL-producing E. coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa
studies.best_model: Regression tree (rpart/CART) - the model the paper uses to establish the prediction (early-warning) model for the number of patients with MDRB infection; no comparative performance metric is reported for it against the random forest

raw.Title: Epidemiology and prediction of multidrug-resistant bacteria based on hospital level
raw.Funder_Names: China Postdoctoral Science Foundation (No. 2021M693593); GuangDong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (No. 2021A1515111146)
raw.Population_Description: Patients with bacterial infection detected at a large teaching hospital (the Eighth Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen, China) between October 2010 and October 2020; only the first result of multiple tests in the same patient was included

raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by random forest IncNodePurity: (1) number of hospital operations; (2) number of type I incision operations; (3) number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues; (4) number of discharged patients; (5) average hospital stay (days); (6) average rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions; (7) rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
raw.Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Programme manager / policymaker

raw.Best_Performing_Model: Regression tree (rpart/CART) - the model the paper uses to establish the prediction (early-warning) model for the number of patients with MDRB infection; no comparative performance metric is reported for it against the random forest

raw.Reported_Limitations: Data came from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so the machine learning model could only produce monthly rather than weekly or daily estimates for real-time prediction; the ecological research design cannot demonstrate causality; the model was built on one hospital, so indicator thresholds may not be generalisable to other hospitals owing to differences in hospital volume
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; the paper reports only age and sex distributions of infected patients (Supplementary Fig. S1) and performs no equity or fairness analysis
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval is stated as not applicable; no other ethical or governance issues are discussed

raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Not otherwise specified; only the first results of multiple tests in the same patient were included
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; Epidemiological surveillance data
raw.Data_Source_Name: The Eighth Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University laboratory information system (LIS); monthly hospital reports
raw.Dataset_Size: Monthly database of 39 hospital-level variables from October 2010 to October 2020
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: One large teaching hospital in the central urban area of Shenzhen, a megacity in southern China with a permanent resident population of 13.43 million
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: The number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) infection per month (variable c4) at hospital level, modelled from 39 hospital-level indicator variables; five MDRB categories analysed: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli), Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Klebsiella Pneumonia (K. pneumoniae), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Haemophilus influenzae; the five MDRB analysed are ESBL-producing E. coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa

raw.Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa); beta-lactams (ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae); methicillin (MRSA)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRB infection is counted as the number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria infection (dependent variable c4), predicted from 39 hospital-level predictor variables using real-world monthly data
raw.AI_Purpose: Use a random forest model and cross-correlation analysis to explore hospital-level factors affecting MDRB infections and their predictive power, and build a regression tree model to predict the number of hospitalised patients with MDRB infection in order to build an early-warning platform for drug resistance
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 (random forest for variable importance; regression tree/CART for prediction); no head-to-head performance metric is reported
raw.Feature_Engineering: 39 factors collected in five groups (hospital operation volume x1-x15, nosocomial infection g1-g8, antibacterial drug use y1-y10, outdoor temperature, incidence of nosocomial infections c1-c3); all variables organised on a monthly basis to build a database; average daily, daily maximum and daily minimum temperature used to adjust for seasonal influence
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Random forest multivariate importance using increases in node purity (IncNodePurity), with the loss function selected through the best segmentation; the highest-ranked variables were carried into cross-correlation and regression tree analysis
raw.Num_Features_Total: 39 independent variables
raw.Num_Features_Selected: Not stated numerically; the highest-importance variables were selected for cross-correlation and regression tree analysis (number of hospital operations, number of type I incision operations, number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, number of discharged patients, average hospital stay, rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions, rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients)
raw.Software_Libraries: pheatmap, randomForest, rpart, rpart.plot, ggplot2 (R version 4.0.3); IBM SPSS version 25.0 for cross-correlation
raw.Other_Metrics: Regression tree thresholds and predicted case counts: emergency rescues <314, hospital operations <1333 and clinical pathway rate >9.3 give an estimated 14 MDRB patients in the hospital in the current month; emergency rescues >314 gives an estimate as high as 77
raw.Overfitting_Method: Random forest selected partly because it prevents overfitting; no cross-validation or train/test split is reported
raw.Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
raw.Clinical_Insights: Surgical, emergency and hospitalised rescue patients showed the highest risk of MDRB infection; more rational perioperative antibiotic use and a higher clinical pathway rate are linked to fewer patients with MDRB infection, while excessive surgical volume and inappropriate antibiotic use in emergency patients may increase MDRB numbers
raw.Generalisability_Details: The model was built on data from one hospital, so the threshold values of the indicators may not be generalisable to other hospitals because of differences in hospital volume
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Model developed on 10 years of monthly hospital-level data from a single hospital; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
raw.Integration_Point: Hospital-level monthly drug-resistance early-warning platform; not integrated into clinical or laboratory systems
raw.End_User_Described: Not explicitly described; the model is intended for hospital-level monitoring and early warning of MDRB infection
raw.Barriers_List: Monthly (not weekly or daily) resolution of the data limits real-time prediction; the ecological design cannot demonstrate causality; the single-hospital model means indicator thresholds may not transfer to hospitals of a different volume
raw.Future_Directions: Improving the accuracy of the data without changing the methods, and wider validation of indicator thresholds across hospitals with different volumes
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 groups of variables / 39 variables in total
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest IncNodePurity (increases in node purity) plus multivariate importance by removing predictor variables from each single tree in the forest
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Hospital-management indicators highlighted as influential, including the number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, the rate of rational perioperative antimicrobial drug use in type I and II incision operations, and the rate of clinical pathways
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data granularity (monthly only), ecological design (no causality), and generalisability (single hospital, hospital-volume-dependent thresholds)
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Data collected from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so only monthly estimates could be produced
raw.Reporting_Clarity: No predictive performance metric (accuracy, AUC or error) is reported for the random forest or the regression tree; results are descriptive (importance rankings, cross-correlation lags, regression tree thresholds)

raw.Funder_Names: UF Informatics Institute; National Institutes of Health - National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH/NIAID) grant #R01AI141810
raw.Population_Description: Adult patients with Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection (BSI-KP): 1,398 patients (1,271 inpatient, 118 outpatient); median Charlson comorbidity index 4.00; 50.7% of inpatients transferred to ICU
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Boosted logistic regression effect sizes (expert-chosen set, ICU population): Betalactam resistance in Klebsiella before or upon the infection (OR 10.12); HIV/AIDS (2.83); Amikacin use upon the infection (2.63); Tobramycin use upon the infection (2.34); Carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella upon the infection (2.23); Ethnicity group - not hispanic (2.06); Infection source - throat/lung (1.78); Vancomycin use upon the infection (1.76); Carbapenem resistance in non-Klebsiella organisms before or upon the infection (1.74); Fluoroquinolone resistance in Klebsiella upon the infection (1.68)

Expert-chosen input set - LASSO 0.778, decision tree 0.684, decision tree depth=6 0.686, random forest 0.761, boosted logistic regression 0.801 (best; sensitivity 0.750, specificity 0.740; ICU 0.726/0.689/0.684), support vector machine 0.623. Full input set - LASSO 0.856, decision tree 0.791, decision tree depth=6 0.792, random forest 0.881, boosted logistic regression 0.885 (best; sensitivity 0.809, specificity 0.849; ICU 0.854/0.810/0.810), support vector machine 0.724. raw.AUROC_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)

raw.Best_Performing_Model: PhageLeads ensemble lifestyle classification (XGBoost temperate-marker predictors) — highest on the review's primary metric (MCC): 0.92 on the phage lifestyle dataset (accuracy 0.96, F1-score 0.95)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Phage lifestyle dataset (423 phages: 240 temperate, 183 lytic), compiled by Mavrich and Hatfull
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation via 10-fold cross-validation plus validation on an independent external dataset (423-phage lifestyle dataset compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull, not used in training): MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. This independent external validation supports level 3.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases (some Cro/CI annotated as 'transcriptional regulators' or 'repressor', integrases as 'DNA-binding protein'/'recombinase', ParA as 'Chromosome partitioning protein'), some protein classes removed due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable and may bias models (hence no lifestyle info used in training); clustered 10-fold CV revealed low conservation for ParA (0.44) and Cro/CI (0.16) markers.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Lytic phages found to carry AMR or virulence genes are unsuitable for therapeutic use: five of 183 lytic phages encoded virulence proteins (increased serum survival proteins ISS, Type III secretion system effectors, Cytolethal distending toxins, Shiga toxins, NleG effectors), one encoded both chloramphenicol resistance (CatA1) and ISS, posing risk of adverse effects / gene transduction into host genomes.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Phage genomics/bioinformatics study developing the PhageLeads ensemble XGBoost tool to predict phage temperate markers and screen for AMR/virulence genes (via ABRicate) for therapeutic phage selection. Best model = PhageLeads lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) validated on the external 423-phage lifestyle dataset. No patient/clinical data; AMR aspect is detection of AMR/virulence genes in phage genomes. Data from NCBI RefSeq (training 188,080 proteins/7686 genomes; validation 45,231 proteins/63 genomes). Web-deployed (www.phageleads.dk).
raw.Unresolved_Items: Best_Performing_Model unit: the paper's best model on its primary (training) dataset would be the individual temperate-marker predictors (integrase/antirepressor MCC 0.92), but the paper's headline application and its reported lifestyle accuracy are for the integrated ensemble lifestyle classifier; I coded the ensemble lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) as the best-performing model. Clinical_Maturity_Level 3 rests on the independent external lifestyle dataset.
raw.Sample_Size: Training dataset: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes (genomes, not patients)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared — 'The authors declare that there are no conﬂicts of interest.'
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Data-level exclusions: proteins <30 amino acids removed; hypothetical proteins and proteins with unclear annotations removed; ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) removed from respective datasets.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype
raw.Data_Source_Name: NCBI RefSeq (phage complete genomes)
raw.Dataset_Size: Training: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes; Validation: 45,231 protein sequences from 63 phage genomes; Lifestyle dataset: 423 phages
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Global public repository data: 8368 phage genomes from 17 families used to train PhageLeads; no geographic framing reported.
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes and virulence genes in therapeutic phage genomes, detected via the ABRicate tool; and classification of phage lifestyle (temperate vs lytic) based on predicted presence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor).
raw.Pathogens: None as study target — the subjects are bacteriophages (therapeutic phage candidates); no specific bacterial pathogen is the outcome organism
raw.Drug_Classes: Phenicols (chloramphenicol resistance gene detected)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Chloramphenicol (resistance gene CatA1, chloramphenicol O-acetyltransferase, detected in Stx2 converting phage vB_EcoP_24B)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Presence/absence of AMR genes (detected by ABRicate comparing predicted ORFs against NCBI, CARD, ARG-ANNOT, Resfinder, MEGARES, EcOH, PlasmidFinder, Ecoli_VF and VFDB databases) and presence/absence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) — gene-presence labels, not clinical MIC/phenotype thresholds.
raw.Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
raw.AI_Purpose: To develop an online single-step tool (PhageLeads) using an ensemble of extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) predictors to determine the presence of temperate markers in phage candidates and, with ABRicate, screen for AMR and virulence genes, in order to rapidly select safe therapeutic phages.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 5 temperate-marker predictors within the PhageLeads ensemble (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) plus the integrated lifestyle classification, compared against baseline BACPHLIP
raw.Feature_Engineering: 1576 protein features extracted from protein sequences using custom scripts (per [26]): 400 dipeptide frequency, 100 reduced amino acid dipeptide frequency, 1000 reduced amino acid tripeptide frequency, 34 PROSITE domain features, and 42 generic protein features from the BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis module.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative feature reduction: for each round the 50 least-contributing features were removed until the minimal number was reached; final features selected based on Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) scores from testing each model on the test dataset. Overall selection driven by feature importance computed by the XGBoost module.
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 626 unique features used for the final predictors (171 integrase, 90 Cro/CI, 59 immunity repressor, 18 ParA, 71 antirepressor; 1576 reduced per predictor to 350, 251, 142, 74, 201 respectively)
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: XGBoost 'scale positive weight' parameter (set = number of negative data / number of positive data) to compensate for unbalanced classes
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Prediction threshold tuning: iterating through incremental threshold values and selecting the threshold with the highest MCC on the training dataset (e.g. 0.252 integrase, 0.363 Cro/CI, 0.472 immunity, 0.03 ParA, 0.389 antirepressor)
raw.Software_Libraries: XGBoost, scikit-learn (StratifiedKFold), python networkx, BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis, DIAMOND, cd-hit, ABRicate
raw.Other_Metrics: Confusion matrix on lifestyle dataset (Lytic 177/7, Temperate 9/231); random 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.97, Cro/CI 0.91, immunity 0.96, ParA 0.90, antirepressor 0.94); clustered 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16); prediction speed 1.6 s/phage for PhageLeads, 8.1 s for gene detection, 2.3 s for BACPHLIP.
raw.Baseline_Method: BACPHLIP (random forest-based phage lifestyle predictor using presence of 206 lysogeny markers via HMM sequence similarity)
raw.Baseline_Performance: BACPHLIP made 7 erroneous predictions on the lifestyle dataset (vs PhageLeads' 16 mispredictions, 7 FP + 9 FN); authors attribute BACPHLIP's higher accuracy to its smaller training data (634 genomes, 5 families)
raw.Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation (two variants: generic random via scikit-learn StratifiedKFold, and clustered using cd-hit at 60% identity where proteins from the same clusters stay in the same bins)
raw.External_Validation_Description: Independent external dataset: the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (240 temperate, 183 lytic) originally compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull [50], on which PhageLeads achieved MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. Also a temporal hold-out validation set of 63 phage genomes dated after March 2018 (45,231 proteins).
raw.Overfitting_Method: Feature reduction — iteratively removing the 50 least-contributing features per round to minimize overfitting probability and prediction time
raw.Generalisability_Details: Clustered 10-fold cross-validation (cd-hit at 60% similarity, proteins from same clusters kept in same bins) assessed prediction of unseen protein clusters; clustered CV MCCs were lower (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16), indicating lower conservation for ParA and Cro/CI and the value of large training datasets.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Independent external validation on the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull) achieving MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95 — evidence of external validation, hence level 3.
raw.End_User_Described: Researchers / laboratory scientists assessing the therapeutic suitability of phages
raw.Barriers_List: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases; removal of some protein classes due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable; low sequence conservation for ParA and Cro/CI markers limiting clustered-CV performance.
raw.Future_Directions: Exploration of three-dimensional protein structures to resolve misannotations, in order to further improve PhageLeads performance; also applicable to predicting lysogenic markers for metagenomic contigs.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance scores calculated from the XGBoost module (used to select final features per predictor)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Ambiguous protein annotations/misannotation; unreliable lifestyle labels from literature; low sequence conservation of specific markers (ParA, Cro/CI); false-positive temperate predictions in lytic phages.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Authors removed proteins <30 amino acids, hypothetical proteins, proteins with unclear annotations, and ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) to reduce misclassification.

raw.Title: Rapid Identification of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Using MALDI-TOF MS and Machine Learning from over 20,000 Clinical Isolates
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort; Prospective cohort
raw.Funder_Names: Taiwan Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST109-2113-M-039-001); China Medical University (CMU109-MF-04); China Medical University Hospital (DMR-109-148 and DMR-110-139)
raw.Population_Description: Clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates (MSSA and MRSA) from patient specimens. Development set: 8,258 CMUH cases (4,309 MRSA, 3,949 MSSA) from the China Medical University Hospital clinical microbiology laboratory, January 2018 to June 2021. External set: an additional 12,101 mass spectra collected 2018-2020 from four hospitals (FYH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH).
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: MALDI-TOF MS spectral peaks (m/z) ranked by SHAP. Top-ranked feature: m/z 6,590 to 6,599; then m/z 5,520 to 5,529; m/z 3,030 to 3,039; m/z 3,760 to 3,769; and m/z 6,550 to 6,559.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: 10 ML algorithms (light gradient boosting machine [LightGBM], gradient boosting, logistic regression, extreme gradient boosting, extra trees, random forest, linear SVM, decision tree, K neighbors and naive Bayes) each run with 5 bin sizes (1-Da, 5-Da, 10-Da, 15-Da, 20-Da) with 5-fold cross-validation, ranked by F1 (Table S1). Selected combination: LightGBM with 10-Da binning. Reported AUC/sensitivity/specificity: CMUH 2018-2019 training 0.91/0.82/0.85; CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test 0.91/0.83/0.85; FYH 0.78/0.83/0.65; NTUH-YL 0.88/0.72/0.88; SHH 0.85/0.74/0.80; HTCH 0.86/0.83/0.73.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: LightGBM with 10-Da binning - the combination selected by the F1 score from 10 ML algorithms x 5 bin sizes; on the primary CMUH data set it reached AUC 0.91, sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.85
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set (1,311 MRSA and 1,145 MSSA isolates)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set (1,311 MRSA and 1,145 MSSA isolates)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set, approximately 2,500 isolates (the primary data set under study); the same AUC of 0.91 is reported for the CMUH 2018-2019 training set
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: A prospective test on approximately 2,500 CMUH isolates (January 2020 to June 2021, AUC 0.91) plus external validation on more than 12,000 isolates from four other hospitals (AUC 0.78-0.88); no CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported.
raw.Reported_Limitations: The rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection; performance was somewhat lower in NTUH-YL, SHH and HTCH than CMUH, and significantly lower at FYH (AUC 0.78) owing to a specificity of 0.65 attributed to Vitek 2 misclassification of MRSA as MSSA.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: No formal harm assessment. The authors state the rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection, and report misclassification at FYH where strains predicted as MRSA were identified as MSSA in the FYH AST reports.
raw.Sample_Size: 8,258 CMUH cases (4,309 MRSA and 3,949 MSSA) for the primary data set; 5,802 CMUH spectra used for model training and internal validation; 12,101 further mass spectra from four external hospitals (20,359 clinical isolates in total)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared - "The authors declare no conflict of interest." and "We declare no competing interests."
raw.Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
raw.Data_Source_Name: De-identified MALDI-TOF MS data deposited in the Zenodo database (record 5502292); clinical data sets from five hospitals (CMUH, FYH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH)
raw.Dataset_Size: 20,359 clinical isolates in total (5,802 CMUH spectra for training/internal validation plus 12,101 external mass spectra)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Four external hospitals chosen as representatives of North Taiwan (SHH), Middle Taiwan (FYH), South Taiwan (NTUH-YL) and East Taiwan (HTCH) plus CMUH in Middle Taiwan - all five sites are in Taiwan.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Clinical samples were collected from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, ascites, pleural fluid, body fluid, sputum, tissue, bile, stool, urine, and other clinical specimens.
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus: binary discrimination of clinical isolates as MRSA or MSSA from MALDI-TOF mass spectra, without conventional AST.
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus - methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin; penicillinase-resistant penicillins)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin (used in the protein-ligand docking simulation); oxacillin and cefoxitin are referred to only in a cited report of false-susceptible results
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: The MRSA/MSSA label is the routine clinical AST result: all MSSA and MRSA strains were confirmed by a Phoenix AST system (CMUH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH) and a VITEK2 AST system (FYH); the ML model predicts this binary label from MALDI-TOF spectra.
raw.AI_Purpose: Machine learning (LightGBM) applied to MALDI-TOF MS spectra to map peak features onto antibiotic resistance and rapidly discriminate MRSA from MSSA, with SHAP-based interpretation of the top features and docking simulation of the leading marker.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 10 ML algorithms, each run with five bin sizes (50 algorithm/bin-size combinations compared with 5-fold cross-validation; Table S1)
raw.Feature_Engineering: MALDI-TOF MS raw data extraction, resampling to a fixed 1 Da sampling rate, TopHat baseline correction, square-root transformation, Savitzky-Golay smoothing, conversion to m/z ratios over 2,000-20,000 Da, min-max scaling to 0-1, and binning of peaks into bins with averaged intensities.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Peak binning (peaks in the same m/z bin treated as one attribute, intensities averaged); bin size and ML algorithm selected by F1 score; SHAP used to rank feature importance.
raw.Num_Features_Total: Not stated numerically - the binned m/z attributes span the m/z 2,000 to 20,000 Da range at the chosen bin size (10 Da in the final model)
raw.Num_Features_Selected: Top 10 molecular features reported by SHAP (Fig. 2); the classifier itself retains all binned m/z attributes
raw.Software_Libraries: LightGBM (light gradient boosting machine); SHAP; Phyre2 for homology modelling; PyRX version 0.8 with PyMol for docking simulation
raw.Other_Metrics: F1 score (used only as the criterion for selecting bin size and algorithm; no numerical F1 value is reported)
raw.Baseline_Method: Head-to-head comparison of five bin sizes across 10 ML algorithms under 5-fold cross-validation, ranked by F1 score (Table S1); no non-ML or clinical baseline is reported.
raw.Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation used to compare bin size and algorithm combinations, with the CMUH 2018-2019 spectra serving as the training and internal validation set.
raw.Train_Test_Split: Training: CMUH cases from 2018 to 2019. Testing: the CMUH 2020-2021 prospective data set and the four external hospital data sets.
raw.External_Validation_Description: An additional 12,101 mass spectra collected during 2018-2020 from Feng Yuan Hospital (FYH), National Taiwan University Hospital Yunlin Branch (NTUH-YL), Shuang Ho Hospital (SHH) and Hualien Tzu Chi Hospital (HTCH); AUC ranged from 0.78 to 0.88.
raw.Overfitting_Method: Generalisability addressed by collecting data from five clinical sites with retrospective and prospective tests rather than by formal overfitting diagnostics.
raw.Clinical_Insights: The top feature at m/z 6,590 to 6,599 was identified as UPF0337 protein SACOL1680, a mutated form of UPF0337 protein SA1452 of MSSA; docking suggests methicillin binds SA1452 but not SACOL1680, a possible mechanism of methicillin resistance.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Isolates were collected from five clinical sites with retrospective and prospective tests specifically to ensure ML model generalization.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Prospective test on approximately 2,500 CMUH isolates (2020-2021) and validation on more than 12,000 isolates from four external clinical sites; no CDS integration or routine clinical use reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory workflow: after MALDI-TOF MS analysis of cultured clinical strains the spectra are classified as MRSA or MSSA by the ML model within about 10 s, instead of the 18 h to 48 h needed by conventional AST methods.
raw.End_User_Described: Physicians - the model can be integrated into current clinical workflows and support physicians in prescribing proper antibiotic treatments
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Following culture, MALDI-TOF analysis of the clinical strain, then the ML model classifies the spectrum as MRSA or MSSA within about 10 s (Fig. 1b), replacing the 18 h to 48 h conventional AST step.
raw.Barriers_List: The rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection; different data formats for identification and AST results across sites required custom data-processing pipelines; lower specificity at FYH (0.65).
raw.Facilitators_List: The MALDI-TOF MS-based ML model can be highly integrated into current clinical workflows and save time for physicians seeking proper antibiotic treatment.
raw.Future_Directions: Integration of the MALDI-TOF MS-based ML model into current clinical workflows to save time for physicians, as a rapid screening assay that complements rather than replaces more sensitive and specific MRSA detection methods.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 (MALDI-TOF MS spectral peaks); the AST phenotype is used only as the outcome label
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapely Additive exPlanations) values
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: First discovery and validation of MRSA markers at this scale; the top feature at m/z 6,590 to 6,599 was identified as a protein whose sequence had not been identified with a reliable bottom-up proteomics method.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific MRSA detection methods; lower model performance at some external sites, with FYH specificity of 0.65 attributed to Vitek 2 misclassification; performance somewhat lower at NTUH-YL, SHH and HTCH than CMUH.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Different clinical sites use different data formats for identification and AST results, requiring regular expressions and text mining to pair clinical information with MALDI-TOF MS data; data preparation and cleaning were needed to ensure MS data quality across the five sites.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Data sizes and performance by clinical site are reported in Table 1; the comparison of bin sizes and ML algorithms is relegated to supplementary Table S1, and no confidence intervals or F1 values are printed.
