raw.Title: Derivation and validation of a risk assessment model for drug-resistant pathogens in hospitalized patients with community-acquired pneumonia
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
raw.Funder_Names: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (grant no. R01HS024277)
raw.Population_Description: Adults aged 18 years or older hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia (principal diagnosis of pneumonia, or secondary pneumonia with respiratory failure/ARDS/respiratory arrest/sepsis) who had blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission; 138,762 patients analysed
raw.Age_Mean_Median: mean 69.5 y (SD 16.2) in the derivation set, N=111,013
raw.Data_Source_Other: Premier Healthcare Database, a multihospital administrative claims/discharge database; Cleveland Clinic Health System (CCHS) hospitals with data elements derived by electronic chart review
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Odds ratios in the final CARM (derivation set, N=111,013): resistant organism in previous year 2.66 (2.3-3.08); invasive mechanical ventilation 2.10 (1.91-2.3); pressure ulcer 1.86 (1.68-2.05); vasopressor administration 1.63 (1.47-1.80); paralysis 1.58 (1.41-1.78); ICU admission 1.55 (1.43-1.67); low functional status/weight loss 1.44 (1.34-1.54); hospital admission in previous year 1.43 (1.31-1.56); admitted from SNF/ICF 1.34 (1.21-1.49); chronic pulmonary disease 1.30 (1.22-1.39); male sex 1.28 (1.21-1.37); current tobacco smoker 0.77 (0.71-0.85)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: CARM (logistic regression): C-statistic 0.71 in the Premier holdout sample and 0.65 in CCHS; DRIP score: C-statistic 0.63 (Premier holdout) and 0.58 (CCHS); 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule and physician prescribing compared by cumulative gain curves
raw.Best_Performing_Model: CARM (Cleveland Clinic Antibiotic Resistance Model), a multiple logistic regression model - highest C-statistic, 0.71 versus 0.63 for the DRIP score in the Premier holdout sample
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Premier 20% random holdout validation sample (CARM linear predictor)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal repeated 10-fold cross-validation and a random 20% Premier holdout sample, plus a fully independent external validation in the CCHS data (0.71 to 0.65 C-statistic); no prospective evaluation or CDS integration reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Administrative database lacking specific laboratory values or vital signs; reasons for missing cultures unknown so selective respiratory culture use could bias; resistant organisms could have been missed; diagnoses and comorbidities from ICD codes subject to differential coding and coding drift; outpatient antibiotics could have lowered culture yields; model developed on 2010-2015 Premier data performed less well on 2017-2019 CCHS data; antibiotic susceptibilities could not be determined where no CLSI break points exist
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: An inescapable tradeoff: a threshold low enough to cover resistant infections requires treating more patients unnecessarily with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a DRIP cutoff of 4 would leave >80% of resistant infections uncovered
raw.Reviewer_Notes: The performance measure reported for the study's own model is the C-statistic (AUROC); 0.71 is the CARM in the Premier 20% holdout validation sample (the derivation-set C-statistic is 0.70, Table 2). No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, AUPRC, kappa, MCC, RMSE or MAE figures are reported for the CARM; the paper reports C-statistics, calibration by deciles and cumulative gain curves. The DRIP score's original sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV are mentioned only as the published values of that external score, not as measures computed here.
raw.Sample_Size: 138,762 patients with pneumonia and blood or respiratory cultures on admission in the Premier database (111,013 derivation set; 27,749 validation set); CCHS validation included all adult patients discharged 2017-2019
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr. Marya Zilberberg: grants from Merck, Lungpacer, Tetraphase, The Medicines Company, J&J and Spero Therapeutics, personal fees from Nabriva, Melinta and Paratek outside the submitted work. Dr. Haessler: SHEA board member 2020-2022 term. Dr. Deshpande: personal funding from Merck and Ferring Pharmaceuticals outside the submitted work. No other authors have potential conflicts to disclose
raw.Sex_Distribution: Female 56,640 (51.0), Male 54,373 (49.0) in the derivation set (N=111,013); male sex is a CARM predictor (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.21-1.37)
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Admissions between July 2010 and June 2015 to any of 177 Premier hospitals with microbiology data: patients aged 18 years or older with a principal diagnosis of pneumonia, or a secondary diagnosis of pneumonia paired with a principal diagnosis of respiratory failure, ARDS, respiratory arrest or sepsis, who had blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia; interhospital transfers; admissions with a diagnosis code for an alternate site of infection (eg, cholecystitis); for patients with multiple hospitalizations only 1 randomly selected admission was included
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
raw.Data_Source_Name: Premier Healthcare Database; Cleveland Clinic Health System (CCHS) hospitals (northeastern Ohio and Florida)
raw.Dataset_Size: Premier: 151,715 pneumonia admissions screened, 138,762 analysed (80% derivation N=111,013; 20% validation N=27,749); CCHS external validation sample: all adults discharged 2017-2019
raw.Ethnicity_Details: Race reported as White 85,654 (77.2%), Black 13,882 (12.5%), Other 11,477 (10.3%) in the derivation set (N=111,013); race (White, Black, or other) was a candidate predictor
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Premier hospitals throughout the United States representing approximately 25% of US admissions, varying in size and including nonprofit, nongovernmental, urban, rural, community and academic medical centres; CCHS validation from 10 northeastern Ohio hospitals and 1 Florida hospital
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission (blood, bronchial or sputum); nares excluded from the outcome definition
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of a cultured organism to first-line CAP therapy: any organism grown from blood or respiratory source (other than the nares) resistant to either a quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin and a macrolide
raw.Pathogens: Any organism grown from blood or respiratory cultures; probable contaminants (eg, coagulase negative Staphylococcus) and organisms not known to cause pneumonia (eg, Enterococcus spp) excluded; methicillin-resistant S. aureus and Pseudomonas named in the guideline/2-factor rule context
raw.Drug_Classes: Quinolones (fluoroquinolones); third-generation cephalosporins; macrolides; beta-lactams
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide (resistance definition); ampicillin and ertapenem named in the resistant-organism footnote; prior-exposure variables cover fluoroquinolone, macrolide, beta-lactam, anti-MRSA agents and aminoglycoside
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary: positive culture with growth of a resistant organism from any blood or respiratory source other than the nares; organisms resistant to either a quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin and a macrolide were counted as resistant to CAP therapy; patients who grew no organisms (or had no sample by a route) were considered negative
raw.AI_Purpose: To validate the DRIP score in a large sample, derive and validate an improved risk prediction model (CARM) for resistance to first-line CAP therapy, and compare the model and the DRIP score with physician prescribing behaviour and the 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 (CARM versus DRIP score), also benchmarked against the 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule and physician prescribing
raw.Feature_Engineering: 43 candidate predictors assembled from ICD-9-CM diagnosis and procedure codes and diagnosis-related groups; comorbidities via HCUP Comorbidity Software version 3.1 (Elixhauser); lifestyle factors from ICD codes or billing for nicotine replacement therapy; previous hospitalisations and antibiotic exposures in the past year; severity indicators on the first hospital day; no laboratory values or vital signs available
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Multiple logistic regression with successive backward elimination of variables maximally reducing the Akaike information criterion (AIC), then removal of variables contributing little to discrimination (C-statistic) based on prevalence, odds ratio, and clinical and statistical judgment
raw.Num_Features_Total: 43 candidate predictors
raw.Software_Libraries: SAS version 9.4 (data management), SAS/STAT version 15.1, R version 3.5 and version 4.0.0; HCUP Comorbidity Software version 3.1
raw.Other_Metrics: C-statistic (AUROC), receiver operating characteristic curves, cumulative gain curves, calibration by risk deciles, slopes and intercepts of logistic regressions of resistance on the CARM linear predictor, outcome prevalence
raw.Baseline_Method: DRIP score; 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule; physician prescribing (actual care provided)
raw.Baseline_Performance: DRIP score C-statistic 0.63 in the Premier holdout and 0.58 in CCHS; a DRIP cutoff of 2 or more covered 53.5% of resistant organisms while treating 34.1% of all patients with broad-spectrum antibiotics
raw.Internal_Validation: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation (20 repeats) in the derivation set and a random 20% Premier holdout sample
raw.Train_Test_Split: Random 80% derivation / 20% validation split of the Premier data (N=111,013 derivation; N=27,749 validation)
raw.External_Validation_Description: CCHS: 10 northeastern Ohio hospitals and 1 Florida Cleveland Clinic Health System hospital; all adult patients discharged between 2017 and 2019 meeting the same inclusion criteria, with data elements derived by electronic chart review; CCHS does not contribute to Premier
raw.Overfitting_Method: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation (20 repeats) in the derivation set, evaluation in a random 20% holdout and an independent external sample
raw.Clinical_Insights: Infection with a resistant organism in the previous year was the strongest predictor; markers of acute illness (need for mechanical ventilation, vasopressors) and chronic illness (pressure ulcer, paralysis) predicted resistant infections; smoking was inversely associated with resistance
raw.Generalisability_Details: External validation confirmed degradation of discrimination in a different health system (C-statistic 0.71 to 0.65) and miscalibration of both models in the highest deciles; the authors argue this is why external validation matters
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal: 20 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation and a random 20% Premier holdout sample. External: fully independent CCHS validation (C-statistic 0.71 to 0.65; miscalibration in high deciles). Model published as a 12-factor web calculator; no prospective evaluation, implementation or CDS integration reported
raw.Integration_Point: Electronic health record as clinical decision support - proposed only: the 12-factor CARM could be incorporated into the EHR as clinical decision support for empiric therapy choice
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians (prescribers choosing empiric therapy for hospitalized CAP patients without culture results); hospitals unable to derive their own local risk models
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The model is applied before culture results are known, to all CAP admissions; each hospital picks a predicted-probability threshold for starting broad-spectrum antibiotics and the cumulative gain curves show the tradeoff between coverage of resistant organisms and broad-spectrum use
raw.Stewardship_Details: Projected only, not measured: a 4% CARM threshold would cover the same 53.5% of resistant organisms while treating only 25% of patients versus 34.1% under a DRIP cutoff of 2 or more; a predicted probability above 11.5% would achieve the same coverage while treating fewer patients
raw.Barriers_List: Most hospitals cannot derive their own local risk factors; the derivation database lacked laboratory values and vital signs; selective culture ordering and missed resistant organisms; ICD coding differences and drift; each hospital must choose its own treatment threshold; no decision-analytic model exists to optimise the threshold
raw.Facilitators_List: All CARM variables are readily available to clinicians at admission; large nationally representative derivation sample; external validation; the 12-factor CARM is published as an online risk calculator that could be built into the EHR
raw.Future_Directions: Determine whether locally derived models outperform the CARM and whether implementing such models improves patient outcomes; decision-analytic optimisation of treatment thresholds
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (sociodemographic, behavioural, healthcare utilisation, pharmacological, microbiological, clinical)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Multivariable logistic regression odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, ranked by odds ratio after backward elimination by AIC
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Chronic-illness markers such as pressure ulcer and paralysis and the inverse association of current smoking were new relative to the DRIP score, which the authors discuss alongside markers of acute illness
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data-source limitations (administrative database without laboratory values or vital signs); selective culture use and possible missed resistant organisms; ICD-coded diagnoses and comorbidities with differential coding and coding drift; outpatient antibiotics lowering culture yield; temporal and geographical differences between the 2010-2015 Premier derivation data and 2017-2019 CCHS data; organisms without CLSI break points excluded
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: No laboratory values or vital signs in the administrative database; cultures obtained in routine care with unknown reasons for missing cultures; diagnoses and comorbidities coded from ICD-9-CM with differential coding across hospitals and drift over time; some patients may have received outpatient antibiotics that lowered culture yields
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear and complete: derivation and validation sets, model predictors with odds ratios and 95% CIs, C-statistics against comparators, calibration by deciles, cumulative gain curves and a limitations section are all reported
raw.Page_References: pp. 1143-1150; Table 1 and Table 2 on pp. 1146-1147; Figure 1 p. 1145; Figures 2-4 pp. 1148-1149

studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug

raw.Title: Deep learning and single-cell phenotyping for rapid antimicrobial susceptibility detection in Escherichia coli
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
raw.Funder_Names: Oxford Martin School (Programme on Antimicrobial Resistance Testing); Wellcome Trust (110164/Z/15/Z); UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BB/N018656/1, BB/S008896/1); UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (Oxford-Nottingham Biomedical Imaging CDT, EP/L016052/1); National Institute for Health Research (NIHR200915; NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre)
raw.Population_Description: Single cells of the laboratory reference E. coli strain MG1655 (untreated and antibiotic-treated) and single cells of six clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6) from human bloodstream infections with differing ciprofloxacin MICs; no patient-level data were accessed
raw.Data_Source_Other: Wide-field fluorescence microscopy images of single bacterial cells (DAPI nucleoid stain, Nile Red membrane stain) acquired in-house; no clinical data source
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Nucleoid structure and organisation (classifier focuses primarily on this), with some attention given to the cell membrane — ranked by post-hoc saliency mapping of single-cell inputs; the co-amoxiclav phenotype was the least visually discriminable
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Segmentation: Mask R-CNN on a ResNet50 backbone (mAP 70 % at IoU 0.5; 92 % maximum total recall), Cellpose, YOLO v8; classification: DenseNet121 (>84 % single-cell accuracy on the holdout experiment) screened against models from the DenseNet, ResNet and EfficientNet families; selected pipeline Mask R-CNN + DenseNet121
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Mask R-CNN (segmentation) + DenseNet121 (classification) — best combination of models; decided on classification accuracy on the holdout test set
raw.Accuracy_Value: >84 % single-cell classification accuracy in the holdout experiments across all antibiotic conditions (the abstract's headline figure for the same models is 80 % single-cell accuracy)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Single cells from the MG1655 lab-reference strain, evaluated on an independent 7th 'holdout' experiment not used for training or hyperparameter optimisation; class-balanced, randomly sampled 1000 cells (800 for co-amoxiclav)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models trained on the MG1655 laboratory strain were validated on an independent holdout experiment and then deployed without retraining on six clinical E. coli blood-culture isolates (EC1-6) with different ciprofloxacin MICs; no prospective clinical evaluation or CDS integration is reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Explicit phenotype classes must be homogeneous across cells and isolates; further work required to validate across more species and antibiotics and to robustly demonstrate correlation with MIC-based susceptibility metrics; specific models must be trained for each antibiotic-species combination, which may not scale well; the assay still requires culture of isolates (not for direct patient specimens)
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: None reported. Risks discussed are assay-performance risks rather than patient harms: reliance on homogeneous phenotype classes (misclassification of cells not showing the full phenotype), possible over-smoothing of population heterogeneity, and the need for per-antibiotic/per-species models
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Analysed bacterial isolates were routinely stored diagnostic cultures; no sampling was undertaken for the study and no patient-related information was accessed, and under the UK Human Tissue Act such isolates required no ethical approval — the paper identifies no ethical or governance risk
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Images-only input: the model sees DAPI/Nile Red micrograph channels, so all predictor-category fields except imaging are No. Per-class performance numbers (sensitivity/specificity/precision/recall) are shown only inside Fig. 3 panels and Supplementary Tables S2/S3, which are not in the PDF text layer, hence the 'No' answers for those metrics.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Per-antibiotic and per-class classifier performance figures and all Supplementary Tables (S2, S3, S5, S6) are image-only or absent from the text layer, so no sensitivity/specificity/precision/F1 values could be quoted for the classification models
raw.Sample_Size: 29,297 manually curated cells in 459 fields of view (segmentation training/cross-validation set); 9,044 cells in 115 fields of view (validation set); 13,247 ground-truth cells in 155 micrographs (segmentation holdout); classification holdout test set of 1,000 cells per antibiotic (800 for co-amoxiclav)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: A.N.K. is a co-founder and shareholder of Oxford Nanoimaging, the company whose wide-field microscope was used for the work; the other authors declare no competing interests
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Laboratory reference E. coli strain MG1655 plus six clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6) recovered from human blood cultures and chosen to span a range of ciprofloxacin MICs
raw.Data_Types_Used: Microscopy images; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype
raw.Data_Source_Name: No named public dataset — in-house micrographs of E. coli MG1655 and Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust clinical isolates
raw.Dataset_Size: 29,297 cells in 459 fields of view (training); 9,044 cells in 115 fields of view (validation); 13,247 ground-truth cells in 155 micrographs (holdout); ~50-200 cells per micrograph
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: clinical isolates from the Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust microbiology laboratory plus the MG1655 laboratory strain; no multi-site or multi-country sampling
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood culture isolates of E. coli
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Single-cell binary classification of E. coli cells as susceptible or resistant from fluorescence micrographs (80 % single-cell accuracy reported in the abstract), plus MIC-related information for ciprofloxacin from the dose-response of susceptible:resistant classification ratios
raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli (laboratory reference strain MG1655 and six clinical isolates EC1-6 from bloodstream infections)
raw.Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin); aminoglycoside (gentamicin); beta-lactam / beta-lactamase-inhibitor combination (co-amoxiclav); rifamycin (rifampicin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin; gentamicin; co-amoxiclav; rifampicin
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptible class = treated cells showing antibiotic-specific cellular phenotypic change; resistant class = untreated cells (phenotype unchanged by treatment); labels are cellular phenotypes, with clinical susceptibility separately defined by MIC/EUCAST breakpoints
raw.AI_Purpose: A deep-learning pipeline (Mask R-CNN segmentation + DenseNet121 classifier, 'DASP') that reads widefield fluorescence micrographs of single bacterial cells and classifies them as susceptible or resistant phenotypes, to provide rapid (30 min) phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility information for E. coli
raw.Num_Models_Compared: A range of segmentation models (Mask R-CNN, Cellpose, YOLO v8) and a range of classification models (DenseNet, ResNet and EfficientNet families) were screened; exact count not stated — per-model accuracies in Supplementary Table S6; the selected pipeline was Mask R-CNN + DenseNet121
raw.Feature_Engineering: None manual — CNNs learn their own convolutional features from the images; preprocessing only: 30-frame averaging, RGB construction from Nile Red/DAPI channels, cross-correlation channel registration, 64x64 resizing, histogram equalisation within the segmentation mask, and on-the-fly augmentation (flips, translations, rotations, cutout, Gaussian blur, brightness, noise)
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: None — learnt CNN features with no manual feature selection; saliency mapping used post hoc to show which image regions drive classifications
raw.Num_Features_Total: No explicit feature count — pixel-level inputs from two fluorescence channels (Nile Red in red, DAPI in green) of 64x64-resized single cells
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Class-balanced datasets: equal numbers of cells drawn randomly from each of the 6 experiments for training, and class-balanced holdout evaluation sets
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over batch size and learning rate for each model, with the best pipeline chosen by classification accuracy on the holdout test set
raw.Software_Libraries: Keras 2.2.4 (classifier); Mask R-CNN implementation adapted from the standard matterport/Mask_RCNN TensorFlow/Keras implementation; Adam optimiser; initial weights from the MS COCO dataset
raw.Other_Metrics: Segmentation quality: precision-recall curves across IoU thresholds, mean Average Precision (mAP) 70 % at IoU 0.5, 92 % maximum total recall (12,147 of 13,247 cells detected); classification: per-class confusion matrices, accuracy and percentage/absolute class counts in Fig. 3; clinical isolates: percentage of susceptible/resistant single-cell classifications per isolate and per ciprofloxacin concentration; dose-response inflection points 0.011 ± 0.001 mg/L (EC1) and 0.49 ± 0.18 mg/L (EC2) versus E-test MICs; Tukey range test p-values
raw.Baseline_Method: Gold-standard growth-based AST: 24 h growth curves in the presence of ciprofloxacin (numerical integration of OD600, normalised to untreated cells) and E-test MIC determination
raw.Baseline_Performance: Dose-response inflection points of the phenotype-based assay were close to the E-test MICs (EC1 E-test MIC 0.008 mg/L vs inflection 0.011 ± 0.001 mg/L; EC2 E-test MIC 0.5 mg/L vs inflection 0.49 ± 0.18 mg/L), and growth ratios followed a relationship reciprocal to the susceptible:resistant phenotype ratio
raw.Internal_Validation: Experimental K-fold cross-validation (one of 6 imaging experiments withheld and rotated, result summed over 6 models) plus an independent 7th 'holdout' experiment used for neither training nor hyperparameter optimisation; class-balanced sampling
raw.Train_Test_Split: Cross-validation dataset: cells pooled from 6 experiments and split randomly into training, validation and test sets without replacement; experimental K-fold: 6 experiments, one withheld for testing; holdout: a separate 7th experiment used only for final evaluation
raw.External_Validation_Description: Models trained on the MG1655 laboratory strain were deployed without retraining on six clinical E. coli blood-culture isolates (EC1-6) with different ciprofloxacin MICs, untreated and treated with 10 mg/L ciprofloxacin for 30 min, to test whether single-cell classifications reflect MIC-defined susceptibility
raw.Overfitting_Method: Independent holdout experiment excluded from training and hyperparameter optimisation; K-fold across separate imaging experiments; class-balanced sampling; augmentation to increase robustness against experimental variation
raw.Clinical_Insights: Correct classifications are driven mainly by nucleoid structure and organisation (with membrane attention); misclassified cells did not display the full expected phenotype because of cell-to-cell heterogeneity, and the method may capture heteroresistance and mixed populations that colony-level ASTs miss
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the method should be applicable to a wide variety of antimicrobials and bacterial species because nucleoid and membrane phenotypes are established across organisms, but note this remains to be evaluated and that specific models must be trained per antibiotic-species combination
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation on MG1655 (K-fold across 6 experiments and an independent 7th holdout experiment) followed by deployment without retraining on six independent clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6); no prospective clinical evaluation, workflow integration or routine use
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory AST workflow — replacing or shortening the culture-based AST step for E. coli by imaging single cells after 30 min of antibiotic exposure
raw.End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratories and clinicians using resistance classification around standard clinical breakpoints such as EUCAST
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinical isolates were prepared untreated or treated with ciprofloxacin at 10 mg/L for 30 min, processed identically to training samples (fixation, DAPI/Nile Red staining, agarose pads, widefield imaging), segmented and then classified cell-by-cell to give sample-wide statistics
raw.Barriers_List: Reliance on homogeneous phenotype classes across cells and isolates; need for validation across more species and antibiotics and robust correlation with MIC-based metrics; a specific model required for each antibiotic-species combination (poor scaling with problem size); the assay still needs cultured isolates and does not yet bypass isolation/growth; predictions below a confidence threshold need more data to calibrate
raw.Facilitators_List: Faster than other single-cell AST candidates because many single cells are interrogated simultaneously per field of view; no continuous tracking of live cells required; results within one bacterial life cycle (30 min); learnt features detect subtle phenotypic changes (e.g. co-amoxiclav) and reduce human bias; automated processing scales with data volume
raw.Future_Directions: Microfluidics to bypass pathogen isolation and culture by concentrating bacteria directly from patient specimens; extension to additional antibiotics and bacterial species; coupling with rapid species identification (e.g. targeted FISH staining); reformulation to scale the modelling task; more data to set prediction-confidence thresholds and confirm dose-response correlation with clinical AST
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Saliency mapping (gradient-based attention heatmaps over single-cell inputs)
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Post-hoc saliency mapping identified nucleoid structure and organisation as the dominant single-cell predictor, with membrane features secondary; the authors note cell-to-cell heterogeneity means some susceptible cells do not show the full phenotype and are misclassified as resistant
raw.Limitation_Categories: Model/class-homogeneity assumptions; need for further validation in more species and antibiotics; scalability of per-antibiotic/per-species model training; residual culture requirement and CFU counts far above those in infected body fluids; limited antibiotic range demonstrated (E. coli only); phenotype plasticity; prediction-threshold calibration requires more data
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Ground-truth segmentation masks required manual data annotation and curation; staining and illumination variation were compensated by histogram equalisation and augmentation; phenotype classes must remain homogeneous for the approach to work
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear — defined metrics, full methods, code and data availability statements, and a limitations section are present
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-12 (Results pp. 2-7; Discussion pp. 7-9; Methods pp. 9-10; data/code availability p. 10; acknowledgements and competing interests p. 12)

studies.title: Simple and Rapid Discrimination of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Based on Gram Staining and Machine Vision
studies.journal: Microbiology Spectrum (American Society for Microbiology); July/August 2023, Volume 11, Issue 4; article 10.1128/spectrum.05282-22
studies.sample_size: 150 staining images (50 clinical S. aureus strains: 33 MSSA and 17 MRSA; one image per strain, 3 experiments repeated)
studies.ai_purpose: To use machine vision (machine-learning analysis of microscope images) to detect the oxacillin-induced colour change in Gram-stained S. aureus and thereby distinguish MRSA from MSSA rapidly, without overnight culture.
studies.pathogens_reported: Staphylococcus aureus - methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)
studies.best_model: ANN (nonlinear artificial neural network) - highest accuracy (0.9733 vs 0.9667) and highest mean AUC (0.9936 vs 0.9930) of the two models; LDA retains the higher specificity (0.9804 vs 0.9608). Metric used: accuracy / mean AUC as stated in the results.

raw.Dataset_Size: 150 staining images (50 strains x 3 parallel experiments)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: the 50 clinical isolates came from one hospital (Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China); no assessment of geographic representativeness is reported.
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Discrimination of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) from methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) by machine-vision analysis of Gram-stained microscope images after oxacillin sodium salt treatment: under oxacillin the MSSA cell wall is destroyed and the cells appear Gram negative (pink), whereas MRSA stays Gram positive (purple).
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus - methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)
raw.Num_Pathogens: 1 (Staphylococcus aureus; both MRSA and MSSA isolates)
raw.Drug_Classes: Cell wall synthesis inhibitors / beta-lactams (oxacillin sodium salt; methicillin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin sodium salt (used experimentally); methicillin (background); penicillin and vancomycin named in the background only
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotype label defined by oxacillin susceptibility: after oxacillin sodium salt treatment the cell wall of methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) is destroyed immediately and the cells appear Gram negative, whereas MRSA is relatively stable and appears Gram positive; the reference classification of the strains was made by agar dilution AST according to CLSI.
raw.Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
raw.AI_Purpose: To use machine vision (machine-learning analysis of microscope images) to detect the oxacillin-induced colour change in Gram-stained S. aureus and thereby distinguish MRSA from MSSA rapidly, without overnight culture.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 (linear discriminant analysis [LDA] and nonlinear artificial neural network [ANN])
raw.Feature_Engineering: Gray statistics-based preprocessing: every staining image was grayscale-stretched to 0-255; the bacterial region of interest was segmented with an automatic global binary threshold from the image histogram; the reduced ROI image was split into red, green and blue channels and the average gray value of each channel (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean) formed the three feature values.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: No formal feature selection: all three extracted features (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean) were fed to both classifiers; PCA and t-SNE were used only for unsupervised visualisation of the feature space.
raw.Num_Features_Total: 3 (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean)
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 3 - all extracted colour features were used; no feature selection step is reported
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Repeated refitting while adjusting parameters until the best model performance was reached (search grid not specified); the ANN was fixed at three layers - one input layer, one hidden layer with 10 nodes and one output layer - with stochastic gradient descent (sgd) for weight optimisation and rectified linear unit (relu) activation in the hidden layer.
raw.Software_Libraries: scikit-learn and seaborn packages in Python (version 3.8); image analyses performed on HALCON (v.12.0; MVTec Software GmbH, Germany)
raw.Other_Metrics: Mean area under the ROC curve (AUC): 0.9930 (LDA) and 0.9936 (ANN); permutation test used to check for overfitting; Student's t test for P values; PCA and t-SNE for unsupervised visualisation of the feature data.
raw.Baseline_Method: LDA (linear discriminant analysis) - named in the paper as the simple and reliable linear model, compared against the more complicated learning-based ANN
raw.Baseline_Performance: LDA: accuracy 0.9667, sensitivity 0.9596, specificity 0.9804, precision 0.9899, F1 0.9744; mean AUC 0.9930
raw.Internal_Validation: 3-fold cross-validation: two folds used for training and the remaining fold for validation, cycled three times until all data had been involved in training and testing
raw.Train_Test_Split: No fixed hold-out split; the 150 images were randomly divided into three folds with 3-fold cross-validation
raw.Overfitting_Method: Permutation test used to check whether the LDA and ANN classifiers modelled from the extracted gray-value features were overfitted (Fig. S52)
raw.Clinical_Insights: The discriminative red-channel gray value reflects the purple (Gram-positive) versus pink (Gram-negative) appearance of the stained cells: when oxacillin destroys the MSSA cell wall the stain is no longer retained and the cells look Gram negative, while MRSA keeps the purple colour - the machine-vision feature therefore tracks a microbiologically meaningful stain change.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors state that the new strategy could be used for other bacteria and represents a new rapid method for clinically identifying antibiotic resistance, with emergency applications; no formal assessment of transportability across sites, populations or instruments is reported.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: 3-fold cross-validation of the LDA and ANN classifiers on 150 staining images from 50 clinical strains; no external data set, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment or CDS integration is reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Not described - the method is a bench microscopy workflow (oxacillin treatment, Gram staining, imaging, MV analysis) and no clinical system or laboratory information system integration is reported.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory (implicit): the method is proposed to fill the stated need for rapid, low-cost clinical identification of MRSA.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Oxacillin sodium salt (256 micrograms/mL) is added to the bacterial suspension, incubated for 30 min at 37 degrees C, washed and Gram stained, the slide is imaged by microscope and the image is analysed by MV to discriminate MRSA from MSSA; the whole process can be completed within 1 h, avoiding overnight incubation.
raw.Future_Directions: The authors propose extending the strategy to other bacteria and developing it as a new rapid method for detecting clinical antibiotic resistance; they also note that because of the high concentration of antibiotics the proportion of pink spheres within MRSA increased, which they attribute to the antibiotic concentration.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: PCA loading coefficients of the first principal component, supported by 3D feature scatter plots and violin plots; no supervised importance metric such as permutation importance or SHAP is reported.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Staining images were normalised by grayscale stretching to eliminate variation from ambient brightness and camera parameters, and the oxacillin concentration and incubation time were optimised to avoid observation errors.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model performance is fully tabulated - Table 1 gives accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 for both LDA and ANN - and the 3-fold cross-validation is described, but the paper has no limitations section, no code or data availability statement, and the ROC curves are cited as Fig. 5e/f in the text while the figure itself is numbered Fig. 6e/f.
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-9 (all nine pages read; references run to p. 9)

raw.Title: Machine learning to predict risk for community-onset Staphylococcus aureus infections in children living in southeastern United States
raw.Funder_Names: National Library of Medicine (1G08LM013190-01); AHRQ K-08 Mentored Clinical Scientist Career Research Development Award (HS024338-01); National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences / NIH (UL1TR002378); NIH / NICHHD, NIDA, NIAID, NIEHS, NCI, NIMHD grants (R01HD092580, T32DA050552, R01AI149527, U01AI148069, UG3AI176853, R01ES033530, P30ES019776, R01CA266572, R21MD017943); CDC (6R49CE003072, 23IPA2312301)
raw.Population_Description: Children <19 years of age treated for community-onset S. aureus infection (CO-MRSA or CO-MSSA) within a single pediatric healthcare system (Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta), 2002–2016; restricted to children with a georeferenced residential address in the 20-county Atlanta Metropolitan Statistical Area (block-group level area data from US Census/ACS).
raw.Age_Range: Children <19 years of age (analysis age groups: 0–3, 4–12, >12 years)
raw.Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Other national / population survey
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Percent contribution (permutation importance in brackets) by model: population density 80.2% (84.1) MRSA 02–05, 84.8% (72.4) MSSA 02–05, 79.9% (89.3) MRSA 06–16, 92.2% (92) MSSA 06–16; proportion black race 4.7% MRSA 02–05; average distance to area hospital 3.7% MRSA 02–05 and 3.6% MSSA 02–05; average distance to day care 3.5% MRSA 02–05 and 3.8% MRSA 06–16; proportion white race 8.6% MRSA 06–16 and 2.1% MSSA 06–16; proportion with a Bachelor’s degree 4.7% MSSA 02–05.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
raw.System_Level_Applications: AMR surveillance / trend prediction; Resource allocation / supply chain
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Four MaxEnt ecological-niche model runs (CO-MRSA 2002–2005 and 2006–2016; CO-MSSA 2002–2005 and 2006–2016); metric = AUC (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation/test 0.769–0.804) plus omission-rate binomial tests; jack-knife AUC for variable importance.
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Evaluation (test) points — highest of the four MaxEnt runs; evaluation AUC range 0.769–0.804 across runs; occurrence points from the 20-county Atlanta MSA dataset
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models developed and evaluated only by random subsampling within the same dataset (75% train / 25% evaluation); no external dataset, no prospective use, no clinical integration.
raw.Reported_Limitations: (1) Only 14 variables selected; other built-environment variables (transportation access, housing quality/type) were incomplete and omitted. (2) Race categories beyond black, white and Asian could not be differentiated, and no Latinx sub-category could be assigned. (3) Cultural/community boundaries differ from census tract or block group boundaries, so community-level cultural influences are not captured. (4) Generalizability may be limited to urban settings in the southeastern U.S.
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race and ethnic disparities in CO-S. aureus infection risk are noted and race is a leading model contributor; the authors caution that neighbourhood race variables need further elucidation because cultural communities are not captured by census block groups.
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Study approved by the institutional review boards with waiver of parental/patient consent; no ethical or governance risks of the machine learning application itself are discussed.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: POINTS OF JUDGEMENT. (1) Unit of analysis: the paper reports four MaxEnt runs (CO-MRSA/CO-MSSA x early/late) on one dataset and names no best run, so Best_Performing_Model is blank with Best_Performing_Model_NA = TRUE; AUROC_Value is the top of the reported evaluation range (0.804). (2) The abstract's AUC ranges (training 0.771–0.824; testing 0.769–0.839) disagree with the Results (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation 0.769–0.804). (3) Data_Types_Used 'Other' = census/ACS block-group socio-economic variables and geospatial distance variables. (4) Study_Setting coded Community because the model is a neighbourhood-level ecological niche model, although the patient data come from a hospital EHR. (5) Interpretability coded Post-hoc: MaxEnt percent contribution, permutation importance and jack-knife are global diagnostics of a fitted model. (6) Reporting_Guideline 'None reported' — no reporting checklist is named; the quote shows the Supporting information list.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Whether the four MaxEnt runs should be treated as four separate models or one model applied to four strata, and whether a per-run AUC (only in Fig 2) should override the reported range. Whether MaxEnt percent contribution/jack-knife should count as intrinsic or post-hoc interpretability. No code, model or repository is shared.
raw.Sample_Size: 16,124 unique patients / occurrence points with community-onset S. aureus (7,867 CO-MRSA; 8,257 CO-MSSA); 15,094 unique occurrence points analysed in the machine learning models
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Children treated for community-onset S. aureus infections from January 2002 through December 2016; first S. aureus culture per unique patient per 12-month calendar year; georeferenced residential address within the 20 counties of Atlanta’s MSA.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Repeated culture results per unique patient excluded (only the first culture per patient per 12-month year counted); patients without a georeferenced address or living outside the 20 counties of Atlanta’s MSA excluded.
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta electronic medical records (EMR); U.S. Census / American Community Survey (ACS) 2010 and 2013 block-group data; Atlanta Regional Commission (ARC) geospatial data
raw.Dataset_Size: 22,366 S. aureus infections (2002–2016) yielding 16,124 unique CO-S. aureus occurrence points (7,867 CO-MRSA; 8,257 CO-MSSA); 15,094 occurrence points entered the MaxEnt models; 2,609 block groups (78% of 3,335)
raw.Ethnicity_Details: Hispanic vs non-Hispanic; among 1,558 Hispanic children with S. aureus infections, 12% had CO-MRSA vs 16% CO-MSSA (p<0.0001); Hispanic ethnicity data not available for 2002–2005.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: 20-county Atlanta MSA, Georgia, USA; analyses included 78% (2,609) of the 3,335 block groups in the MSA; data from a single pediatric healthcare system (Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta) covering >90% of pediatric hospitalisations for this condition.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Microbiology culture from source of infection which resulted in positive S. aureus; majority of community-onset disease was skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI).
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance status of community-onset S. aureus infection: CO-MRSA vs CO-MSSA, classified by oxacillin susceptibility, modelled as the spatial probability of occurrence of each type across the 20-county Atlanta MSA.
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA, and methicillin-sensitive, MSSA)
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin susceptibility used as the marker of methicillin resistance)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (defines MRSA vs MSSA)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Community-onset defined as a positive S. aureus culture within 48 hours between healthcare visit date and specimen collection date; resistance to oxacillin categorised as MRSA and susceptibility to oxacillin as MSSA.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 4 MaxEnt model runs (CO-MRSA early and late; CO-MSSA early and late)
raw.Feature_Engineering: All area variables aggregated to census block group level; Euclidean distances to daycares, K-12 schools and children’s hospitals rasterised and averaged per block group using zonal statistics; rasters aligned at ~328 feet (100 m) resolution (QGIS v3.22, GDAL); duplicate infections within the same raster removed.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: A priori selection of 14 area-level variables previously reported as CO-MRSA/CO-MSSA risk factors; MaxEnt feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) chosen by lowest AIC using ENMeval
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 14 (all area variables retained in the four MaxEnt runs; model feature classes reduced to linear, quadratic and hinge)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) selected on lowest AIC using R package ENMeval v2.0.3; all other MaxEnt settings kept at default
raw.Software_Libraries: MaxEnt software v3.4.4; R package ENMeval v2.0.3; QGIS v3.22; ArcGIS Pro 2.9; GDAL/OGR; SAS 9.4 (PROC GLIMMIX)
raw.Other_Metrics: Training AUC 0.771–0.837 and evaluation AUC 0.769–0.804 for the four MaxEnt runs (abstract reports testing AUC 0.769–0.839); predicted omission rate binomial tests; AUC jack-knife for variable importance; odds ratios with 95% CI for the multilevel models.
raw.Baseline_Method: MaxEnt ROC plots against a random-prediction (AUC = 0.5) reference line; comparison of the machine learning results with previously reported spatial and multilevel regression analyses
raw.Baseline_Performance: Random prediction reference line only; no baseline score quantified
raw.Internal_Validation: Random subsampling: 75% of occurrence points for training, 25% held out for model evaluation; predicted-omission binomial test; jack-knife test of variable importance
raw.Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% evaluation (per run, randomly subsampled occurrence points)
raw.Overfitting_Method: Total number of variables limited to 14 to avoid collinearity and model overload; duplicate occurrence points within a raster removed; only three MaxEnt feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) retained after AIC-based selection
raw.Clinical_Insights: Densely populated areas were the single largest predictor of CO-MRSA and CO-MSSA occurrence; population density alone performs nearly as well as all variables; distance to day care and hospitals contributes; race contributed more in CO-MRSA models than CO-MSSA; poverty and education contributed little despite high-density areas having higher poverty and lower education.
raw.Data_Repository: Supporting information files (S1 Table XLSX, S2 Table CSV); no external repository named
raw.Generalisability_Details: Findings are limited to geographic areas similar to the study area — an urban setting in the southeastern U.S.; the authors suggest comparing with settings that have multiple healthcare systems for children.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Evidence = random-subsampling evaluation of the four MaxEnt runs on held-out occurrence points from the same 20-county dataset (no external validation).
raw.Integration_Point: Population / area-level risk mapping at census block-group scale within the Atlanta MSA; not a point-of-care tool
raw.End_User_Described: Local public health agencies and communities; hospitals (for surveillance and prevention planning)
raw.Barriers_List: Built-environment variables (transportation access, housing quality/type) not available or incomplete; race/ethnicity categories collapsed (cannot identify beyond black, white, Asian; no Latinx sub-categories); cultural/community boundaries differ from census units; generalizability limited to similar urban southeastern U.S. settings; household crowding contribution may be underestimated after removal of duplicate raster locations.
raw.Facilitators_List: Large georeferenced dataset spanning more than 10 years; hospital system captures >90% of paediatric admissions for this condition; block-group scale keeps all variables at the same spatial scale (MAUP eliminated).
raw.Future_Directions: Re-run the MaxEnt models replacing non-contributing variables with ‘access’ variables; further elucidate neighbourhood-level race factors and compare with settings that have multiple paediatric healthcare systems.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 8 (clinical, microbiological, laboratory, healthcare utilisation, sociodemographic, environmental, temporal, geographic)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: MaxEnt percent contribution and permutation importance (Table 6); jack-knife test of AUC with each variable in isolation and excluded
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Population density was by far the single most important predictor (80–92% contribution); proximity to paediatric congregate care (day care centres) and hospitals also predicted risk; household crowding contributed <1%, contrary to prior expectations.
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: MaxEnt feature classes — linear, quadratic and hinge features selected on lowest AIC via R package ENMeval v2.0.3 (quadratic and hinge features capture non-linear relationships and interactions)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Variable selection / data completeness; race and ethnicity classification; generalizability and single health system; neighbourhood and cultural boundary mismatch.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Data for candidate built-environment variables were not as complete as the variables selected and were therefore excluded; race/ethnicity recorded only as black, white, Asian or Hispanic.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: AUC ranges are inconsistent between the abstract (training 0.771–0.824; testing 0.769–0.839) and the Results (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation 0.769–0.804), and per-run AUC values appear only in Fig 2; the four MaxEnt runs are described collectively.

studies.title: The use of infrared spectroscopy and artificial neural networks for detection of uropathogenic Escherichia coli strains’ susceptibility to cephalothin
studies.journal: Acta Biochimica Polonica (Vol. 60, No 4/2013, pp. 713-718; actabp.pl)
studies.sample_size: 109 uropathogenic E. coli strains (10 colonies per strain; 1090 IR spectra in total)
studies.ai_purpose: Classification of uropathogenic E. coli strains as cephalothin susceptible/resistant from their ATR/FTIR infrared spectra by designed artificial neural networks (MLP, RBF).
studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug
studies.best_model: MLP 30-9-2 (multilayer perceptron, 30 input - 9 hidden - 2 output neurons) for the two-group sensitive / 'non-sensitive' task: 92.64% correctly classified strains in the validating set (Table 4, ID 1) - the highest accuracy reported for any network in the paper.

raw.Title: The use of infrared spectroscopy and artificial neural networks for detection of uropathogenic Escherichia coli strains’ susceptibility to cephalothin
raw.Journal_Source: Acta Biochimica Polonica (Vol. 60, No 4/2013, pp. 713-718; actabp.pl)
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation

raw.Population_Description: 109 uropathogenic E. coli strains isolated from urine samples of hospitalised patients with urinary tract infection (wards of hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008), stored at -80 degrees C; 10 colonies per strain harvested, giving 1090 IR spectra.
raw.Data_Source_Other: Clinical E. coli isolates from urine cultures of hospitalised patients (hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008); ATR/FTIR spectra measured in-house.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Experiment 1 (3 groups): 10 MLP networks - validating-set correct classifications 83.43% (MLP 30-8-3) descending to 76.69%; 10 RBF networks - validating 58.90% down to 55.21%. Experiment 2 (2 groups): 10 MLP networks - validating 92.64% (MLP 30-9-2) down to 90.80%; 10 RBF networks - validating 65.03% down to 63.80%. Metric reported throughout is the percentage of correctly classified strains in the training / testing / validating subsets (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5).
raw.Best_Performing_Model: MLP 30-9-2 (multilayer perceptron, 30 input - 9 hidden - 2 output neurons) for the two-group sensitive / 'non-sensitive' task: 92.64% correctly classified strains in the validating set (Table 4, ID 1) - the highest accuracy reported for any network in the paper.
raw.Accuracy_Value: 92.64% correctly classified strains (validating set, MLP 30-9-2, two-group task)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Validating subset (15% of the 1090 IR spectra); two-group sensitive / 'non-sensitive' classification
raw.Sensitivity_Value: 93.23% of cephalothin-sensitive strains correctly classified (validating set, best two-group network MLP 30-9-2)
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validating set; true cephalothin-sensitive strains (two-group task)
raw.Specificity_Value: 91.9% of 'non-sensitive' strains correctly classified (validating set, best two-group network)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Validating set; 'non-sensitive' strains (intermediate + resistant combined, two-group task)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Performance is assessed on a randomly held-out validating subset (15%) of the same 1090 spectra; no external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no decision-support integration.
raw.Reported_Limitations: The main limitation of the technique is the need for a large number of learning data, which grows with network complexity; the best three-group network's 83.43% is 'decidedly unsatisfactory'; performance for resistant (67.5%) and intermediate (77%) strains is much worse than for sensitive strains (95%).
raw.Sample_Size: 109 uropathogenic E. coli strains (10 colonies per strain; 1090 IR spectra in total)
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Other
raw.Dataset_Size: 1090 bacterial IR spectra
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: 109 E. coli strains isolated from urine of patients in the wards of hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008; no other site, region or country.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: urine samples (of hospitalised patients with urinary tract infection)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Susceptibility/resistance of uropathogenic E. coli to cephalothin, coded first as three groups (sensitive / intermediate / resistant) and then as two groups (sensitive vs 'non-sensitive').
raw.Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (first-generation cephalosporin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Cephalothin
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptibility to cephalothin determined by an ATB UR5 (bioMerieux) susceptibility test: 51% of strains sensitive, 27% resistant and 22% intermediate; in the second experiment intermediate and resistant strains were merged into one 'non-sensitive' group.
raw.AI_Purpose: Classification of uropathogenic E. coli strains as cephalothin susceptible/resistant from their ATR/FTIR infrared spectra by designed artificial neural networks (MLP, RBF).
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 20 networks per experiment (10 MLP + 10 RBF; Tables 1-2 and 4-5) = 40 in total
raw.Feature_Engineering: ATR/FTIR spectra pre-treatment: baseline fixed, calculation of the first derivative, scaling to the range 0-1; each colony spectrum averaged from 25 scans
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Wavenumbers related to cephalothin resistance identified by statistical methods; 30 input neurons used in the final topologies
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Manual comparison of network architectures: number of hidden neurons and the activation function varied across ten networks per experiment
raw.Software_Libraries: Statistica 10 (StatSoft)
raw.Other_Metrics: Percentage of correctly classified strains per class and per subset (training / testing / validating). Validation subset of the best three-group network (Table 3, MLP 30-8-3): sensitive 95%, intermediate 77%, resistant 67.5% correctly classified. Best two-group network: sensitive 93.23%, 'non-sensitive' 91.9%.
raw.Baseline_Method: Principal component analysis (PCA) and cluster analysis (CA)
raw.Baseline_Performance: PCA and CA did not differentiate the E. coli strains (data not shown)
raw.Internal_Validation: Random split of the 1090 IR spectra into independent learning (70%), testing (15%) and validating (15%) subsets
raw.Overfitting_Method: Network complexity used as a secondary selection criterion after the number of correct classifications in the validation subset
raw.Clinical_Insights: Resistance information in the spectrum is dispersed rather than localised: specific enzymes (e.g. beta-lactamase) and transmembrane proteins may be reflected in the spectrum, but the features are spread over its whole length rather than concentrated in one peak.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors conclude that ATR/FTIR plus ANNs 'may allow' rapid differentiation of strains by resistance/sensitivity, but no transportability analysis across sites, instruments or populations is reported.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only - random learning (70%) / testing (15%) / validating (15%) split of the 1090 IR spectra from the same 109 strains.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The assay is positioned inside the diagnostic pathway: a life-threatening infection needs correct antibiotic treatment within hours of symptom onset, and chemometric methods would allow susceptibility to be determined within several hours.
raw.Barriers_List: ANNs need a large number of learning data, and larger learning sets are required as network complexity grows; conventional resistance testing is labour- and time-consuming; the best three-group result was 'decidedly unsatisfactory'; complex E. coli phenotypes distort the spectra.
raw.Facilitators_List: ATR/FTIR is fast, cheap, non-invasive and needs no special sample preparation; neural networks resist certain data distortions and recognise patterns better than PCA/CA; susceptibility results could be obtained within hours.
raw.Future_Directions: Use of modern chemometric methods (FTIR, MALDI-TOF) to determine bacterial drug susceptibility within several hours.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data requirements (need for large learning sets that grow with network complexity); model performance (unsatisfactory overall accuracy in the three-group task, poor recognition of resistant and intermediate strains); biological variability distorting the spectra.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Differences remaining after first-derivative conversion are slight and unstable, so resistant/sensitive strains cannot be separated on them; phenotype differences distort the IR spectrum and can be mistaken for random noise.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model comparison tables are complete (topology, error and activation functions, training/testing/validating percentages), but the selected wavenumbers are never listed and the PCA/CA comparison is reported only as 'data not shown'.
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-6 of the text layer (journal pp. 713-718)

raw.Title: Predicting future hospital antimicrobial resistance prevalence using machine learning

raw.Data_Source_Other: IQVIA monthly antibiotic (pharmacy dispensing) usage data
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Top-10 features per pathogen-antibiotic model ranked by mean absolute SHAP (Tables 1-4). Generally: previous resistance to the same pathogen-antibiotic combination, resistance in a different pathogen to the same antibiotic, and usage of the same / same-class antibiotic. e.g. for E. coli amoxicillin/clavulanic acid the top feature was 'E. coli amoxicillin/clavulanic acid-res, prev1' (SHAP 2.87)

raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Six models compared by mean absolute error (MAE) on the held-out test set (FY2021-2022): (1) previous value taken forwards; (2) difference of previous two years taken forwards; (3) linear trend forecasting (LTF); (4) XGBoost default parameters; (5) XGBoost tuned hyperparameters; (6) XGBoost with usage features only. XGBoost best overall; previous-value forwards similar/slightly higher MAE; difference-forwards worst, then LTF.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (lowest mean absolute error on the test set)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation on a temporal held-out test set: models trained on resistance up to FY2020-2021 (with 3-fold CV hyperparameter tuning) and evaluated on FY2021-2022 as the test outcome. No external dataset and no prospective deployment.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Representativeness of tested isolates for the population served; imperfect antibiotic-usage denominator (bed-days); aggregation to financial years loses within-year seasonality; short time series (main statistical limitation); only one-year-ahead prediction; number of training examples too small for better-than-default hyperparameters.
raw.Sample_Size: 119 hospital Trusts (hospital groups), each a training/test example; 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations, up to 6 financial years
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: D.W.E. declares lecture fees from Gilead, outside the submitted work; all other authors declare no competing interests.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded Trusts testing <100 isolates per year; excluded Trust-pathogen-antibiotic-FYs with <=10 susceptibility results; 19 Trusts with <100 tested isolates/FY excluded (16 specialised Trusts).

raw.Data_Source_Name: UKHSA Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS); IQVIA
raw.Dataset_Size: 119 Trusts across up to 6 financial years, 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations
raw.Missing_Data_Method: XGBoost learns, at each decision-tree split, the classification of the missing-value group that minimises MAE; small-number (<=10 results) cells excluded; usage missing for only a few Trusts in the highest-usage antibiotics.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: 138 hospital groups (Trusts) across England for FY2016-2022; 119 retained (data from ~98% of hospital microbiology laboratories); bloodstream infections representative via widespread testing in a high-income setting.

raw.Drug_Classes: Tetracyclines (doxycycline); macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin); lincosamides (clindamycin); glycopeptides (vancomycin); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin); third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime, ceftazidime, cefpodoxime, ceftriaxone); aminoglycosides (gentamicin); carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem); penicillin/beta-lactam combinations (co-amoxiclav, piperacillin/tazobactam)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: doxycycline/tetracycline; erythromycin; clarithromycin; clindamycin; vancomycin; ciprofloxacin; third-generation cephalosporins; gentamicin; carbapenems; co-amoxiclav; piperacillin/tazobactam; ceftazidime
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Percentage of isolates resistant to each antibiotic per Trust per financial year; intermediate susceptibility treated as susceptible (EUCAST increased-exposure recommendation).
raw.AI_Purpose: Predict future antimicrobial-resistance prevalence at hospital-Trust level from historical aggregate resistance and antimicrobial usage, to target interventions and allocate resources.
raw.Feature_Engineering: Time-series feature engineering: each Trust contributes one row of lagged historical features (resistance prevalence prev1-prev3/4, usage prev1-prev6); usage standardised to DDDs per 100 bed-days; optional feature selection by SHAP-importance threshold above white-noise.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Refitting models using only features with feature importance (mean absolute SHAP) above white-noise level
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: 3-fold cross-validation on the training dataset to tune number of estimators, maximum depth, and minimum child weight
raw.Software_Libraries: XGBoost; SHAP
raw.Other_Metrics: Mean absolute error (MAE) as the primary performance metric; mean absolute SHAP values for feature importance / model interpretability.
raw.Baseline_Method: Previous value (last resistance prevalence) taken forwards; difference between the previous two years taken forwards; linear trend forecasting (LTF)
raw.Baseline_Performance: Previous value forwards similar to, or slightly higher MAE than XGBoost; difference-forwards worst (highest MAE), then LTF
raw.Internal_Validation: 3-fold cross-validation on the training dataset for hyperparameter tuning
raw.Train_Test_Split: Calendar-time split: training outcome FY2020-2021 (with up to 6 prior FYs of features), test outcome FY2021-2022
raw.Overfitting_Method: Hyperparameter tuning (CV), feature selection, and feature engineering to improve generalisability; authors note over-fitting was reduced though performance barely improved.
raw.Clinical_Insights: SHAP ranked features showed previous resistance to the same pathogen-antibiotic combination, resistance in a different pathogen to the same antibiotic, and usage of same / same-class antibiotics among the top features, indicating the model exploits cross-pathogen and cross-antibiotic resistance/usage relationships.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Domain knowledge used to standardise usage across Trusts (DDDs and occupied beds); authors relate their results to European/national studies and note assumptions are reasonable in a high-income setting.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: temporal train/test split (test outcome FY2021-2022) with 3-fold CV hyperparameter tuning on the training set; no external dataset, no prospective or deployed use.
raw.Future_Directions: As time series lengthen, deep learning (LSTM and transformer) models become viable; predicting >1 year ahead (autoregressive or encoder-decoder architectures); incorporating community antibiotic-usage features; potential quarterly granularity when numbers permit.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: mean absolute SHAP values (computed on the test set, averaged across Trusts)
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Mean absolute SHAP feature-importance analysis; XGBoost inherently learns non-linear interactions between features
raw.Limitation_Categories: Bias/representativeness (tested isolates vs population served); measurement (imperfect usage denominator); aggregation/seasonality (financial-year aggregation); time series length (too short for deep learning & multi-step); training sample size (too small to gain from hyperparameter tuning).
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Uncommon outliers possibly reflecting data-quality issues; likely some large outliers remain despite data cleaning; Trust assignation in laboratory-only data historically poor (hence mandatory-surveillance linkage); possible supply interruptions and COVID-19 impacts.
