raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary VRE positivity from electronic medical records: the dependent variable of the logistic regression was colonization (0 = no, 1 = yes); patients were labelled VRE-positive (cases) if they had VRE acquisition during the outbreak period and all other patients, whether tested or not, were assumed VRE negative (controls).
raw.AI_Purpose: To improve existing nosocomial outbreak investigation by applying machine learning (decision tree) and graph-theoretical network analysis to identify risk factors for VRE colonization, determine which patients should be screened, and locate transmission hot spots (devices, rooms, employees), and to compare the resulting prioritised screening with traditional proximity-based contact screening.
raw.Feature_Engineering: No bespoke feature construction: the classification tree was built with the same independent and dependent variables as the logistic regression (the variables in Table 1); a minority-class oversampling step produced equal numbers of positive and negative samples.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Logistic regression: most parsimonious model by forward selection then backward deletion, P > .10 inclusion criterion; decision tree: covariate importance ranking used to reveal the most predictive variables
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Minority class oversampling, resulting in equal numbers of positive and negative samples
raw.Software_Libraries: Python 3.7: pyodbc, numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, networkx, pytorch, seaborn, bokeh, Holoviz, Holoviews; R version 3.5 or newer: data.table, ggplot2, tableone, survey
raw.Other_Metrics: Decision-tree feature importance (Table 3); screening efficiency: 40.0% fewer screenings compared with the current gold standard (95% CI, 17.3 – 54.6); screening benefit: 102 (95% CI, 66 – 138) VRE-positive patients detected who were missed by proximity-based screening
raw.Baseline_Method: Proximity-based contact screening, described as the current gold standard (patients screened if hospitalized in the same room and ward as a newly detected VRE-positive patient in the prior 7 days)
raw.Internal_Validation: Model validation on the oncology ward, which screened all patients every week, so that for each week the predicted VRE-positive cases from the model could be compared with the observed cases (ground truth); performance summarised as screening efficiency and screening benefit relative to proximity-based screening.
raw.Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
raw.Clinical_Insights: The decision tree provided thresholds that split the data appropriately and allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization. The network analysis identified 3 pathways linking the 560 VRE cases (healthcare personnel, medical devices, patient rooms) and produced a daily hotspot list of rooms, devices and employees ordered by likelihood of being colonized.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The method provides the basis for a smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially for data-driven outbreak monitoring; the authors add that data-science interpretations should consider data-source maturity, the scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: predictions compared with the oncology ward's weekly screening ground truth within the same hospital; the authors state the study was monocentric and could have been improved by validating against data from another hospital.
raw.Integration_Point: Outbreak management: the daily hotspot list is sent to the organisational unit that disinfects rooms and medical devices, and the network-graph method produces a prioritised screening list for patients in place of proximity-based contact screening.
raw.End_User_Described: The organisational unit involved in disinfecting rooms and medical devices, plus those deciding how to isolate patients and clean devices and rooms.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The new prioritised screening list derived from the network graph is compared with the current gold-standard proximity-based screening; the hotspot list orders devices, healthcare personnel and patient rooms by likelihood of being colonized so that isolation, disinfection and potential screening of personnel can be targeted.
raw.Barriers_List: Lack of a fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse, which slowed implementation; information on physicians and other key personnel absent from the time and resource management system, so employee contacts were limited to nursing staff; only IT-tracked (larger, non-portable) medical devices captured; data-source integration and operationalisation were the most time-consuming and resource-intensive steps; the popularity of machine-learning methods can lead to an analysis-driven approach ("85% of data science projects fail").
raw.Facilitators_List: Availability of a hospital-wide, fully integrated data warehouse as a prerequisite for fast implementation and actionable results; a clear project mandate with metrics for success defined before the project started; data maturity, scope of included sources and consideration of confounding factors.
raw.Future_Directions: A smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially data-driven outbreak monitoring; defining appropriate metrics at project initiation; validation against data from another hospital; consideration of data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Decision-tree feature importance (the rank of the covariate in splitting the data set: the higher the importance, the earlier the covariate is used in the branching process)
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: The decision-tree analysis allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization; number of rooms stayed in and patient-device interactions highlighted environmental contamination as an important factor.
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Decision tree with a maximum depth of 6 levels, motivated by the complex interactions and multiple collinearities seen in the fitted statistical models; collinear variables were not estimated in the multivariable logistic model (Table 2 note).
raw.Limitation_Categories: Monocentric / single-institution design and lack of external validation; incomplete data on physician and other personnel contacts; only IT-tracked medical devices; no fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse; data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Interactions documented by healthcare workers were limited to nursing employees because physician interactions are not documented at that granularity for in-patient care; for medical devices only interactions tracked in the IT systems were included, limiting the study to larger, often non-portable devices.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: The article reports models, variables, software and the validation ward clearly, but the computation of the screening-efficiency and screening-benefit metrics is deferred to the Supplementary Material, and no discrimination metric (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC) is reported for any model.
raw.Page_References: Article pp. 1–7 (journal pp. 246–252); methods pp. 2–3; Table 1 p. 2; Table 2 p. 4; results pp. 4–5; Table 3, Table 4, limitations and funding p. 6

studies.title: Computer-aided diagnosis using embedded ensemble deep learning for multiclass drug-resistant tuberculosis classification
studies.sample_size: 5,039 CXR images in the primary dataset (4,030 training / 1,009 testing); 760 images in the web-application test; 33 physicians in the usability test
studies.ai_purpose: To build an embedded ensemble deep learning CAD system (TB-DRD-CXR) that classifies drug-resistant TB types from a single CXR image and returns a recommended treatment regimen so physicians have AI support for the drug-resistance diagnosis decision.
studies.best_model: The proposed heterogeneous ensemble deep learning model (EfficientNetV2B3 + EfficientNetV2M + ConvNeXtSmall with HyVaN-AMIS decision fusion; experiment 16, which used image segmentation, augmentation, CLR and HyVaN-AMIS) - highest AUC (95.1%), F-measure (94.8%) and accuracy (93.4%) of the 16 experiments.

raw.Title: Computer-aided diagnosis using embedded ensemble deep learning for multiclass drug-resistant tuberculosis classification
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Imaging Analysis
raw.Funder_Names: Research and Graduate Studies, Khon Kaen University, Thailand
raw.Population_Description: Chest X-ray (CXR) images of tuberculosis patients from the open TB Portal dataset (5,039 CXR images: 1,608 DS-TB, 470 DR-TB, 2,098 MDR-TB, 108 pre-XDR-TB, 755 XDR-TB); a separate usability evaluation involved 33 physicians from 14 large hospitals in northeastern Thailand (aged 28-58).
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Proposed heterogeneous ensemble (EfficientNetV2B3 + EfficientNetV2M + ConvNeXtSmall, HyVaN-AMIS fusion; experiment 16): AUC 95.1%, F-measure 94.8%, accuracy 93.4%. Table 2 comparison (AUC / F-measure / accuracy): DenseNet201 75.4/73.8/72.5; ResNet101 72.8/71.2/69.4; NASNetMobile 52.7/50.4/48.3; EfficientNetB7 93.1/91.9/90.7; EfficientNetV2B3 67.4/65.4/63.1; EfficientNetV2M 92.8/90.4/89.5; ConvNeXtSmal 90.3/87.9/86.8. Sixteen parameter combinations (Table 4) ranged from AUC 67.4%/F 63.8%/accuracy 65.1% (experiment 1) to AUC 95.1%/F 94.8%/accuracy 93.4% (experiment 16).
raw.Best_Performing_Model: The proposed heterogeneous ensemble deep learning model (EfficientNetV2B3 + EfficientNetV2M + ConvNeXtSmall with HyVaN-AMIS decision fusion; experiment 16, which used image segmentation, augmentation, CLR and HyVaN-AMIS) - highest AUC (95.1%), F-measure (94.8%) and accuracy (93.4%) of the 16 experiments.
raw.Accuracy_Value: 93.4% (multiclass, test set)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Held-out test set of the TB Portal dataset (20%; 1,009 CXR images)
raw.F1_Population_Set: Held-out test set of the TB Portal dataset (20%; 1,009 CXR images)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Held-out test set of the TB Portal dataset (20%; 1,009 CXR images)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evidence stops at internal validation: the ensemble was trained on 80% of the TB Portal dataset and evaluated on a held-out 20% (1,009 CXR images) with no external dataset. The web application was tested on 760 further Portal images and by 33 physicians for usability, but no prospective clinical evaluation or CDS integration is reported.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Fast image analysis gave relatively unstable results (a stated shortcoming); the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types documented in the clinical literature, so the model should be retrained with new data; the recommended regimen must be kept current with WHO/national guidelines or the software becomes a distraction.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: If the recommended treatment regimen is not kept up to date, the software ceases to be an aid and becomes a distraction for physicians.
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not framed as an equity analysis, but the authors argue the low-cost mobile application suits practitioners in resource-constrained settings and may reduce unnecessary tests and procedures.
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Developers are said to need to make such applications transparent, safe and compliant with privacy and ethical norms to earn trust; no formal governance or regulatory assessment is reported.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Judgement calls: (1) Study_Setting coded Tertiary / hospital - the AI development is in silico on a public image archive, but the application was implemented and evaluated with physicians at 14 large hospitals. (2) Study_Design also ticks Qualitative (acceptability / usability) because a 33-participant task-based SUS evaluation was run; that evaluation is quantitative in instrument but is the review vocabulary's only home for an acceptability/usability study. (3) Provider_Facing_Applications deliberately omits 'Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)' because the model predicts the drug-resistance class from CXR images, which is neither genotypic nor spectral; the same output is captured under Diagnosis / species identification. (4) Accuracy/F1/AUROC values are for the best model (experiment 16, multiclass: AUC 95.1, F-measure 94.8, accuracy 93.4 on the held-out 20% test set). The 96.1% figure quoted in the abstract/conclusion is the deployed web application's accuracy on 760 further Portal images, and the 96.7% in the abstract is the SUS score, not a model metric. (5) Sensitivity, specificity and PPV are coded No: the paper reports only AUC, F-measure and accuracy. (6) Software_Language is Not specified - only TensorFlow (library) and HTML/JavaScript (web front end) are named, never the modelling language. (7) Lifecycle_P5 is ticked because a working web application was built and used by 33 physicians, while Clinical_Maturity stays at level 2 for lack of external validation. (8) Subgroup/performance-disparity fields are coded No; the per-class accuracy breakdown (Figure 4, Table 6) is part of the classification result, not a demographic subgroup analysis.
raw.Sample_Size: 5,039 CXR images in the primary dataset (4,030 training / 1,009 testing); 760 images in the web-application test; 33 physicians in the usability test
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: No competing interests declared: the authors state the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Frontal, AP or PA chest X-ray views held in the TB Portal dataset with a TB drug-resistance class assigned at data entry from the DST profile (five classes).
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Rifampicin-resistant (RR) and isoniazid-resistant (Hr) TB were not assigned to any TB Portals dataset and, lacking detailed DST profiles to reorganise them, were not part of the classifier implementation.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Imaging
raw.Data_Source_Name: TB Portal / Portal dataset (tbportals.niaid.nih.gov)
raw.Dataset_Size: 5,039 CXR images (4,030 training; 1,009 testing)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: The training/testing data come from the TB Portal, an open global drug-resistant-TB image-sharing platform, so the images are not from one country; the usability evaluation was limited to 33 physicians in northeastern Thailand, and the authors note the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types seen in practice.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: chest X-ray (CXR) images; frontal, AP or PA views
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multiclass classification of drug-resistance type from a single CXR image into five WHO categories: DS-TB, DR-TB, MDR-TB, pre-XDR-TB and XDR-TB.
raw.Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis drugs: first-line anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin), fluoroquinolones, and group A anti-TB drugs (bedaquiline, linezolid).
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: isoniazid, rifampicin, fluoroquinolone, bedaquiline, linezolid
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: TB type assigned at data entry from the drug susceptibility test (DST) profile, per WHO 2021 criteria: DS-TB no resistance; MDR-TB resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin; pre-XDR-TB MDR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone; XDR-TB pre-XDR-TB plus resistance to one additional group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid).
raw.AI_Purpose: To build an embedded ensemble deep learning CAD system (TB-DRD-CXR) that classifies drug-resistant TB types from a single CXR image and returns a recommended treatment regimen so physicians have AI support for the drug-resistance diagnosis decision.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 8 (7 homogeneous CNN architectures plus the proposed heterogeneous ensemble in Table 2); 16 parameter-combination experiments in Table 4
raw.Feature_Engineering: Lung segmentation (two-model ensemble: patch CNN plus custom U-Net with 64*64 patches and a 20% lung-patch threshold), downscaling/resizing/normalising and patch extraction, three augmentation groups (A1-Aug reflection and linear scaling, A2-Aug rotation (-10 to 10 degrees)/translation (0-5 pixels)/shear (0-30 degrees), A3-Aug PCA-based perturbation), and two learning-rate strategies (ADADELTA and cyclical learning rate).
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Manual setting of per-architecture batch sizes (EfficientNetV2B3 16, EfficientNetV2M 2, ConvNeXtSmall 8; 2, 3, 5, 12, 10 and 8 for the comparison CNNs), 200 epochs, and learning-rate strategy (ADADELTA vs cyclical learning rate).
raw.Software_Libraries: TensorFlow (web application); custom U-Net architecture
raw.Hardware_Details: Intel i7 2.1 GHz (8 core) CPU, 32 GB RAM, Tesla V100 GPU (16 GB GPU RAM)
raw.Other_Metrics: Time-based efficiency (ET) 4.16 goals/minute and overall relative efficiency (ORE) 100% for the web application; System Usability Scale (SUS) score 96.7; model size (MB), training time (minutes) and testing time (seconds per dataset) in Table 2; correct / wrong classification counts in Tables 1 and 6.
raw.Baseline_Method: Homogeneous single-CNN and ensemble baselines: DenseNet201, ResNet101, NASNetMobile, EfficientNetB7, EfficientNetV2B3, EfficientNetV2M and ConvNeXtSmal (Table 2), plus the 'defender' configuration with no segmentation, no augmentation, ADADELTA and UWA (Table 4).
raw.Baseline_Performance: Proposed method vs the CNN baselines: +28.8% (DenseNet201), +93.4% (NASNetMobile), +2.99% (EfficientNetB7), +48.0% (EfficientNetV2B3), +4.4% (EfficientNetV2M) and +7.6% (ConvNeXtSmal) accuracy; on average 30.6% more accurate than the state-of-the-art methods; within Table 4 segmentation added 25.8%, augmentation 8.1%, CLR 4.2% and HyVaN-AMIS 2.3% accuracy over their defender settings.
raw.Internal_Validation: Hold-out test set: 80% training / 20% testing, 200 epochs
raw.Overfitting_Method: Data augmentation (A1-Aug, A2-Aug, A3-Aug) to enlarge the training set
raw.Clinical_Insights: Grad-CAM heatmaps are read clinically: innermost lung area for DR-TB, upper regions of both lungs for MDR-TB, middle-to-lower innermost area for Pre-XDR-TB, and the lower innermost areas of both lungs for XDR-TB; the model uses all six lung areas for non-TB classification.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors state the model should be retrained with new data because the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types seen in the real world, and that fast-image analysis results were unstable.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only (80/20 train-test split of the TB Portal dataset, 4,030/1,009 CXR images); the deployed web application was then tested on 760 further Portal images (96.1% correct) and by 33 physicians for usability (SUS 96.7). No external dataset, no prospective clinical evaluation and no CDS integration is reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Standalone web/mobile browser application (TB-DRD-CXR, https://itbru.com/TDRC/index.html) to which physicians upload or live-capture a CXR image; the server returns the predicted drug-resistance class and a recommended regimen. Not EHR- or LIS-integrated.
raw.End_User_Described: medical staff and physicians; a pharmacist maintains the regimen list
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Users submit a CXR image file (or capture one live through the camera); a server makes the diagnosis and returns the drug-resistance class with treatment recommendations; the pharmacist updates the treatment plan; physicians use the recommendation as a guideline but must also weigh the patient's own information and drug response.
raw.Barriers_List: Keeping the recommended regimen up to date with changing WHO / national DR-TB guidelines (otherwise the software distracts rather than helps); the Portal dataset missing drug-resistance types seen in practice; unstable results in fast image analysis.
raw.Facilitators_List: Speed and accuracy of results, real-time analysis of large data volumes, specific treatment recommendations for clinicians, low cost without costly equipment or extensive training, and suitability for resource-constrained settings.
raw.Future_Directions: Retrain the model with new data covering the drug-resistance types missing from the Portal dataset; research how best to interpret rapid image analysis; test other CNN ensembles; add automatic detection of drug-resistant types from photo galleries; explore unsupervised learning / clustering (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN) on the labelled data.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Model/system limitations: unstable results in fast (live camera) image analysis; dataset coverage - the Portal dataset lacks the drug-resistance types most common in the real world; dependence on keeping the treatment regimen current with WHO/national guidance.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Dataset coverage and image-variability concerns: the Portal dataset does not include all documented drug-resistance types, and CXRs come from various sources and technologies so image quality between lab and physician can vary.
raw.Page_References: pp. 1 (title, DOI, abstract), 3-4 (TB Portal dataset, 5,039 CXR images, 80/20 split), 8 (Table 1 strategies, Table 2 KPIs), 10 (Table 4, 16 experiments), 12-13 (best model and baseline comparison, Table 5), 14 (Table 6 web-application test, ET/ORE, SUS), 15 (Grad-CAM), 17-18 (limitations, future work), 19 (funding, conflicts, data availability).

studies.title: PREDICTION OF MUL TIDRUG-RESISTANT BACTERIA IN URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
studies.sample_size: 414 patients with a UTI diagnosis (125 MDR, 289 non-MDR)
studies.ai_purpose: To evaluate the applicability of a predictive model (the Gonzalez del Castillo clinical scale) of infection by multidrug-resistant microorganisms in UTIs treated in an emergency department, in order to identify patients at high risk of multidrug resistance and guide empirical antibiotic treatment.
studies.pathogens_reported: Escherichia coli (n = 241; 68 multidrug-resistant), Klebsiella pneumoniae (n = 53; 24 multidrug-resistant), and, in the MDR definition, MRSA, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae (including Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium and Acinetobacter baumannii.
studies.resistance_type: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; Other

raw.Title: PREDICTION OF MUL TIDRUG-RESISTANT BACTERIA IN URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
raw.Population_Description: Adult patients seen in an emergency department with a diagnostic suspicion of UTI and significant isolation of bacteria in urine culture; 414 patients, mean age 77.6 (SD 16.8) years, of whom 125 (30.2%) had an infection caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism.
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Items of the Gonzalez del Castillo scale with their point weights: previous colonization 15; institutionalization 8; indwelling urinary catheter 6; severe dependence 5; > 3 cycles of antibiotics in the previous year 4; antibiotic treatment in < 3 months 4; skin and soft tissue infection 4; congestive heart failure 3; end-organ damage diabetes mellitus 3; recurrent urinary tract infections 3; hospital admission in < 3 months 3; age >= 80 years 2; moderate dependence 2; mild dependence 0.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: One model only, no comparators: the Gonzalez del Castillo et al. risk scale (six risk-point groups), evaluated on 414 ED patients with UTI. AUC-ROC 0.79 (95% CI 0.76-0.83); at the optimal cut-off of 9 points sensitivity 76.8%, specificity 71.6% and PPV 60.2%.
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture (Gonzalez del Castillo scale score as the independent variable)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The Gonzalez del Castillo score, developed in another emergency department population, was applied to 414 patients with UTI and positive urine culture at a single ED and its discrimination was measured (AUC-ROC 0.79, optimal cut-off 9 points). The authors state that this is the first application of the scale to positive urine cultures and call for validation in other EDs, so no prospective evaluation or clinical decision support integration is reported (level 3).
raw.Reported_Limitations: Retrospective analysis with possible bias in data collection; antibiotic therapy at home and in long-term facilities was taken from community electronic information systems, so patients treated or admitted outside that setting are not captured; single ED with a high percentage of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and a high proportion of patients from residential centres, so results should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: The study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of the Hospital Santa Pau (reference No: IIBSP-OAM-2022-86). No specific ethical or governance risks of applying the predictive score are discussed.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre retrospective study of a published clinical risk score (Gonzalez del Castillo scale), not a machine-learning model: no model training, no code or data sharing, no fairness analysis, no decision-support platform. The score's outputs are point-based risk categories for empirical antibiotic prescribing in the ED.
raw.Sample_Size: 414 patients with a UTI diagnosis (125 MDR, 289 non-MDR)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: None of the authors has any potential financial conflict of interest.
raw.Sex_Distribution: Female 284 (68.5%) of the total sample (MDR group 75 [60.0%]; non-MDR group 209 [72.3%])
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Patients seen in an emergency department with diagnostic suspicion of UTI and significant isolation of bacteria in urine culture (adult patients with a diagnosis of UTI and positive urine culture).
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Repeat visit episodes for the same patient were excluded.
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: Hospital Santa Creu i Sant Pau (Barcelona, Spain) shared clinical history and the primary-care electronic prescription system; no named public dataset.
raw.Dataset_Size: 414 patients (MDR n = 125; no MDR n = 289)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Not described: only the proportion missing is reported (missing information for a complete score calculation < 5% in all variables considered, most importantly antibiotherapy in the 3 previous months 4.5% and > 1 UTI episode in the previous year 4.5%); no imputation or exclusion method is stated.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: one emergency department of a 650-bed tertiary-level hospital in Barcelona, Spain, with approximately 140,000 ED visits per year. The authors state that the results should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine (urine culture)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Infection by a multidrug-resistant microorganism: a UTI was considered to be caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism when caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium or Acinetobacter baumannii.
raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli (n = 241; 68 multidrug-resistant), Klebsiella pneumoniae (n = 53; 24 multidrug-resistant), and, in the MDR definition, MRSA, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae (including Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium and Acinetobacter baumannii.
raw.Num_Pathogens: Not reported as a single count; the MDR definition names 6 organism groups (MRSA; multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp.; ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae; carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae; Enterococcus faecium; Acinetobacter baumannii).
raw.Drug_Classes: No drug classes analysed: multidrug resistance is defined by organism/mechanism (methicillin resistance, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas, ESBL production, carbapenemase production).
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; Other
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary outcome: UTI caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism versus not, where a UTI due to a multidrug-resistant microorganism was considered to be caused by any of MRSA, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium, and Acinetobacter baumannii. Infection by a resistant pathogen is the dependent variable.
raw.AI_Purpose: To evaluate the applicability of a predictive model (the Gonzalez del Castillo clinical scale) of infection by multidrug-resistant microorganisms in UTIs treated in an emergency department, in order to identify patients at high risk of multidrug resistance and guide empirical antibiotic treatment.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single published risk scale; no comparator models)
raw.Feature_Engineering: None by the authors: the items of the published Gonzalez del Castillo score (age >= 80 years, congestive heart failure, end-organ damage diabetes mellitus, indwelling urinary catheter, recurrent urinary tract infections, institutionalization, > 3 cycles of antibiotics in the previous year, previous colonization, antibiotic treatment in < 3 months, hospital admission in < 3 months, functional status, skin and soft tissue infection) were applied with the weights assigned in the original scale.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: None: all items of the published Gonzalez del Castillo scale were retained as printed.
raw.Num_Features_Total: 12 items (functional status counted once, with 3 levels)
raw.Software_Libraries: Stata V. 13.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX)
raw.Other_Metrics: PPV 60.2% and NPV 86.7% at the optimal cut-off of 9 points (NPV quoted on p. 4); sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for each of the six risk-score groups (Table 3); 139 patients (33.6%) classified as high risk (> 9 points); odds ratios for each risk factor (Table 2).
raw.Baseline_Method: None: the score was applied alone, with no comparator model or naive baseline; performance is only compared qualitatively with the score's original development study.
raw.External_Validation_Description: The Gonzalez del Castillo et al. score, developed in a different emergency department population, was applied without modification to 414 patients seen in one ED with UTI and positive urine culture; discrimination (AUC-ROC 0.79, 95% CI 0.76-0.83) and an optimal cut-off of 9 points were evaluated in this independent sample.
raw.Clinical_Insights: Previous colonization with a multidrug-resistant pathogen carries the highest score (15 points) and only about 10% of patients had a known prior multidrug-resistant pathogen; previous antibiotic therapy did not differ significantly between patients with and without MDR UTI although it was frequent overall; the authors conclude that the classic single risk criteria are inadequate and that risk factors must be combined in a score.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The results come from a single ED with a high prevalence of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and many patients from residential centres, and the authors state they should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles; they argue the data may be applicable to most EDs in their environment given the global spread of resistance and population ageing.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: External application of a published score to an independent single-centre sample with discrimination measured (AUC-ROC 0.79, 95% CI 0.76-0.83) and a proposed cut-off of 9 points; no internal development, no prospective evaluation, no integration into clinical systems and no routine use reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical decision point when prescribing empirical antibiotic treatment: ED patients with suspected UTI and positive urine culture pending identification; the score is proposed as an aid to prescribing, not as a software integration.
raw.End_User_Described: The attending physician: the scale should be considered an aid to prescribing, without replacing the attending physician's clinical judgement.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The score is applied in the ED to patients with suspected UTI and positive urine culture, particularly outside the local antibiotic therapy protocols in the sepsis code, to support the decision on empirical treatment; it is an aid to prescribing and does not replace the physician's clinical judgement.
raw.Barriers_List: Retrospective design with possible bias in data collection; antibiotic exposure data limited to patients treated or admitted within the community electronic information systems; single ED with a high percentage of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and many patients from residential centres, limiting generalisability; sensitivity and specificity did not reach the optimal cut-off points (> 80%).
raw.Facilitators_List: The score helps predict many of the daily situations attended in the ED and is especially useful outside the local antibiotic therapy protocols in the sepsis code; it combines several risk factors into one tool and is proposed as an aid to prescribing.
raw.Future_Directions: Future studies should demonstrate the usefulness of this scale for bacterial isolates in samples of different sources; the authors also call for validation in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (clinical; microbiological; pharmacological; healthcare utilisation; sociodemographic; geographic - place of origin)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: A-priori clinical point weights assigned by the Gonzalez del Castillo et al. score; no statistical importance measure was computed.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Study design (retrospective, data-collection bias); data completeness (antibiotic exposure outside the community electronic systems not captured); setting/generalisability (single ED, high MDR prevalence, elderly, residential-centre patients); performance (sensitivity and specificity below the optimal > 80% cut-off).
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing information for a complete score calculation was < 5% in all variables considered, the most important being antibiotherapy in the 3 previous months (4.5%) and > 1 UTI episode in the previous year (4.5%); antibiotic therapy at home and in long-term facilities was captured from community electronic information systems, so patients treated or admitted outside that setting are missed.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear for a clinical validation study: study period, single-centre setting, population, outcome definition, metric definitions and 95% CI are reported, with the metrics shown per risk group. No code or data availability statement and no reporting guideline is named.
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-6 (full article text layer); key evidence: p. 1 (abstract, aim, DOI), p. 2 (methods, population, MDR outcome definition, AUC-ROC), p. 3 (scale weights, Table 2, optimal cut-off, missing data), p. 4 (Table 3 metrics, limitations of comparison with the development study), p. 5 (limitations, competing interest), p. 6 (article summary).

raw.Data_Source_Other: Urine samples supplied by the bacteriology laboratory at Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC); FTIR spectra measured in-house for the study

raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF): accuracy 98% for taxonomic classification (combined E. coli + K. pneumoniae vs other UTI bacteria). RF for ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative: AUC 0.90, accuracy 80%, sensitivity 81%, specificity 80%, PPV 59%, NPV 92% (Table 2). RF for ESBL-positive vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms: AUC 0.82, accuracy 77%, sensitivity 79%, specificity 70%, PPV 89%, NPV 52% (Table 3). Several sophisticated classifiers were screened but only RF is named; UMAP used for dimensionality reduction/visualisation and PCA did not show good cluster separability.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random forest (RF) classifier

raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random forest classifier developed and evaluated on a single-centre urine-spectra dataset using 5-fold cross-validation, with 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter estimation (number of features and number of trees); no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical integration is reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: The success rate of identifying ESBL bacteria was not especially high; enlarging the dataset is expected to enable more sophisticated classifiers and improve success rates; linking spectral changes to a specific biological element of the cell is difficult because of the limitation of infrared spectroscopy
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Study performed under the approval of the Ethical Helsinki Board from Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC); no safety hazards, serious risks or dangers reported; no other ethical or governance issues discussed
raw.Sample_Size: 2249 urine samples infected with E. coli or K. pneumoniae (1746 E. coli, 503 K. pneumoniae) out of 2616 samples from 2616 different patients; the ESBL analysis used 591 ESBL-positive and 1658 ESBL-negative isolates
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Urine samples from patients infected with Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae; other UTI gram-negative bacteria were excluded because of their low incidence
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Bacteria other than E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae (367 samples infected with other UTI bacteria) were not included in the ESBL classification because of their low incidence
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC) bacteriology laboratory urine sample collection
raw.Dataset_Size: 2616 urine samples from 2616 different patients (2249 infected with E. coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae, 367 with other UTI bacteria); the ESBL classification used 591 ESBL-positive and 1658 ESBL-negative isolates
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: urine samples supplied by the bacteriology laboratory at Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC), Beer-Sheva, Israel
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: urine
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of bacteria obtained directly from patient urine as ESBL-positive or ESBL-negative, regardless of species, plus differentiation of resistant isolates by mechanism of resistance (ESBL production vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms)
raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae; a mixed group of other UTI bacteria (367 samples) used only in the preliminary taxonomic classification
raw.Num_Pathogens: 2 (Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae) plus a mixed 'other UTI bacteria' group
raw.Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (resistance to all cephalosporins defines ESBL-positive; another mechanism defines resistance to at least one cephalosporin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: cephalexin, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime axetil, cefuroxime, ceftazidime
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative established by the classical methods (MALDI-TOF species identification and disk diffusion ESBL testing) as the gold standard; ESBL-positive samples were resistant to all cephalosporins, and the second sub-category was ESBL-negative but resistant to at least one cephalosporin antibiotic by another mechanism
raw.AI_Purpose: To examine the potential of FTIR spectroscopy-based machine learning (random forest) to detect ESBL-producing bacteria directly from patient urine within about 40 minutes and to differentiate resistance mechanisms, without identifying the bacterial species first
raw.Num_Models_Compared: Several classifiers were screened ('several sophisticated classifiers were applied'); only the random forest is named and reported. UMAP and PCA were used for dimensionality reduction/visualisation, not as predictive models.
raw.Feature_Engineering: Atmospheric compensation; Savitzky-Golay smoothing with 13 points; spectra cut to the 1800-900 cm-1 fingerprint region; Concave Rubber Band baseline correction (64 equal-sized ranges, minima fitted with a polynomial and subtracted, repeated five times); vector normalisation and offset correction; second derivative of the spectra used in all analyses
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Mutual information (MI) score per wavenumber of the second-derivative spectra, wavenumbers arranged in descending MI order; nested K-fold multiple iterations adding five features at a time until the best-performing set was found
raw.Num_Features_Total: Not stated; candidate features are the individual wavenumbers of the second-derivative spectra in the 1800-900 cm-1 fingerprint region
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 100 (mutual-information selected features for the ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative stage; number not stated for the other stages)
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Instance weighting: costs proportional to the inverse priors of the training set, raising the weight of the smaller class
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set to estimate the number of features and the number of classifier trees
raw.Hardware_Details: Nicolet-i10 infrared microscope FTIR spectrometer with a liquid nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector, transmission mode; spectra measured 4000-650 cm-1 with 128 co-added scans at 4 cm-1 resolution
raw.Other_Metrics: AUC 0.90 for ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative classification (Table 2); AUC 0.82 for ESBL-positive vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms (Table 3); accuracy 98% for the taxonomic classification (Table 1)
raw.Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation (data divided into five equal subsets maintaining the class ratio; four train, one test, repeated five times); 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter estimation
raw.Train_Test_Split: Cross-validation rather than a single split: four of five subsets used for training and the fifth for test, rotated five times
raw.Clinical_Insights: The main spectral changes between ESBL-positive and ESBL-negative isolates are in amide I (1728-1627 cm-1), amide II (1627-1520 cm-1) and the carbohydrate region (1196-900 cm-1); absorption of ESBL-negative isolates is significantly lower in the carbohydrate region (1200-1000 cm-1) and at the 1081 cm-1 carbohydrate band; the differences may partly reflect plasmid-borne resistance genes rather than ESBL production alone
raw.Generalisability_Details: The next step would include all gram-negative UTI bacteria once sufficient data are collected from low-incidence bacteria; enlarging the dataset is expected to allow more sophisticated classifiers and better success rates
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal 5-fold cross-validation with nested 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameters on a single-centre urine-spectra dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported
raw.Integration_Point: None described; the method is proposed for use in bacteriology laboratories
raw.End_User_Described: bacteriology laboratories and prescribing physicians
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: A patient's urine sample is received, measured by FTIR spectroscopy and classified by the trained random forest as ESBL-positive or ESBL-negative within about 40 minutes, instead of at least 48 hours with classical phenotypic methods, so that physicians can prescribe targeted antibiotics instead of random broad-spectrum antibiotics
raw.Future_Directions: Include all gram-negative UTI bacteria once enough data are collected from low-incidence bacteria; enlarge the dataset to enable more sophisticated classifiers and improve the success rates
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 (laboratory / microbiological spectroscopic features: selected wavenumbers of the second-derivative FTIR spectra)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mutual information (MI) scores calculated for each wavenumber of the second-derivative spectra, ranked in descending order
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: The 1081 cm-1 band associated with carbohydrates identified as a unique biomarker that is lower in ESBL-negative isolates; absorption in the carbohydrate region (1200-1000 cm-1) is significantly lower in ESBL-negative than ESBL-positive isolates
raw.Limitation_Categories: Not especially high success rate; difficulty linking spectral changes to a specific biological element because of the limitation of infrared spectroscopy; single-centre urine samples; only E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae included
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Spectral differences between ESBL-positive and ESBL-negative spectra are subtle and minimal; sample preparation must follow a strict protocol to ensure a high signal-to-noise ratio because the biomolecular changes due to resistance are minor

raw.Reported_Limitations: No full-text interrogation possible for all assessed articles; a single bibliographic database (Scopus) used, which may decrease documents identified through NER; English-language search restriction (language bias); imprecise sampling terms in abstracts; One Health definitions not specific and needing refinement.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Risk that literature-derived signals are misread as true burden: where research capacity is limited, few publications may reflect lack of research resources rather than low disease burden ('observing limited disease burden may be due to a lack of resources for research and nothing is reported').
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Capacity imbalances between LICs and HICs; scarce integrated AMR research in African LICs; no LIC publications covering all five One Health sectors; only one of the 100 most cited papers related to LICs; LICs have few publications across all pathogen types.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Bibliometric / NLP evidence-gap analysis of the published AMR literature (254,738 articles, 2003-2023), not a clinical prediction study: no patients, isolates, laboratory results or clinical outcomes. raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella spp.; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter spp.; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Enterobacter spp.; Acinetobacter baumannii; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Proteus spp.; Campylobacter spp.; Shigella spp.; Enterococcus faecium; Enterococcus faecalis; Haemophilus influenzae; Neisseria gonorrhoeae; Staphylococcus epidermidis; Proteus mirabilis; Enterobacter cloacae; Helicobacter pylori; Serratia spp.; Salmonella typhi; Streptococcus pyogenes; Streptococcus agalactiae; Serratia marcescens; Klebsiella oxytoca; Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; Vibrio cholerae; Providencia spp.; Morganella spp.; Enterobacter aerogenes; Clostridioides difficile; Salmonella paratyphi

raw.Drug_Classes: Methicillin (penicillinase-resistant penicillins), carbapenems, vancomycin (glycopeptide), penicillin, ampicillin (aminopenicillin), cephalosporins/ESBL-producing strains, fluoroquinolones, macrolides (clarithromycin), and colistin, sulfonamide and tetracycline resistance genes
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin, carbapenems, vancomycin, penicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, clarithromycin, colistin
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: XDR; ESBL; AmpC; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; VRE; Other
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: AMR is a term-presence label: an article is counted as AMR research when the title, keywords or abstract contains 'antimicrobial resistance' and related terms, and its One Health sector(s) are assigned from the presence of AMR words in the abstract (Tables S1-S3). ARB, ARG and pathogen-drug topics are coded by mention frequency.
raw.Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
raw.AI_Purpose: To apply AI/NLP methods to the whole AMR literature: harvest and sort 254,738 articles into a database and inverted-index information retrieval system, extract research country, ARB and ARG information, categorise articles into One Health sectors, and map global AMR research activity to expose knowledge gaps and guide One Health solutions.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 (single AI/NLP categorisation pipeline, benchmarked against manual screening of 3,000 papers; no model-to-model comparison)
raw.Feature_Engineering: NLP text pre-processing: tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, and noun phrase / alias / abbreviation extraction; inverted indexes built for each noun phrase for Boolean (conjunction, disjunction, negation) complex searches.
raw.Software_Libraries: lxml / ElementTree in Python; spaCy via R package Spacyr (version 1.2.1); a pre-trained transformer-based AI model for POS tagging
raw.Other_Metrics: Search speed (~0.6 microseconds per query); percentage of papers correctly categorised (97.4 % AMR, 98.5 % One Health sector); quantification methods and bias level of the AI classification results in Tables S1-S3.
raw.Baseline_Method: Manual screening by two reviewers (Cai Chen and Shu-Le Li) of titles, abstracts and full texts, with disagreements resolved by a senior researcher; each paper received a manual identification score (0 = false, 1 = true) for AMR relevance and category membership.
raw.Internal_Validation: Manual verification of 3,000 randomly sub-selected papers from the same database; manual scores compared with the predicted scores of the AI-based identification.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the database and AI method can be updated and reinterrogated over time as a general method for quantifying AMR trends across sectors and countries, but caution that literature-based AI cannot capture burden where research capacity is limited.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Highest evidence is internal validation: the NLP/AI model was benchmarked against manual screening of 3,000 papers randomly sub-selected from the same Scopus database, and the categories were assigned from AMR word presence in abstracts. No external dataset, prospective use, EHR/LIS integration or clinical deployment is reported. An open-access database and retrieval system are offered for future use.
raw.Integration_Point: Research literature database and information retrieval system (no clinical care pathway, EHR or LIS integration described)
raw.End_User_Described: Users of the AMR database and information retrieval system, for whom a user manual is provided ('the detailed guidance for users is provided in the user manual').
raw.Barriers_List: Limited laboratory infrastructure, incomplete National Action Plans, inadequate financial support in low-income settings, limited local research capacity, poor harmonisation of methods between sectors, and single-database (Scopus) plus English-language literature coverage.
raw.Facilitators_List: Capacity building (new laboratories, instruments, guidance and training, integrated monitoring), increasing co-developed research outputs, harmonising culture-based and molecular methods across sectors, and the open-access database with NLP methods for equitable data sharing.
raw.Future_Directions: Reduce capacity imbalances between LICs and HICs, harmonise methods across sectors (culture-based with genomic/metagenomic), refine One Health term definitions, and update/reinterrogate the database over time.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 (free-text / NLP terms from titles, keywords and abstracts)
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Co-occurrence network analysis of One Health sector terms; hierarchical clustering of term-by-year matrices to define research stages
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data availability (no full-text interrogation of all articles); single bibliographic database (Scopus); English-language restriction (language bias); imprecise sampling terms in abstracts; One Health definitions not specific and needing refinement.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Titles, keywords and abstracts may not reflect a manuscript's true content; imprecise sampling terms in abstracts reduce NER recall; One Health definitions are not specific, so sector terms need refinement.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Methods and results are described in narrative form with heavy deferral to supplemental tables (S1-S31) not in the main text, so feature lists, bias quantification and per-country tables are not verifiable from the PDF alone; the text layer carries typos ('perfomed', 'limitaitons').

raw.Data_Source_Other: ARTEMIS transnational antimicrobial resistance monitoring system (DebugIT)
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Low-frequency EMD components (the residue / mean trend and components C6+) add the most forecasting value; high-frequency components C1 and C2 degrade accuracy (by 4.6% and 1.0%); components C3–C5 have no significant impact (gains −0.4% to +0.1%).

DECF and DECS significantly outperformed the other models (P≤.004); DECS marginally better than DECF but not significantly (P≈.05). DECF 135 wins / 17 losses; DECS 118 wins / 25 losses.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: DECS

raw.Reviewer_Notes: Forecasting / method-development study combining empirical mode decomposition (trend extraction) with a k-nearest-neighbor forecaster on retrospective, weekly aggregated antibiogram data from a single institution (HUG, Geneva, Switzerland); unit of analysis is 26 organism–antibiotic resistance time series. Best-performing model DECS (not significantly better than DECF).
raw.Sample_Size: 26 organism–antibiotic resistance time series, each comprising 520 weekly data points (January 2002–December 2011); minimum 350 weeks training, 170 test points.
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: CL serves currently as a PLOS ONE editor.
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Epidemiological surveillance data
raw.Data_Source_Name: ARTEMIS (DebugIT transnational antimicrobial resistance monitoring system)

raw.Specific_Antibiotics: AMI (aminoglycoside); AMP (aminopenicillin/ampicillin); AMC (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid); FEP (cefepime); CF3 (3rd-generation cephalosporin); FLU (fluoroquinolone); SXT (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); TZP (piperacillin-tazobactam); CAR (carbapenem); CAZ (ceftazidime); CIP (ciprofloxacin); PEN (benzylpenicillin); CLI (clindamycin); MAC (macrolide)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Weekly resistance rate = percentage of resistant antibiogram results out of the total antibiograms (including intermediate results), computed per organism–antibiotic time series.
raw.Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
raw.AI_Purpose: To build a novel, fully data-driven method combining trend extraction (empirical mode decomposition) with a k-nearest-neighbor machine learning forecaster to provide timely short- and medium-term forecasting of antibiotic resistance trends for enhanced biosurveillance systems.
raw.Feature_Engineering: Resistance time series decomposed by EMD into IMF components plus a residue; non-contributing high-frequency components filtered out; remaining components delay-embedded into vectors of dimension m.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Relevant EMD component selection via DECF (frequency threshold — components with cycle < 10 weeks excluded) or DECS (Wu & Huang statistical significance test against the first IMF); optimal embedding dimension m by fractal dimension.
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Leave-one-out cross-validation to determine the number of nearest neighbours k; optimal embedding dimension m determined by the fractal-dimension method (also tested against naive m={3,6,10}).
raw.Baseline_Method: Random walk (RW)
raw.Baseline_Performance: RW 1-week-ahead MAE across the KP/SA series 1.40–10.97 (largest errors of all models; e.g., KP7 10.97, SA6 1.40)
raw.Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation adapted to time-series forecasting
raw.Train_Test_Split: Minimum 350 weeks training; test set of 170 data points.
raw.CV_Folds: Leave-one-out (one future point held out at a time)
raw.Overfitting_Method: Four time series (EC 4, KP 2, PA 5, SA 5) used to determine the optimal embedding dimension were excluded from the final training and test sets to avoid overfitting bias.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The trend extraction and forecasting methodologies make no assumption about the underlying data model, so the authors state the method could be generalized to other time-varying clinical events and readily applied to ward-specific data.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Leave-one-out cross-validation on a decade of weekly resistance time series (internal validation only) — no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Proposed as input to clinical decision support systems for antibiotic prescribing and to outbreak-detection biosurveillance (not deployed).
raw.End_User_Described: Care providers / clinicians (empirical therapy) and infection control groups
raw.Future_Directions: Investigating correlation of other time-dependent clinical factors (e.g., antibiotic consumption) with decomposed resistance trends; combining the forecasting methodology with burst detection models to improve prediction accuracy.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Relative gain in mean absolute error (MAE) from incrementally including higher-frequency EMD components
raw.Limitation_Categories: Ward-level aggregation; limited to resistant pathogens; bursting patterns not testable; irregular (null-containing) time series not investigated
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Data aggregated across wards; time series limited to pathogens with some level of resistance; null-containing (irregular) series not investigated.

raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random 7:3 split of a single-centre cohort into training (n = 91973) and validation (n = 39417) cohorts, with bootstrap resampling (1000 resamples); no external or prospective evaluation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Exclusion of patients with incomplete variables may cause selection bias; single-centre design; external effectiveness and generalizability require multicentre studies.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Retrospective single-centre development and internal validation of a logistic-regression nomogram for CRO infection. Performance is reported only as AUC (training 0.935, validation 0.937) with calibration and decision curves; no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV/F1 figures are given. Class imbalance (CRO 0.49%) is not addressed.
raw.Sample_Size: 131390 hospitalized patients (inpatients): training cohort n = 91973, validation cohort n = 39417
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors report no conflicts of interest relevant to this article.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized patients who received at least one microbial culture during hospitalization.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: (1) Patients with polymicrobial bacteria including MRSA, VRE infections, or invasive fungal disease; (2) patients with any unknown epidemiology and clinical information; (3) age ≤ 18 years.
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Dataset_Size: 131390 inpatients (training n = 91973; validation n = 39417)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case analysis only: patients with unknown epidemiology and clinical information were excluded, and exclusion of patients with incomplete variables is acknowledged as a source of selection bias; no imputation reported.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre (Pudong New Area People’s Hospital, Shanghai, China); no multicentre or non-Chinese data; generalisability to other regions untested.

raw.Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: CRO infection diagnosed according to CDC criteria: positive culture of CRO plus high clinical suspicion from the patient’s clinical symptoms, signs and examination results (e.g. fever patterns, inflammatory markers).

raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 (univariable logistic regression and multivariable logistic regression nomogram)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Age categorised by percentile into <40, 40-62, 63-75 and >75 years; other variables recorded as binary indicators (e.g. temperature above 38 degrees for two days) or as two-level categories (duration of antibiotic therapy <5 vs ≥5 days; length of hospital stay <10 vs ≥10 days).
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate logistic regression screening, then multivariable logistic regression; non-significant variables were not included in the nomogram
raw.Num_Features_Total: 18 candidate predictor variables (the listed variables excluding the CRO infection outcome)
raw.Other_Metrics: AUC (training cohort 0.935; validation cohort 0.937); calibration curve; decision curve analysis (DCA); odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals
raw.Internal_Validation: Random 7:3 split into training (n = 91973) and validation (n = 39417) cohorts; bootstrap with 1000 resamples
raw.Clinical_Insights: The nomogram is built from the 9 independent risk factors; duration of antibiotic therapy (days) was the variable with highest predictive ability for CRO infection, and the tool is intended to flag patients at risk early.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Single-centre Chinese cohort; the authors state that clinical feasibility should be evaluated by assessing external effectiveness and generalizability in multicentre studies.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Random 7:3 internal split with a held-out validation cohort (AUC 0.937 validation vs 0.935 training) and 1000-resample bootstrap; single centre, no external validation and no prospective evaluation.
raw.Integration_Point: Clinician decision-making (no EHR/LIS integration or workflow described)
raw.End_User_Described: clinical doctors
raw.Facilitators_List: All model variables are easily obtained from routine clinical data, which supports clinical applicability
raw.Future_Directions: External effectiveness and generalizability should be assessed in multicentre studies
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Nomogram point scale from the multivariable logistic regression model (individual point values shown only in Fig. 1)
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Temperature above 38 degrees for two days had not previously been reported as a risk factor for CRO infection but was included in the nomogram (and was significant in both univariate and multivariate analysis).
raw.Limitation_Categories: selection bias from excluding patients with incomplete variables; single-centre design; need for external/multicentre validation
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: incomplete variables and unknown epidemiology/clinical information (patients excluded rather than imputed); repeat isolates from the same site excluded and only initial isolates considered
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear for methods, model performance (AUC, calibration, DCA), ethics and limitations; the nomogram point values appear only in Fig. 1 and no accuracy/sensitivity/specificity figures are reported; no reporting guideline named.
raw.Page_References: Key content: title/abstract p. 1; methods pp. 2-3; Tables 1-3 pp. 3-5; nomogram and validation figures pp. 3 and 6; discussion/limitations p. 7; end matter p. 7

studies.title: Accurate prediction of antimicrobial resistance and genetic marker of Staphylococcus aureus clinical isolates using MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning - a cross DRIAMS and Taiwan database

studies.ai_purpose: To compare the efficacy and accuracy of various ML classifiers on MALDI-TOF MS profiles for predicting antimicrobial resistance to tier 1 antibiotics and the mecA genetic marker in clinical S. aureus, and to test transfer learning from a large national database (DRIAMS) to an institutional database (CS)
studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
studies.best_model: LightGBM - highest AUROC/AUPR on the primary (CS) database: oxacillin resistance by agar dilution accuracy/AUROC/AUPR 0.88/0.96/0.97 and mecA existence AUROC/AUPR 0.955/0.963 (Table 1). raw.Title: Accurate prediction of antimicrobial resistance and genetic marker of Staphylococcus aureus clinical isolates using MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning - a cross DRIAMS and Taiwan database
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
raw.Funder_Names: Chung Shan Medical University (grant number: CSMUH No: CS1-23228)
raw.Population_Description: Clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates: 4874 S. aureus (788 ORSA, 4086 OSSA) from DRIAMS and 416 invasive S. aureus isolates (189 ORSA, 227 OSSA) from the CS database (Chung Shan Medical University Hospital), of which 183 (44.0%) were mecA-positive MRSA and 233 (56.0%) mecA-negative MSSA
raw.Data_Source_Other: Public MALDI-TOF MS / antimicrobial susceptibility database (DRIAMS) plus an institutional clinical microbiology database (CS)
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP (Shapley value) top features: 2423-2426 m/z, 4496-4499 m/z and 3764-3767 m/z (top five overlapping features for oxacillin resistance by agar dilution and mecA presence); 2423-2426 m/z among the top three for ERY, CLI, TET and TMP/SMX; 3020-3023 m/z and 4523-4526 m/z (top five for ERY and CLI resistance among ORSA); 7169-7172 m/z (OSSA, ERY and CLI resistance)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: LightGBM; MLP (Multilayer Perceptron); Random Forest; KNN (K Neighbors Classifier); Ada Boost; Logistic Regression; plus a Deep Neural Network (DNN) with transfer learning for crossing databases. Metrics reported: accuracy, AUROC, AUPR. Examples: DRIAMS ORSA - MLP clindamycin AUROC/AUPR 0.81/0.90 and tetracycline 0.87/0.94; LightGBM erythromycin 0.81/0.87 (Supplementary Table 1). CS database ORSA - KNN best except tetracycline (LightGBM better) (Supplementary Table 2). CS database S. aureus with LightGBM - mecA existence 0.878/0.955/0.963; oxacillin resistance (agar dilution) 0.876/0.961/0.969; oxacillin resistance (Vitek 2) 0.845/0.931/0.926 (Table 1). DNN with transfer learning from DRIAMS - oxacillin 0.893/0.891/0.834; clindamycin 0.842/0.781/0.851; erythromycin 0.921/0.818/0.936; tetracycline 0.632/0.639/0.620; TMP/SMX 0.947/0.917/0.886 (Table 2)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: LightGBM - highest AUROC/AUPR on the primary (CS) database: oxacillin resistance by agar dilution accuracy/AUROC/AUPR 0.88/0.96/0.97 and mecA existence AUROC/AUPR 0.955/0.963 (Table 1). The paper also names MLP as superior for most tier 1 antibiotics among ORSA in DRIAMS and KNN for ORSA in the CS database (except tetracycline), so no single model is best across databases
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: S. aureus isolates from the CS database (n = 416); oxacillin resistance determined by agar dilution
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: S. aureus isolates from the CS database (n = 416); oxacillin resistance determined by agar dilution (0.961 in Table 1)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model development with ten-fold cross-validation on the two source databases (each fold used once as the testing set); Table 2 refits the DNN with 60% CS training, 20% validation and 20% prediction. No prospective or routine-clinical evaluation is reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Two databases with distinct phylogenic strains, sample sizes, susceptibility profiles and MALDI-TOF instruments; retrospective datasets used for model development; no standard protocol for MALDI-TOF MS with ML (pre-processing, training, validation, testing); efficacy and speed limited by mass spectra quality and resolution and by noise/variability in small datasets
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethical approval reported from two committees; ML-based resistance prediction is presented as a research tool, with the authors cautioning about comparing performance across models, study designs and datasets
raw.Sample_Size: 4874 S. aureus isolates (788 ORSA, 4086 OSSA) from DRIAMS; 416 invasive S. aureus isolates (189 ORSA, 227 OSSA) from the CS database
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest in relation to this study.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Non-duplicate, clinically invasive S. aureus strains (isolated from sterile sites) collected from September 2018 to August 2021 in the CS database; S. aureus clinical isolates with MALDI-TOF MS profiles from DRIAMS
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Duplicate isolates excluded (only non-duplicate strains were collected)
raw.Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype
raw.Data_Source_Name: DRIAMS (Database of Resistance Information on Antimicrobials and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectra); CS database (Chung Shan Medical University Hospital, Taiwan)
raw.Dataset_Size: DRIAMS: over 300 000 fungal and bacterial MALDI-TOF MS isolates from four laboratories, of which 4874 S. aureus were analysed; CS database: 416 invasive S. aureus isolates
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: DRIAMS isolates come from four clinical microbiology laboratories in Switzerland; the CS database is a single medical centre in central Taiwan. The two-database comparison is transnational but neither sample is population-representative of a defined catchment
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: clinically invasive S. aureus strains (isolated from sterile sites)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antimicrobial resistance of Staphylococcus aureus against tier 1 antibiotics (oxacillin, erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and presence of the mecA gene
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin); macrolides (erythromycin); lincosamides (clindamycin); tetracyclines (tetracycline); folate pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (OX); erythromycin (ERY); clindamycin (CLI); tetracycline (TET); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptible vs intermediate/resistant classification for each tier 1 antibiotic; oxacillin MIC <=2 mg/L classified as OSSA, otherwise ORSA (CLSI); presence/absence of mecA by PCR classified as MRSA and MSSA
raw.AI_Purpose: To compare the efficacy and accuracy of various ML classifiers on MALDI-TOF MS profiles for predicting antimicrobial resistance to tier 1 antibiotics and the mecA genetic marker in clinical S. aureus, and to test transfer learning from a large national database (DRIAMS) to an institutional database (CS)
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 5 ML classifiers compared on the same spectra (Adaboost, MLP, KNN, LightGBM, LR), plus Random Forest and LR described in the methods and a DNN with transfer learning for cross-database prediction
raw.Feature_Engineering: Mass spectra binned into 3 m/z bins from 2000 m/z to 20000 m/z giving a 6000-dimensional vector per sample; variance stabilisation of m/z, smoothing, baseline removal, intensity calibration and trimming; inter-peak distance ratio (IDR) used to refine peak identification
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: No explicit feature selection reported; all binned m/z features (6000-dimensional vector) were used by the models, with SHAP used only to quantify the contribution of individual m/z features
raw.Num_Features_Total: 6000 (3 m/z bins from 2000 to 20000 m/z per sample)
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 6000 (all binned features used); the top 20 impactful features are reported for interpretation via SHAP
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: AUPRC (area under the precision-recall curve) reported alongside AUROC because of the imbalanced nature of the classes; Ada Boost described as adjusting weights of incorrectly classified instances in imbalanced data
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Extensive tuning of model hyperparameters using cross-validation within the training data
raw.Other_Metrics: AUPR (area under precision-recall) reported alongside accuracy and AUROC for every model; no sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, kappa, MCC, RMSE or MAE
raw.Baseline_Method: Comparison with previously published DRIAMS performance for oxacillin resistance (AUROC/AUPR 0.80/0.49) and head-to-head comparison of the ML classifiers within each database
raw.Baseline_Performance: Published DRIAMS oxacillin resistance AUROC/AUPR 0.80/0.49, versus 0.93/0.93 with the Vitek 2-based model in the current study
raw.Internal_Validation: Ten-fold cross-validation: the dataset was split into ten equal parts and each portion served in turn as the testing set; Table 2 used 60% CS training with 20% validation and 20% prediction, and DRIAMS-based fine-tuning
raw.Train_Test_Split: Ten-fold cross-validation (nine portions training, one testing per fold); transfer learning experiment: 60% CS training, 20% CS validation, 20% CS prediction
raw.Overfitting_Method: Increase in sample size for conservative training and layer transfer via transfer learning to avoid overfitting; ten-fold cross-validation and within-training hyperparameter tuning to keep performance consistent with the limited dataset sizes
raw.Clinical_Insights: Overlapping m/z features (2423-2426, 4496-4499 and 3764-3767 m/z) predict both mecA presence and oxacillin resistance, and 2423-2426 m/z also contributes to resistance prediction for ERY, CLI, TET and TMP/SMX; grouped features outperform single peaks such as 2415 +/- 2.00 m/z, which only predicts PSM-mec
raw.Generalisability_Details: Performance depends on database characteristics and the ML algorithm; differences in phylogenic strains, sample size, susceptibility profiles, MALDI-TOF instruments and technical variability explain the divergent predictive contributions; transfer learning from DRIAMS improved ERY, CLI and TET prediction in the CS database but not OX or TMP/SMX
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Ten-fold cross-validation on the source databases is the only validation performed; the transfer-learning model is evaluated on held-out CS data (20%). No prospective use or clinical deployment is reported
raw.End_User_Described: Not explicitly described; the work is framed as expanding the scope of clinical microbiology (species identification plus resistance and genetic-marker prediction)
raw.Barriers_List: Two databases with distinct phylogenic strains, sample sizes, susceptibility profiles and MALDI-TOF instruments; retrospective model development; absence of a standard protocol for MALDI-TOF MS with ML; data quality/resolution, noise and variability limiting efficacy and speed of algorithms
raw.Facilitators_List: A large-scale transnational source database (DRIAMS) that improves ERY, CLI and TET prediction through transfer learning; grouped MALDI-TOF features as robust predictive markers; precision-recall and AUROC metrics for imbalanced classes
raw.Future_Directions: Future studies should focus on optimising data quality and developing more efficient algorithms to balance the trade-offs between resolution, computational complexity, and predictive performance
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP - Shapley additive explanations values (Shapley value) quantifying the individual contribution of each m/z bin
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Overlapping m/z features 2423-2426, 4496-4499 and 3764-3767 were among the top five for predicting oxacillin resistance (agar dilution) and mecA presence, and 2423-2426 m/z was among the top three features for the other four tier 1 antibiotics; no overlapping feature was found for DRIAMS
raw.Limitation_Categories: Database heterogeneity (strains, sample size, susceptibility profiles, MALDI-TOF instrument); retrospective design; no standard MALDI-TOF+ML protocol; data quality and resolution; small dataset size and noise
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Mass spectra quality and resolution, noise and variability especially in smaller datasets, instrument calibration, sample preparation and pre-processing all affect predictive efficacy and speed
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Main text reports accuracy/AUROC/AUPR per model, group and database for the LightGBM/DNN analyses; the per-antibiotic results for the five ML classifiers and the bin-size analyses are in Supplementary Tables 1-4, which are not part of the PDF text layer
