raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of chest X-ray images into five classes - TB-negative (non-TB), drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB), drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) - with a recommended treatment regimen returned by the TB-DRC-DSS.
raw.Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis (anti-TB) drugs; no specific agent or drug class is named - the paper refers to the recommended TB treatment regimen that the pharmacist updates.
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: The label of each CXR image is the patient's drug-susceptibility category obtained from drug susceptibility testing (not read off the image): binary DS-TB vs DR-TB pairs and the MDR-TB and XDR-TB resistance categories.
raw.AI_Purpose: Detect TB and classify the drug-resistance category from a chest X-ray image, and provide treatment recommendations, through the TB-DRC-DSS decision support system.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 12 proposed models (N-1 to N-12) compared with one another, plus performance compared against 13 published methods from the literature
raw.Feature_Engineering: Lung-field image segmentation with a modified U-Net (EfficientNetB7 encoder), image augmentation, cropping, normalisation and enhancement of the CXR images before the three heterogeneous CNNs, followed by UWA / AMIS-WCE / AMIS-WLCE decision fusion of the CNN outputs.
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: AMIS metaheuristic used to find the optimal decision-fusion weights (Wi and Sij); fixed training settings of batch sizes 16 (MobileNetV2), 2 (EfficientNetB7) and 8 (DenseNet121), 200 epochs and the Adam algorithm
raw.Software_Libraries: TensorFlow; HTML and JavaScript for the web application; CNN architectures MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB7, DenseNet121 and a modified U-Net with EfficientNetB7 encoder
raw.Other_Metrics: Confusion matrices (Figure 1); per-class accuracy (non-TB 98.99%, DS-TB 92.2%, DR-TB 97.1%, MDR-TB 88.7%, XDR-TB 91.1%); average percentage difference versus prior methods (Table 4); TB-DRC-DSS per-class % correct classification (Table 8); six-item user agreement questionnaire scored out of 10 (Table 9).
raw.Baseline_Method: Published single-architecture and feature-based comparators (VGG16, ResNet50, EfficientNet, MobileNetv2, FuseNet, MAG-SD, CoroNet, TBXNet) and prior drug-resistance models (Karki et al. ResNet18, Tulo et al. mediastinal shape, Jaeger et al. texture/shape/edge, Kovalev et al., Ureta and Shrestha CNN)
raw.Baseline_Performance: Portal dataset, DS vs DR: best prior AUC 93.6 (Tulo et al.) and 79.0 (Karki et al.) vs proposed 97.2 AUC / 95.2 accuracy. Dataset A: best comparator TBXNet 98.9 vs proposed 99.4; Dataset B: TBXNet 99.2 vs proposed 99.3; Dataset C: TBXNet 95.1 vs proposed 97.4.
raw.Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation on the 5,606-image training set, with a separate 1,408-image (20%) held-out test set for final evaluation
raw.Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test (5,606 training images, 1,408 test images)
raw.Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers in the modified U-Net decoder to improve generalisation and prevent over-fitting; residual blocks to avoid vanishing gradients; data augmentation
raw.Clinical_Insights: The Grad-CAM heatmaps show which lung sectors drive each class: non-TB uses all six lung areas, DS-TB the lung interior from top to bottom, DR-TB the upper left and right sectors, and MDR-TB and XDR-TB the lower and upper left/right sectors, with MDR-TB using the inner and XDR-TB the outer portion of the lung.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Performance is compared across datasets from different sources and countries (Dataset A: Montgomery County and Shenzhen; Dataset B: Belarus; Dataset C: Kaggle), but there is no discussion of applicability to other patient populations or settings.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: five-fold cross-validation of the 5,606-image training set and a held-out 1,408-image test set; the model was then embedded in the TB-DRC-DSS web application, tested on 428 images drawn at random from the test dataset and rated by 31 medical staff. No external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported.
raw.Integration_Point: TB-DRC-DSS web application: the user uploads a CXR image, the deep learning model predicts the disease type, and the system returns medication recommendations for that disease
raw.End_User_Described: Physicians who are TB specialists (pulmonologists and internal medicine); the pharmacist administers the TB-DRC-DSS and updates the treatment regimen prescribed to the physician
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Medical staff upload CXR image files from their personal computers; the image is forwarded to a server that diagnoses the disease and suggests appropriate drugs and medications; the pharmacist updates the treatment regimen; the recommendation is sent back to the user.
raw.Future_Directions: Three research gaps: (1) develop a more accurate model for multiclass drug-resistant classification and TB detection (better image segmentation, augmentation and normalisation, and denoising); (2) extend the web application to support therapy follow-up and further decisions based on the recommended protocol; (3) let the pharmacist follow WHO treatment regimens, record the patient's drug reaction and use data mining to adapt the regimen as resistance emerges.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Grad-CAM (GradCAM heatmap visualisations on the X-ray images)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Accuracy ceiling (classification is not 100% accurate) and scope for better image preprocessing (segmentation, augmentation, normalisation, denoising); web application lacks therapy follow-up and downstream decision support; regimens must be updated as treatment resistance emerges, requiring WHO-conformant pharmacist input and data mining of patient drug reactions.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Drug-susceptibility labels associated with each image are not produced from the image itself but obtained through drug susceptibility testing, and the analysis pools heterogeneous public datasets from different countries and institutions.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Generally clear, with minor internal inconsistencies: Table 9 is headed '30 doctors' while the text and abstract report 31 medical staff, and the 'Total' row of Table 8 sums the percentage columns to 463.8% and 36.2%.

studies.title: Development of Predictive Models to Inform a Novel Risk Categorization Framework for Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli–Caused Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection

raw.Title: Development of Predictive Models to Inform a Novel Risk Categorization Framework for Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli–Caused Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection
raw.Journal_Source: Clinical Infectious Diseases (CID), Infectious Diseases Society of America; volume 79, issue 2, pp. 295–304
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
raw.Funder_Names: GSK
raw.Population_Description: Female patients aged ≥12 years with a UTI diagnosis (no evidence of complicated UTI) and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of diagnosis; enrollees also needed documented pyuria and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result for at least 1 agent in the 4 antibiotic classes of interest.
raw.Age_Mean_Median: Mean age ranged from 49.7 to 50.4 years across the training and test cohorts for each antibiotic class
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Top predictors by absolute standardized log odds ratio: race; number of previous UTI episodes (recurrence); US Census Bureau region (particularly residence in the South); prior nonsusceptibility to β-lactams; prior treatment with fluoroquinolones.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: LASSO models (per antibiotic class; the paper's optimal algorithm, test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72); random forest algorithms (compared against LASSO via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation, not selected as optimal); 4 final logistic regression models built on the union of the top 10 LASSO predictors — mean (SE) test-cohort AUROC 0.67 (0.010) for NTF, 0.66 (0.004) for SXT, 0.66 (0.005) for β-lactams, 0.72 (0.005) for fluoroquinolones.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) predictive models — named the optimal predictive algorithm across all 4 antibiotic classes on mean AUROC and clinical interpretability; test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Test cohorts (temporal validation); LASSO predictive models for nonsusceptibility to each of the 4 antibiotic classes
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were internally bootstrapped and temporally validated in the test cohorts of the same EHR dataset (training 1 October 2016–31 December 2018; test 1 January 2019–29 February 2020). No external validation was performed; the authors call for validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations, so the highest level supported is internal validation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: 1) Models and framework are not a decision algorithm recommending optimal antibiotic treatment; 2) population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates could not be included because the data were unavailable (Census Bureau region used as a proxy); 3) models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, limiting generalisability to diverse US populations; 4) models were anchored on the date of the susceptibility test result rather than the uUTI diagnosis date.
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race was identified as a predictor of nonsusceptibility and the authors note it should not be given a causal interpretation or used alone to inform treatment decisions, because it correlates with socioeconomic indicators that were not available in the data.
raw.Sample_Size: 87 487 patients with confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test results (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: R. K. S. is a paid consultant to GSK. W. Y. C., K. K.-S., D. I., F. K., C. G., M. M., L. P., and J. R. are employees of Analysis Group, Inc., a consultancy that received funding from GSK to conduct this study. A. V. J., F. S. M.-G., P. S., D. F., M. T. P., and J. H. are employees of and shareholders in GSK. R. C. has served as a paid consultant to GSK.
raw.Sex_Distribution: All female (study population restricted to female patients ≥12 years)
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Female patients ≥12 years of age with a diagnosis of UTI, without evidence of complicated UTI, and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis; documentation of pyuria within ±7 days of diagnosis; and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result of the urinary E. coli isolate for at least 1 agent within the 4 antibiotic classes of interest within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Evidence of complicated UTI
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: Optum's de-identified Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset
raw.Dataset_Size: 87 487 patients (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), assuming data were missing at random; results were largely consistent using MICE versus a complete case analysis.
raw.Ethnicity_Details: Race distribution reported as 85.1%–85.5% White across training and test cohorts (model predictor categories: White [ref.], Black, Asian, Other/unknown); ethnicity (e.g. Hispanic/Latino) is not separately reported.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Patients were mostly from the Midwest (63.8%–66.3%) and mostly White, across US Census Bureau regions; US-only data, so generalisability to other populations is limited.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: urine culture; urinary E. coli isolate
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Nonsusceptibility (intermediate or resistant) of the patient's urinary E. coli isolate to each of 4 antibiotic classes: NTF, SXT, β-lactams, and fluoroquinolones (4 separate endpoints/models).
raw.Drug_Classes: Nitrofurantoin (nitrofuran); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (folate-pathway inhibitor); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Nitrofurantoin (NTF); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones; fosfomycin is mentioned only as another first-line guideline option.
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Nonsusceptibility at the class level was defined by a urinary E. coli isolate categorized as “intermediate” or “resistant” to at least 1 of the respective antibiotic agent(s) within each class based on susceptibility test results.
raw.AI_Purpose: To develop and validate predictive models estimating the probability that a female patient's urinary E. coli isolate is nonsusceptible to each of 4 antibiotic classes for uUTI, to identify key predictors of nonsusceptibility, and to build a novel risk categorization framework (low/moderate/high risk) to inform empiric prescribing.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithm types compared (LASSO and random forest) via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation; 8 fitted models in total (4 LASSO models and 4 final logistic regression models, one per antibiotic class)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Candidate features (demographics, clinical characteristics, microbiology-related characteristics) were evaluated over a 12-month lookback period prior to the susceptibility test result date; Table 3 footnotes show window-based derivations (e.g. previous UTI episodes excluding the uUTI diagnosis date; antibiotic treatment from 6 months prior to 3 days preceding diagnosis; counts of oral antibiotic prescriptions and ED visits).
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO, with the top 10 predictors per class ranked by absolute standardized log odds ratio; the union of the top 10 predictors across the 4 LASSO models (22 features) was used in the final logistic regression models.
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 22 features for each final logistic regression model (union of the top 10 predictors from the 4 LASSO models)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation used to select the optimal algorithm (LASSO vs random forest); LASSO models fitted in the training cohort with internal bootstrap validation.
raw.Software_Libraries: SAS (version 9.4, SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina) and Python (version 3.9); no specific libraries named
raw.Other_Metrics: AUROC with standard error; predicted probability distributions (mean/SD, median/IQR, min–max) versus observed nonsusceptibility rates; calibration (mean calibration and calibration plots); odds ratios with 95% CIs and P values; proportions of patients in each risk category.
raw.Baseline_Method: Previously published predictive models for antibiotic nonsusceptibility in uUTI (reference 17); US prevalence of nonsusceptibility to each antibiotic class is used as the comparator for the risk categories.
raw.Internal_Validation: Internal bootstrap validation of the LASSO models in the training cohort (mean AUROC and SE); temporal validation in the test cohorts with the SE of the AUROC derived using 200 bootstrapping samples; model selection by (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation.
raw.Train_Test_Split: Temporal split: susceptibility test result date 1 October 2016–31 December 2018 = training cohort; 1 January 2019–29 February 2020 = test cohort.
raw.Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
raw.Clinical_Insights: The risk categorization framework separates risk better than US prevalence alone: a patient's probability of a truly nonsusceptible SXT isolate rises to 53.9% if their isolate is categorized high risk and falls to 15.3% if low risk, versus a 25.4% baseline prevalence; the proportion of patients with high-risk isolates was 3- to 12-fold higher among those with truly nonsusceptible isolates.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, with E. coli–caused uUTI, which may limit applicability to diverse US populations and to uUTI caused by other uropathogens; race and Census Bureau region were retained as predictors to improve external validity; future validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations is proposed.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal bootstrap validation in the training cohort and temporal validation in the test cohorts (same Optum EHR dataset, different time periods); no external or prospective validation is reported.
raw.Integration_Point: Not integrated; proposed future integration into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool that would present patients' predicted probabilities and risk profiles to clinicians.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians treating uUTI (to inform empiric prescribing)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians would derive an isolate's predicted probabilities of nonsusceptibility to the 4 antibiotic classes, generate risk profiles, and integrate the framework into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool to assist empiric treatment decisions; the models are not a decision algorithm.
raw.Barriers_List: Models are not a decision algorithm; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were unavailable; models developed among mostly White patients from the Midwest (limited generalisability); predictions anchored on the susceptibility test result date rather than the uUTI diagnosis date; race cannot be interpreted causally or used alone for treatment decisions.
raw.Facilitators_List: First evaluation of nonsusceptibility to 4 commonly prescribed antibiotic classes for uUTI in the US using a large rich EHR database; features identified from a comprehensive literature search plus clinical expert input; two complementary approaches (predictive models with temporal validity and a risk categorization framework).
raw.Future_Directions: Validate the models in different clinical settings and in ex-US populations, and recalibrate them to include population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates; use the models and framework to develop a data visualization tool integrated into clinical workflows.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Absolute standardized log odds ratio from the LASSO models (top 10 predictors per model, combined across models).
raw.Limitation_Categories: Framing/scope (not a decision algorithm); missing data on population-level features (local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates); population representativeness / generalisability (mostly White, Midwest, E. coli only); timing of the prediction anchor (susceptibility test result date vs uUTI diagnosis date); race cannot be interpreted causally and socioeconomic indicators were unavailable.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing information on candidate features was limited and results were largely consistent using MICE versus complete case analysis; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were not available in the data source.
raw.Page_References: Article pp. 295–304 (CID 2024;79(2)); abstract p. 295; methods pp. 296–297 (data source, population, endpoints, model development); results pp. 297–301 (final model performance Table 2 p. 299; predictor log ORs Table 3 pp. 300–301); limitations pp. 302–303; conclusions pp. 303–304. Page 11 is a pharmaceutical advertisement, not part of the article.

raw.Title: Development a risk prediction nomogram for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in gastrointestinal fistula patients during the perioperative period
raw.Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
raw.Funder_Names: Anhui Provincial Department of Education institutions key scientific research project (2023AH053380, 2022AH052319); Health Commission of Anhui Province Key Scientific Research projects (AHWJ2022a026); Jiangsu Provincial Department of Science and Technology key research and development projects (BE2021727)
raw.Population_Description: 266 hospitalised patients with gastrointestinal fistulas who underwent surgical treatment at Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital (Jan 2022-Jul 2024); 157 (59.02%) tested positive for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection and 109 (40.98%) tested negative; the 266 cases were randomly split 2:1 into a training cohort (n=177) and a validation cohort (n=89).
raw.Age_Mean_Median: 56.23 ± 16.02 years (training cohort, n=177); 55.22 ± 15.77 years (validation cohort, n=89)
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Nomogram points assigned to the six independent predictors: preoperative neutrophil level 100 points (highest), preoperative WBC level 92.1 points, postoperative WBC count 34.2 points, secondary surgery 30.3 points, length of hospital stay 20.3 points, postoperative CRP level 13.8 points.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: One model was developed and evaluated: a nomogram built from multivariable logistic regression with six independent predictors (secondary surgery, length of hospital stay, preoperative WBC, preoperative neutrophil count, postoperative WBC, postoperative CRP). Reported performance - AUC 0.905 (95% CI 0.864-0.947) in the training cohort and 0.793 (0.690-0.896) in the validation cohort; accuracy 0.825/0.693; sensitivity 0.889/0.692; specificity 0.781/0.694; PPV 0.736/0.545; NPV 0.911/0.810; Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.970 (training) and 0.674 (validation). No comparator models were evaluated.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Nomogram based on multivariable logistic regression (the only model developed and evaluated; decision metric = AUC 0.905 in the training cohort and 0.793 in the validation cohort)
raw.Accuracy_Value: 0.825 (training cohort); 0.693 (validation cohort)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was developed on a training cohort and evaluated on a validation cohort created by randomly splitting the same 266 single-centre patients 2:1, with discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow) and DCA reported for both. No external cohort and no prospective evaluation: the authors state further prospective studies are necessary before widespread clinical application, so the highest level the evidence supports is internal validation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Retrospective single-centre design subject to some degree of selection bias; limited number of case observations from a small sample size and a single centre; further prospective studies needed to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; antibiotic use was not included as a factor because of the complexity of antibiotic-therapy information (many patients had already received antibiotics before transfer).
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval by the medical ethics committee of Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital; study conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki with written informed consent from all participants; the paper declares no generative-AI use. No AI-specific governance, deployment or monitoring risk discussion.
raw.Sample_Size: 266 patients with gastrointestinal fistulas (157 multidrug-resistant-positive, 109 negative); 329 pathogenic strains isolated
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
raw.Sex_Distribution: Training cohort (n=177): female 79, male 98. Validation cohort (n=89): female 41, male 48.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: (1) Diagnosis of gastrointestinal fistula: any discharge from the gastrointestinal tract, which may include abdominal abscesses or spontaneous drainage through a stoma; (2) undergoing surgical treatment during hospitalisation; (3) perioperative cultures of sputum, blood, pus, bile, etc. indicating infections with multidrug-resistant bacteria and fungi; (4) diagnosis of multidrug-resistant bacteria defined as bacteria resistant to three or more commonly used antimicrobial agents that are typically sensitive.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: (1) Patients with gastrointestinal fistulas who did not receive surgical treatment; (2) patients who died within 24 hours post-surgery or were discharged.

raw.Dataset_Size: 266 patients with gastrointestinal fistulas; 329 pathogenic strains isolated (84 Gram-positive, 215 Gram-negative, 30 fungal)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Indicators with more than 20% missing values were discarded before the multivariable analysis (this is why preoperative PCT and CRP were excluded from the multivariate model).
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre study: all 266 patients were enrolled at Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital, Hefei, China; the authors acknowledge a small sample size from a single centre, and there is no external or geographically distinct validation cohort.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Perioperative cultures of sputum, blood, pus, bile; resistant strains came from blood (26%), drainage (17%), sputum (15%), pus (14%) and conductor housings (12%)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas during the perioperative period (positive perioperative cultures; 157/266 patients, 59.02%)

raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Multidrug resistance is defined as bacteria that exhibit resistance to three or more commonly used antimicrobial agents that are typically sensitive; the study outcome is a positive perioperative culture (sputum, blood, pus, bile, etc.) for multidrug-resistant bacteria or fungi, with resistance mechanisms (CRE, ESBL, CR-PA, CR-AB) and per-antibiotic resistance rates reported separately.
raw.AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a risk-prediction nomogram for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas during the perioperative period, so that clinicians can assess infection risk before surgery and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single nomogram based on multivariable logistic regression; no comparator models were developed or benchmarked)
raw.Feature_Engineering: No engineered transformations reported: 37 candidate indicators were taken directly from the hospital information system (surgical characteristics, comorbidity, clinical outcome, ICU and hospital stay, and preoperative/postoperative laboratory values) and screened by univariate then multivariable logistic regression; 'postoperative' was defined as the most recent test at the specimen that indicated multidrug-resistant bacteria or fungal infection, or results 5-10 days post-surgery if there was no such infection.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate logistic regression screening followed by variable selection in a multivariable logistic regression model
raw.Num_Features_Total: 37 clinical indicators (training cohort)
raw.Software_Libraries: R packages: regplot (nomogram), pROC (ROC curve/AUC), rmda (decision curve analysis)

raw.Internal_Validation: The 266 included cases were randomly divided 2:1 into a training cohort (n=177) for model development and a validation cohort (n=89) for assessing predictive performance; discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test) and decision curve analysis were reported for both cohorts.
raw.Train_Test_Split: Random 2:1 split; training cohort n=177, validation cohort n=89
raw.Clinical_Insights: The authors read the nomogram weights clinically: secondary surgery (reoperation) is a considerable setback that heralds adverse clinical outcomes and is itself an independent risk factor; prolonged hospital and ICU stays create a favourable environment for multidrug-resistant organisms; preoperative WBC/neutrophil and postoperative WBC levels reflect systemic inflammatory status; and postoperative CRP is an independent risk factor, so the model informs targeted infection prevention and rational antibiotic use.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors state that although the study was divided into training and validation cohorts, further prospective studies are necessary to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; the small single-centre sample also limits generalisability.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Evidence for the level: 2:1 random split of the 266 single-centre patients into training (n=177) and validation (n=89) cohorts, with AUC 0.905 (training) and 0.793 (validation), Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.970 and 0.674, and DCA in both cohorts. No external validation, no prospective evaluation, no CDS integration - internal validation only.
raw.Integration_Point: Perioperative risk assessment of patients with gastrointestinal fistulas requiring surgery, to identify those at high risk of multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.
raw.End_User_Described: healthcare providers / clinicians
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Limited: the nomogram is proposed for use during the perioperative period to assess the risk of multidrug-resistant infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas requiring surgery and to support targeted infection prevention strategies and selection of antibiotics based on drug-sensitivity results; no workflow, pathway or integration detail is given.
raw.Future_Directions: Prospective randomised controlled studies are planned for further exploration; prospective studies are needed to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; antibiotic use should be incorporated in future analyses.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Nomogram points assigned from the multivariable logistic regression model (each independent risk factor given a specific weight in points, preoperative neutrophil level highest at 100 points)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Study design / setting (retrospective, single centre, selection bias, small sample); absence of prospective validation before clinical application; missing predictor data (antibiotic use not analysed because of complexity, preoperative PCT/CRP excluded for missingness).
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: A certain proportion of preoperative PCT and CRP values were missing, so these indicators were excluded from the multivariable analysis; antibiotic-use data were incomplete/too complex to analyse because many patients had already received antibiotics before transfer; indicators with more than 20% missing values were discarded.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear and internally consistent for design, cohort flow, predictors and model performance, with AUC, calibration and DCA all reported; values differ between the abstract/Table 7 (AUC 0.905/0.793) and the results text (AUC 0.92/0.78), and the text layer carries kerning artefacts (e.g. 'preoperat i v eW B Cl e v e l'), but no ambiguity in the reported figures.
raw.Page_References: PDF pages 1-15 (article text pp. 1-14; reference list on p. 15)

raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables; Microscopy images
raw.Dataset_Size: >800 images from 150 P. mirabilis isolates
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates came from patients at one institution in Isfahan, Iran; representativeness beyond this setting is not discussed.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Catheters from patients diagnosed with catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs)/UTIs; Gram-stained smears of the isolates
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary classification of P. mirabilis isolates as antibiotic-resistant (with strong biofilm formation) vs sensitive (with weak biofilm formation) from microscopic image radiomics features.
raw.Pathogens: Proteus mirabilis (Escherichia coli K12 and Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853 used as biofilm assay control strains)
raw.Drug_Classes: Penicillins; beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations; carbapenems; cephalosporins; monobactams; aminoglycosides; fluoroquinolones; folate pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); tetracyclines; nitrofurans
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: ampicillin-sulbactam, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, ampicillin, meropenem, cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-clavulanic acid, cefixime, aztreonam, amikacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (plus tetracycline and nitrofurantoin in the susceptibility results)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; ESBL
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Isolates grouped as resistant (strongly biofilm-forming) vs sensitive (weakly biofilm-forming); per-drug resistance by CLSI breakpoints; MDR defined as resistance to at least one agent in >=3 antimicrobial classes (Magiorakos et al.); ESBL detected by double-disc diffusion synergy test.
raw.AI_Purpose: To assess ML algorithms that classify P. mirabilis isolates as antibiotic-resistant or sensitive using radiomics features extracted from simple light-microscopy images of Gram-stained bacteria.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 7 (KNN, DT, NB, LR, SVM, MLP, RF)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Image preprocessing (convolutional-autoencoder denoising, RAVEL normalisation, manual ROI masks in 3D Slicer) followed by radiomics feature extraction: first-order statistics, shape-based, texture-based (GLCM, GLDM, GLRLM, GLSZM, NGTDM), intensity-based and wavelet-based features.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator)
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: No explicit resampling; the authors argue RF's bootstrapped samples and random feature subsets mitigate class imbalance
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: KNN n_neighbors tuned by comparing accuracy; n_neighbors = 6 selected
raw.Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (including its 'metrics' subpackage); 3D Slicer Radiomics extension (v.4.11)
raw.Hardware_Details: Canon (EOS R5) camera mounted on a light microscope; aperture f/16, exposure time 1/60, ISO 100
raw.Other_Metrics: Confusion matrix and ROC curves; area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) as summary measure
raw.Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation within the training set; 20 % hold-out test set
raw.Overfitting_Method: 5-fold cross-validation to mitigate overfitting; LASSO feature selection to remove irrelevant/intercorrelated features
raw.Clinical_Insights: Authors hypothesise that membrane modifications (lipopolysaccharide changes, efflux pumps) in resistant P. mirabilis alter Gram-stain dye uptake, producing the radiomics differences exploited by the model.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Small image number may limit generalisability; high bacterial density in images (more magnified images might improve performance); simple microscopy gives limited spatial, temporal and contextual information.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Only internal validation: 20 % hold-out test set and 5-fold cross-validation on the same 150-isolate image dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment described.
raw.Integration_Point: None described; the model is proposed as a rapid laboratory classification of microscopic images of Gram-stained isolates rather than an integrated clinical system.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians, for predicting antibiotic resistance and personalising treatment
raw.Barriers_List: Small number of images limiting generalisability; high bacterial density in the images; limited spatial, temporal and contextual information from simple microscopy; variability and artifacts from sample preparation and image acquisition.
raw.Facilitators_List: Light microscopy: minimal sample preparation, reduced experimental time and cost, broader accessibility; non-destructive repeated imaging; imaging under near-physiological conditions.
raw.Future_Directions: Use more magnified microscopic images; uncover the biological mechanisms driving the wavelet-feature/resistance correlation; extend to enhance applicability and precision of ML-based resistance classification.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) coefficients
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Wavelet-transformed radiomics features (mainly GLSZM, GLDM and first-order features) were the most informative for resistance classification — a novel finding for microscopy-image-based resistance prediction.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Sample size / image count; image characteristics (bacterial density, magnification); inherent limits of simple microscopy; sample preparation and acquisition variability/artifacts.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Variability and artifacts from sample preparation and image acquisition could affect reliability and reproducibility, mitigated by using a bacteriologist to discern staining artifacts and standardised protocols.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Methods reported in detail; all seven algorithms compared with a full metric table (Table 1); the extracted feature list is deferred to Supplementary 1.

raw.Title: Predictive phage therapy for Escherichia coli urinary tract infections: Cocktail selection for therapy based on machine learning models
raw.Journal_Source: PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), 2024, Vol. 121, No. 12, e2313574121
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
raw.Funder_Names: Canine Welfare Grant from The Dog's Trust; National Council of Science and Technology of Mexico (CONACYT); University of Edinburgh; University of Glasgow; Roslin Institute PhD studentship supported by the BBSRC
raw.Population_Description: 314 uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) strains from urinary tract infections in canine (n = 203) and human (n = 111) patients in the Edinburgh area (human urine n = 81 and human blood n = 30 isolates), whole genome sequenced; a further 10 newly isolated clinical strains were held back for validation
raw.Data_Source_Other: Study-generated interaction dataset: 314 sequenced E. coli isolates challenged with 31 phage in artificial urine growth assays (plus Illumina whole genome sequences)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: 31 Random Forest regression models (one per phage, MUVR package, recursive feature reduction); average RMSE 8-23 across models (interaction score range 0-100); classifier metrics at a threshold of 60 with F1 highest for the generalist phage CHAP1 (0.83)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest ML model for the generalist phage CHAP1 (highest F1 = 0.83; F1 chosen as the performance metric)
raw.F1_Population_Set: 301 of the 314 isolates, used for model training and testing; one 75-25 split with 10-fold cross-validation
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest evidence level is external validation: models trained on 301 of the 314 isolates were applied to 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains not in the training set, and predicted bespoke cocktails were compared with observed bespoke cocktails and a general cocktail in artificial urine and canine urine
raw.Reported_Limitations: Proof-of-principle study with a single species (E. coli) and 31 phage; artificial urine cannot reproduce the variability of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host factors); most genomic features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so receptor and resistance mechanisms cannot be dissected; a high rate of False Negatives can leave too few phage predicted active for cocktail design; feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples untested; wider adoption requires changes in licensing and management of expectations
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False Negatives are preferred to False Positives from a cocktail perspective, but a high False Negative rate can leave a paucity of phage predicted as active; antagonism was seen where a general cocktail scored higher (worse) than its best constituent phage, and bacterial resistance evolved against the general cocktail for some strains
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: ML models replicate biases in their training datasets (illustrated by phage A01, whose imbalanced dataset produced a model prone to False Negatives), and accuracy falls when models are applied to strains from a different population structure
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Safety and registration issues for predictive phage therapy, and licensing plus management of expectations of clinicians and the public
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Extra review notes: (a) the study's unit of analysis is one Random Forest model per phage, so the best model is taken as CHAP1 (F1 = 0.83, the highest and the one the paper highlights); (b) the paper reports no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, AUROC, NPV, AUPRC, kappa, MCC, MAE or calibration figures in the article text - recall and precision values live in SI Appendix Fig. S2, which is not in the PDF; (c) no antimicrobial susceptibility testing, no patient-level clinical data and no environmental/SES variables are used; (d) no compute hardware is described
raw.Unresolved_Items: Numeric recall and precision for the CHAP1 model are in SI Appendix Fig. S2 and per-model RMSE in SI Appendix Table S2 - not available in the article PDF, so Sensitivity_Reported/Precision_PPV_Reported are answered No per the spec note; the number of protein-variant features in the initial model is never stated; whether the Supplementary-Materials field means 'the study has SI' or 'the extractor used SI' is ambiguous
raw.Sample_Size: 314 E. coli isolates (203 canine, 81 human urine and 30 human blood); 301 of the 314 used for ML model training and testing after filtering fragmented assemblies
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interest.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: E. coli isolates from canine and human urinary tract infections (plus human bacteraemia blood isolates) that were whole genome sequenced; for the ML analysis, isolates whose assemblies were not fragmented (<600 contigs), giving 301 of the 314 isolates
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates with fragmented assemblies (>=600 contigs) were excluded from ML model training and testing, leaving 301 of the 314 isolates
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: Enterobase (workspace:97040, ecoli_train); Illumina sequencing by MicrobesNG
raw.Dataset_Size: 31 phage x 314 isolates (>9,000 interactions, each in triplicate against a no-phage control); >27,000 growth curves in total
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Strains were collected from canine and human patients presenting at local clinics in the Edinburgh area only; the authors describe the collection as representative subpopulations rather than a geographically comprehensive sample of UPEC
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: urine (E. coli isolated from canine and human urinary tract infections) and blood (human bacteraemia isolates)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phage activity (phage susceptibility) of each E. coli isolate, quantified as an interaction score: the ratio of the area under the growth curve with phage to that of the no-phage control x 100
raw.Drug_Classes: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins (named as first-line UTI antibiotics in humans and pets; background, not modelled)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; fluoroquinolones; cephalosporins (background only; no antimicrobial susceptibility testing performed)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary Infection/No Infection label from the measured and predicted interaction scores at a threshold of 60: score <60 = infection (active interaction), score >60 = no infection
raw.AI_Purpose: To train ML models on bacterial whole genome sequence features to predict phage activity against individual E. coli isolates, so that effective phage cocktails can be selected without manual screening
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 31 (one Random Forest model per phage)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Pangenome analysis (panaroo v1.2.9) of the 301 bacterial sequences to define predicted genes as protein variants (PVs), encoded as binary presence/absence vectors for each isolate
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive feature reduction using the MUVR package: an initial model with all PVs, then top-ranking features retained to build a smaller model, repeating while RMSE stayed similar
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: F1 chosen as the performance metric to account for class imbalance; imbalanced interaction datasets (up to 85:15) were investigated for model bias via confusion matrices; a predefined F1 cutoff of 0.6 used for practical selection
raw.Software_Libraries: MUVR (random forest regression and feature reduction); panaroo (v1.2.9); prokka (v1.14.5); gplots (v3.1.3); Enterobase Tool Kit (EToKi); SkanIt Software (Thermo); PRISM (GraphPad)
raw.Other_Metrics: RMSE (score prediction); F1, recall and precision (classification at threshold 60); False Positive and False Negative counts for the CHAP1 model (7% FN, 10.8% FP); paired t tests with P values for cocktail comparisons
raw.Internal_Validation: One 75-25 training/testing split with 10-fold cross-validation (MUVR)
raw.External_Validation_Description: 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains (3 canine and 7 human) not used in model training were genome sequenced and run through the models; predicted and observed bespoke cocktails were then tested in artificial urine and canine urine
raw.Generalisability_Details: Models should hold within a similar population structure to the training set but accuracy falls on strains from different population structures; the strain collection covers local canine and human UPEC isolates only, and more generalist phage are needed to make cocktail selection broadly applicable
raw.Maturity_Evidence: External validation on 10 independent sequenced clinical isolates: predicted bespoke cocktails were more effective than a generic cocktail and comparable to bespoke cocktails built from measured activity
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical laboratory diagnostic sequencing: isolate genome sequence is fed to the models to select phage cocktails for the patient
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians (human and veterinary) and the general public as recipients of phage therapy; expectations of both must be managed
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Direct sequencing of nucleic acids from clinical samples (e.g. urine) gives the bacterial genome, which is run through the phage ML models to predict active phage and build a bespoke cocktail, with the interaction dataset continually reinforced by new observations
raw.Barriers_List: Artificial urine cannot capture the complexity of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host response); most genomic features are unannotated grouped genes; class imbalance limits model reliability for narrow-host-range phage; feature extraction from long-read/mixed samples untested; licensing and expectation management needed for clinical adoption
raw.Facilitators_List: High-throughput interaction platforms (e.g. 50 x 96-well plates) can generate the required training datasets quickly; direct sequencing of clinical samples already works for E. coli in canine urine; generalist phage with higher activity increase model reliability and cocktail options
raw.Future_Directions: Include more generalist phage in interaction datasets and prefer phage targeting at least 30% of the population (class imbalance below 85:15); combine associative and function-based features in future phage selection pipelines; test feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples; continually reinforce the learning dataset with clinical sequencing; move into clinical practice with licensing and expectation management
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Recursive feature reduction / top-ranking feature selection with the MUVR package; no named features or importance values are reported
raw.Limitation_Categories: Methodological: unannotated genomic features, no functional dissection, class imbalance, proof-of-principle scope, untested long-read/mixed-sample feature extraction. Applicability: artificial urine does not represent real urine; local strain population only. Translation: licensing, registration, safety, expectation management
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: High-quality training sets with phenotypic interaction data are critical; interaction datasets for some phage were highly imbalanced (up to 85:15); most features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so functional meaning is uncertain
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear: the interaction-score definition, the threshold of 60, and the formulas for precision, recall and F1 are all given in Materials and Methods, with per-model RMSE and F1 reported
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-9 (main article); model results pp. 3-6; Materials and Methods pp. 7-8

raw.Inclusion_Criteria: 1. Patients hospitalized at Jinhua Central Hospital from January 2021 to December 2023. 2. Patients meeting the CDC criteria for A. baumannii infection. 3. Clinically infected AB specimens include sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions and puncture fluid. 4. Only the first AB infection in each patient. 5. XDRAB defined as a strain susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline).
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: 2. Patients infected with pathogens other than AB or colonized with AB without clinical infection. 3. Patients with AB infection detected within 48 hours of admission, transferred out within 48 hours of admission, who died, or who abandoned treatment. 4. Patients with significant missing clinical data. (Also: contaminated samples or duplicate strains from the same patient.)
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: Jinhua Central Hospital (single-centre electronic medical records and laboratory systems)
raw.Dataset_Size: 559 patients; 35 candidate variables screened by LASSO
raw.Missing_Data_Method: VIM package used to visualize missing-value distribution; factors with more than 10% missing values excluded; MICE package multiple imputation for factors with less than 10% missing values.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre in Jinhua, Zhejiang, China (Jinhua Central Hospital), January 2021 - December 2023; the authors acknowledge geographic bias and limited generalizability.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions, and puncture fluid
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: XDRAB infection (nosocomial) among hospitalized A. baumannii-infected patients, modelled against non-XDRAB AB (NXDRAB) infection.
raw.Pathogens: Acinetobacter baumannii (extensively drug-resistant, XDRAB; and non-XDRAB AB)
raw.Drug_Classes: aminoglycosides; carbapenems; quinolones; beta-lactamase inhibitors; broad-spectrum cephalosporins
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: tobramycin; amikacin; gentamicin; imipenem; meropenem; levofloxacin; ciprofloxacin; piperacillin-tazobactam; cefoperazone-sulbactam; ceftazidime; ceftriaxone; cefepime
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: XDRAB is defined as a strain of A. baumannii susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline); the outcome is XDRAB infection versus non-XDRAB AB infection.
raw.AI_Purpose: To establish a practical infection prediction model (LASSO regression variable selection plus multivariable logistic regression, visualized as a nomogram) that lets clinicians assess the risk of XDRAB infection and guide early isolation and treatment.
raw.Feature_Engineering: ICU admission time recoded into three intervals (no ICU admission / 1-7 days / >7 days) calculated from admission to first AB detection; hypoproteinemia defined as serum albumin below 30 g/L; NLR and other blood parameters collected.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation (lambda.1se = 0.03450), keeping 10 non-zero-coefficient features for the multivariable logistic regression.
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 10 (non-zero coefficients at lambda.1se); 8 retained as independent risk factors in the nomogram
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross-validation to determine the lambda value; lambda.min = 0.0065 (24 variables) versus lambda.1se = 0.03450 (10 variables), lambda.1se selected.
raw.Software_Libraries: glmnet; rms; VIM; MICE (R packages)
raw.Other_Metrics: C-index 0.932 (training) / 0.929 (testing); AUC 0.9322 (training) and 0.9291 (test); Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; OR with 95% CI for each risk factor; decision curve analysis and clinical impact curve.
raw.Baseline_Method: Univariate comparison of XDRAB versus NXDRAB groups (independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test for continuous variables, chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables).
raw.Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples from the training set; C-index 0.932; Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; calibration curve close to the 45-degree line.
raw.Train_Test_Split: 7:3 randomization by R software - training set 391 cases, test set 168 cases
raw.External_Validation_Description: Test set of 168 cases from the same 7:3 random split of the single-centre cohort (AUC 0.9291); not an independent external cohort - the authors state external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
raw.Overfitting_Method: LASSO penalisation to reduce dimensionality and multicollinearity-induced overfitting; internal validation by 1000 bootstrap samples.
raw.Clinical_Insights: Clinicians can quickly assess the risk of XDRAB infection from existing clinical data and implement timely isolation and treatment; early transfer from ICU to general wards for eligible patients could reduce risk; rational use of carbapenems and b-lactamase inhibitors remains crucial.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Single-centre, single-country cohort; coefficients may vary under different circumstances; external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples (C-index 0.932) and a held-out test set (AUC 0.9291) drawn from the same single-centre cohort; the authors state external validation with other institutions, regions and countries is still necessary - no prospective or deployed use.
raw.Integration_Point: Early risk assessment of hospitalized patients (nomogram scoring from existing clinical data) to trigger timely isolation and treatment.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians score the nomogram from existing clinical data to assess XDRAB risk and implement timely isolation and treatment; the paper notes early transfer out of the ICU for eligible patients.
raw.Future_Directions: External validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries; prospective studies to validate the findings further; more prospective studies on glycaemic control and XDRAB infection.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (sociodemographic, behavioural, clinical, laboratory, pharmacological, healthcare utilisation)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO regression coefficients at lambda.1se and multivariable logistic regression odds ratios; nomogram points scaled from the regression coefficients.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Single-centre design / geographic bias / limited generalizability; retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems (incomplete data, intended factors not included); selection bias; need for external validation and prospective studies.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems may be incomplete and some intended factors could not be analysed; individual missing values in continuous variables handled by exclusion (>10% missing) or MICE multiple imputation.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear, TRIPOD-guided reporting of variable selection, model development, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical utility.

raw.Title: Pioneering Klebsiella Pneumoniae Antibiotic Resistance Prediction With Artificial Intelligence-Clinical Decision Support System-Enhanced Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry: Retrospective Study
raw.Journal_Source: Journal of Medical Internet Research (J Med Internet Res)
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
raw.Funder_Names: Tri-Service General Hospital (grant numbers TSGH-D-113105 and TSGH-D-113106)
raw.Population_Description: Routine clinical bacterial specimens (165,299) submitted to the microbiology laboratories of Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospitals, Taiwan, January 2021-December 2023; 11,996 identified as Klebsiella pneumoniae, of which 11,127 (LEV) and 11,623 (CIP) had non-intermediate AST results. No patient-level demographic data reported.
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Top 15 m/z spectral features (m/z segment ranges of 2035-2040, 2067-2072, 2166-2171, 2180-2185, 2688-2695, 2759-2764, 3143-3152, 4363-4368, 4567-4572, 5278-5283, 5379-5384, 7238-7253, 7703-7708, 9136-9145 and 9532-9544); ranked by feature importance values (m/z segments with importance <0.01 filtered as background noise) and correlation with resistance in heat maps
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random forest classifier (RF) - highest area under the curve of 0.95 for both levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin resistance
raw.Accuracy_Value: 0.87 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.86 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.Sensitivity_Value: 0.88 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.89 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.Specificity_Value: 0.86 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.82 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.Precision_PPV_Value: 0.81 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.86 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.F1_Value: 0.85 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.87 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
raw.F1_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.AUROC_Value: 0.95 (random forest, testing AUC, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin validation sets; training AUC 0.99)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were developed on January-September specimens and validated on October-December specimens from the same hospital network; validation was against culture-based AST. No external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no routine clinical use is reported, so the highest level the paper's own evidence supports is internal validation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Dataset balancing and feature selection intricacies; intermediate AST results introduce uncertainty and their exclusion (869 LEV, 373 CIP) may have omitted significant data, affecting generalizability to intermediate cases; resistance mechanisms not mediated at the protein-peptide level or outside m/z 2000-20,000 are not captured; further validation required
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: No formal equity analysis; the authors argue the approach is relevant to low- and middle-income countries where antibiotic use is escalating and access and stewardship are challenged
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: No specific ethical or governance risks discussed; IRB approval obtained (TSGHIRB No. C202305073), informed consent waived for the retrospective design, data anonymized
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Judgements recorded: (1) the study builds two parallel models (levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin) rather than one; the random forest is the best-performing model for both, so the performance Value fields report the random forest figure for each drug, labelled by drug; (2) Clinical_Maturity_Level coded 2 (internal validation) because the validation set is a later time window of the same hospital-network dataset, not an external dataset; (3) Data_Source coded 'Laboratory information system' - the data are routine hospital microbiology MALDI-TOF MS spectra and VITEK 2 AST results, no registry or EHR is named; (4) Funding_Source coded 'Public' - grants from the study hospital (TSGH), a public National Defense Medical Center hospital, conflicts declared 'None declared'.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Which of the two parallel models (levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) is the review's single unit of analysis is not settled by the paper; both are reported. Also unresolved: whether a model validated on a later time window of the same 5-hospital dataset counts as internal validation (coded 2) or partial external validation.
raw.Sample_Size: 11,996 KP specimens identified from 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,127 specimens analysed for LEV resistance and 11,623 for CIP resistance
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Klebsiella pneumoniae specimens identified by MALDI-TOF MS that underwent AST for levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin with the VITEK 2 system
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Specimens with intermediate AST results: 869 excluded from the LEV analysis (leaving 11,127) and 373 from the CIP analysis (leaving 11,623)
raw.Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
raw.Data_Source_Name: No public dataset named - local Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospital MALDI-TOF MS/AST data (January 2021-December 2023)
raw.Dataset_Size: 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,996 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (11,127 LEV analysis, 11,623 CIP analysis)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single country (Taiwan); specimens from Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospitals, no wider geographic sampling reported
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: bacterial specimens / Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) specimens (routine clinical samples; specimen site not stated)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae to levofloxacin (LEV) and ciprofloxacin (CIP), classified from MALDI-TOF MS spectra using machine learning
raw.Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (quinolones)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Levofloxacin (LEV); ciprofloxacin (CIP)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype from VITEK 2 AST interpreted with CLSI clinical breakpoints; specimens with intermediate results excluded
raw.AI_Purpose: Develop a web-based artificial intelligence-clinical decision support system (AI-CDSS) that combines machine learning with MALDI-TOF MS spectra to predict Klebsiella pneumoniae resistance to levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin and speed up diagnosis to guide antibiotic choice
raw.Feature_Engineering: m/z ranges segmented into 1-unit intervals with a +/- 2-unit tolerance for grouping; peak intensity values for resistant and susceptible strains extracted and logarithmically transformed; segments with feature importance below 0.01 filtered out as background noise
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Feature importance thresholding (segments with a feature importance value below 0.01 removed as background noise)
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Resampling with sklearn.utils: downsampling of over-represented classes and upsampling of underrepresented classes
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search for each model; best parameters in Multimedia Appendix 1
raw.Software_Libraries: sklearn.utils (used for resampling); models include XGBoost and light gradient boosting machine (LGBM)
raw.Other_Metrics: No metrics beyond training/testing AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and F1-score were reported (Tables 1 and 2); ROC curves presented graphically
raw.Baseline_Method: Logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis as comparator algorithms; traditional culture-based AST as the clinical reference standard
raw.Baseline_Performance: Ciprofloxacin: logistic regression testing AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.78; LDA testing AUC 0.80, accuracy 0.77 (versus random forest AUC 0.95, accuracy 0.87)
raw.Internal_Validation: Temporal hold-out: October-December specimens used as the validation set, validated against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
raw.Train_Test_Split: Temporal split - January to September specimens for training, October to December specimens for validation
raw.Clinical_Insights: The same top 15 m/z spectral features are associated with resistance to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, suggesting a universal resistance mechanism despite the different modes of action; these spectral markers could support rapid resistance detection
raw.Generalisability_Details: Exclusion of intermediate AST results may have omitted significant data and affected model generalizability to intermediate cases; future work should add intermediate cases and diverse data modalities to broaden applicability; further validation required
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Temporal validation of the models on October-December specimens at Tri-Service General Hospital against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases); no external cohort, no prospective evaluation, no documented routine clinical use
raw.Integration_Point: Web-based AI-CDSS embedded in the microbiology/AST workflow: a culture sample is collected, MALDI-TOF MS spectra are analysed and the system predicts LEV/CIP resistance to inform antibiotic choice
raw.End_User_Described: health care professionals (clinicians)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Sample collection, MALDI-TOF MS analysis and AI-CDSS resistance prediction integrated into the antibiotic resistance-testing workflow; predicted resistance determination in approximately 3 days versus the conventional 4-day timeline for standard AST
raw.Stewardship_Details: Antimicrobial stewardship benefit is claimed (faster resistance determination is said to enhance stewardship and ensure appropriate and effective treatment) but no stewardship outcome was measured
raw.Barriers_List: Resistance mechanisms not mediated at the protein-peptide level or outside m/z 2000-20,000 are not captured; intermediate AST results excluded and remain unpredictable; dataset balancing and feature selection are intricate; limited data and antibiotic access challenges in low- and middle-income countries
raw.Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is already indispensable for rapid and accurate microorganism identification in routine laboratories; ML plus MALDI-TOF is a faster route than NGS/PCR; a web-based AI-CDSS is easily distributed to health care professionals
raw.Future_Directions: Incorporate intermediate AST cases and diverse data modalities to broaden applicability to a wider array of antibiotic-resistant organisms; further validate the results
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance values (m/z segments with importance below 0.01 filtered as background noise) plus correlation heat maps of the top 15 m/z segments
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: A shared set of top 15 m/z spectral features predicts resistance to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, suggesting a universal mechanism of resistance despite the different modes of action; the authors state no prior study had applied ML with MALDI-TOF to quinolone resistance in KP
raw.Limitation_Categories: Dataset balancing and feature selection complexity; uncertainty and data loss from excluding intermediate AST results; incomplete coverage of resistance mechanisms (non-protein-mediated, m/z outside 2000-20,000); need for further validation
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Intermediate AST results create label uncertainty and were excluded; genotypic data may not align with phenotype, but spectra are used instead of genotypes
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model algorithms, grid-search tuning (Multimedia Appendix 1), preprocessing, temporal split and per-model metrics for both drugs (Tables 1 and 2) are reported; the language, libraries and hardware are not fully specified
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-12 (abstract and title p. 1; methods pp. 2-3; results and tables 1-2 pp. 5-6; discussion pp. 8-9; data availability and conflicts p. 9; appendices and PMID p. 10-12)

raw.Funder_Names: UKRI (BBSRC BB/X018156/1; MRC MR/X005895/1; EPSRC EP/Y018842/1)
raw.Population_Description: 35,777 M. tuberculosis isolates with WGS (> 20-fold coverage) and corresponding phenotypic drug-susceptibility test (pDST) data, sourced from 66 countries across all WHO regions
raw.Data_Source_Other: Public repositories/archives of Illumina whole genome sequences with linked phenotypic drug-susceptibility test data for M. tuberculosis isolates
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Aggregated counts of rare variants per gene (highest total information gain for aggregated pncA mutations, PZA); loss-of-function variants (ethA 15/32 prioritised, pncA Glu173fs OR 182.28, Rv0678, Rv2752c); RIF- and INH-resistance mutations rank highly (permutation feature importance/information gain)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) and gradient boosted trees (GBT) on feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; best AUC per drug (Table 2): INH RF + F2 96.50; RIF RF + F2 96.60; EMB GBT + F1 91.70; PZA GBT + F2 88.30; STM RF + F2 89.60; AMK RF + F1 90.70; CAP RF + F2 84.10; KAN GBT + F2 91.00; CIP GBT + F2 95.40; OFL GBT + F2 88.10; MOX GBT + F2 89.10; ETH GBT + F2 86.30; LEV GBT + F1 93.50; RFB GBT + F2 94.90. External comparisons: DE19 (GBT-CRM, AUC 95.5-97.9), KO19 (AUC 84.4-97.8), GR22 (CNN, AUC 82.3-98.1), TB-Profiler (sensitivity 87-97% first-line, 79.2-92.2% second-line)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random forest with the F2 feature set (RF + F2) - highest AUC in the study (RIF, AUC 96.6)

raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)

raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)

raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Monomorphic SNPs, variants in non-unique regions of the genome (e.g. pe/ppe genes) and variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded; only loci with a non-major allele frequency > 0.1% (F1/F2) or > 0.5% (F3) were retained
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
raw.Data_Source_Name: "35k" dataset: publicly available M. tuberculosis WGS and pDST data (sample accession numbers in the GitHub repository SSID08/TB-ML)
raw.Dataset_Size: 35,777 isolates (from 50,723 sourced); F1 56-143 variants, F2 895-1428 variants, F3 5603-10,487 variants
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates sourced from 66 countries covering all WHO regions: Europe 13,381 (37.4%), Africa 8756 (24.5%), South East Asia 5518 (15.4%), Western Pacific 3964 (11.1%), Americas 3176 (8.9%), Other 982 (2.8%)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary phenotypic drug resistance (pDST) to each of 14 anti-TB drugs, plus MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, Low resistance, High resistance, Resistant/Extreme) based on ECOFF thresholds
raw.Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (INH, RIF, EMB, PZA); second-line injectables (STM, AMK, CAP, KAN); fluoroquinolones (CIP, OFL, MOX, LEV); rifabutin (RFB); ethionamide (ETH); bedaquiline (BDQ) and clofazimine (CLF) in the loss-of-function and MIC analyses
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: INH, RIF, EMB, PZA, streptomycin (STM), OFL, MOX, levofloxacin (LEV), amikacin (AMI), capreomycin (CAP), kanamycin (KAN), CIP, ethionamide (ETH) and RFB; BDQ and CLF also analysed
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistance/susceptibility from pDST for each drug; MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, 'Low' resistance, 'High' resistance, and Resistant ['Extreme']) based on recommended ECOFF thresholds; genotypic MDR/pre-XDR/XDR categories from TB-Profiler
raw.AI_Purpose: To apply and evaluate ensemble tree-based machine learning (RF, GBT) on a large-scale WGS and pDST dataset to predict binary drug resistance for 14 drugs and MIC phenotypes, and to characterise drug-resistance mutations
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithms (RF, GBT) across feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; 4 external comparators (DE19, KO19, GR22, TB-Profiler)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Presence/absence (one-hot) encoding of SNPs and indels as 1/0 in a numpy matrix; F1 supplemented with aggregated counts of rare variants (MAF < 0.1%) predicted by SnpEff to have moderate-to-high functional impact (F1 + ); lineage predicted by TB-Profiler appended to the feature matrices
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: bedtools intersect to retain drug-resistance-associated genes from the TB-Profiler list; MAF filtering (> 0.1% for F1/F2, > 0.5% for F3); permutation feature importance to rank variants
raw.Num_Features_Selected: F1 56-143 variants; F2 895-1428 mutations; F3 5603-10,487 variants
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Randomised Grid Search with stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set (specified parameters and ranges, Table S7)
raw.Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (v1.4.1), XGBoost Python API (1.7.6), numpy; TB-Profiler; SnpEff (v5.1); BWA-mem (v0.7.17); Trimmomatic (v0.39); samtools; GATK GenotypeGVCFs (v4.1.3.0); bedtools (v2.31); MASS and nnet packages in R
raw.Other_Metrics: Conditional odds ratios for LOF variant associations; relative-risk ratios from multinomial ordinal regression across MIC categories; information gain from permutation feature importance
raw.Baseline_Method: Deelder et al. 2019 (DE19, GBT-CRM); Kouchaki et al. 2019 (KO19, best ensemble tree model with dimensionality reduction); Green et al. 2022 (GR22, CNN); TB-Profiler (in-silico rule-in classification)
raw.Baseline_Performance: DE19 (n = 16,507) GBT models AUC 95.5-97.9, sensitivity 69.7-91.1%, specificity 94.2-98.9%; KO19 (n = 13,167) AUC 84.4-97.8; GR22 (n = 22,615) AUC 82.3-98.1 with higher sensitivity across all drugs; TB-Profiler sensitivity 87-97% first-line and 79.2-92.2% second-line
raw.Internal_Validation: 20% hold-out test dataset plus stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set with randomised grid search for hyperparameter and classification-threshold optimisation
raw.Overfitting_Method: MAF filtering to control the number of input features; 80/20 train-test split with hold-out evaluation; stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.Clinical_Insights: Loss-of-function mutations in pro-drug activation genes (pncA for PZA, ethA for ETH, mshA) as resistance mechanisms; Rv0678 LOF mutations linked to BDQ/CLF cross-resistance via MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux; putative novel markers Rv3861 Ile27fs (STM) and Rv1907c Asp48fs (INH) absent from the WHO catalogue; inhA promoter variants associated with extreme INH resistance
raw.Data_Repository: GitHub repository: https://github.com/SSID08/TB-ML (contains sample accession numbers, feature importance values and analysis code)

raw.Facilitators_List: Standardised containerised environments (Docker containers within ML-TB) for model comparison and reproducibility; interpretable targeted feature sets (drug-specific regions); aggregation of rare variants to capture under-sampled resistance mutations

raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Prospective cohort
raw.Population_Description: Non-duplicate MRSA screening specimens (nasal and inguinal/perineal ESwabs) from patients at a Swiss tertiary care centre: 6,771 specimens used to train PhenoMATRIX, 17,223 sequential specimens for validation (09 February 2022 - 08 May 2023) and 1,409 sequential specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS (23 May 2023 - 03 July 2023). No patient-level characteristics reported.
raw.Data_Source_Other: Digital chromogenic culture plate images (CHROMID MRSA) captured on the Copan WASPLab; ground truth from technologists' manual reading of the same images
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
raw.Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Infection prevention and control team
raw.Delivery_Platform: Laboratory information system (LIS) integrated; Instrument / device embedded
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: PhenoMATRIX (CNN image-classifier of chromogenic plates): sensitivity 99.9% (95% CI 99.2-99.9), specificity 99.1% (95% CI 99.0-99.2) on 17,223 validation specimens, 146 false positives (0.85%), 2 false negatives; PhenoMATRIX PLUS: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 92.1-100), specificity 95.2% (95% CI 93.8-96.1) on 1,409 specimens, PPV 40%, NPV 100%, 67 false positives (4.8%), 0 false negatives, 100% accuracy of automatic release of the 1,297 negative results; manual reading of culture images (comparator/reference standard).

raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: 1,409 non-duplicate specimens analysed by PhenoMATRIX PLUS (23 May 2023 - 03 July 2023)
