No randomised or external-site evaluation and no clinical decision-support integration is reported.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Impact on personnel load and productivity not measured; downstream effects in the clinical wards (e.g. unnecessary infection control measures) require further study; patient outcomes, antimicrobial prescribing and cost-savings not assessed.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Automated screening of chromogenic culture plate images (PhenoMATRIX / PhenoMATRIX PLUS) at a single Swiss tertiary centre; no patient-level demographic or clinical data. Abstract reports PhenoMATRIX sensitivity 99.8% while the results text and Table 1 give 99.9% (866/868 = 99.77%) and the abstract positivity rate 5% (866/17,223) differs from the results text 5% (868/17,223). The '100% accuracy' statement refers to the automatic release of negative results to the LIS and the automatic discharge of negative plates, not to classification accuracy.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Whether PhenoMATRIX or PhenoMATRIX PLUS is this review's unit of analysis: the two software versions were assessed on different, non-overlapping specimen sets (17,223 validation specimens vs 1,409 specimens), so no head-to-head comparison exists and the paper names neither as best.
raw.Sample_Size: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens (validation phase); 6,771 non-duplicate specimens (machine learning phase); 1,409 non-duplicate specimens (PhenoMATRIX PLUS)

raw.Data_Types_Used: Imaging; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: CHROMID MRSA chromogenic plates (bioMerieux) imaged on the Copan WASPLab; Copan 490CE.A ESwabs

raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) from nasal and inguinal/perineal screening ESwabs on chromogenic media: agreement of PhenoMATRIX/PhenoMATRIX PLUS image classification with the manual reading (sensitivity, specificity).
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Other organisms named only as mixed-growth false positives: Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Bacillus sp.
raw.Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is detection of methicillin resistance (cefoxitin/mecA), not an antimicrobial class outcome.
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: cefoxitin (disk diffusion AST confirming methicillin resistance)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA; Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA positive/negative on CHROMID MRSA chromogenic plates (presumptively positive = green colonies on manual reading); positives confirmed by qPCR targeting femA and mecA and by disk diffusion AST on all femA-positive isolates.
raw.AI_Purpose: Automated reading of chromogenic culture plate images: sorting plates as MRSA positive/negative, automatic release of negative results to the LIS and automatic discharge of negative plates from the incubators.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 (PhenoMATRIX and PhenoMATRIX PLUS; assessed on different specimen sets)
raw.Feature_Engineering: No hand-crafted features: several high-resolution digital images per plate taken under different light and exposure conditions at two incubation time points (0 h and 18 h) fed to the CNN.
raw.Other_Metrics: Positive predictive value 40% and negative predictive value 100% (PhenoMATRIX PLUS); false positive rate 4.8% (67/1,409) for PhenoMATRIX PLUS and 0.85% (146/17,223) for PhenoMATRIX; MRSA positivity rate 5% (868/17,223) and 3.2% (45/1,409); TAT and time-of-day distributions of image availability; 100% accuracy of automatic release and plate discard for the 1,297 negatives.
raw.Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the digital culture images by technologists (reference standard); qPCR targeting femA and mecA plus disk diffusion AST for confirmation of presumptive positives.
raw.Baseline_Performance: Manual reading was the reference standard: PhenoMATRIX PLUS showed 100% sensitivity (no false negative among 1,409 specimens) and 95.2% specificity; for PhenoMATRIX, 99.9% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity against manual work-up.
raw.Internal_Validation: Temporal validation: settings trained on 6,771 specimens and validated on 17,223 non-duplicate specimens prospectively analysed between 09 February 2022 and 08 May 2023; discrepancies reviewed by clinical microbiologists.
raw.Train_Test_Split: Training: 6,771 non-duplicate specimens (machine learning phase); validation: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens; separate evaluation: 1,409 specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Authors state the software could be implemented, after thorough validation, on a broad panel of culture-based analyses such as urines, GBS screening and other infection-control screening specimens.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Performance of both versions established against manual reading on consecutive routine specimens, with PhenoMATRIX PLUS prospectively releasing negative results to the LIS and discarding negative plates in the routine workflow; no external or randomised evaluation.
raw.Integration_Point: Bacteriology laboratory WASPLab line (imaging after 18 h of incubation) with automatic notification of negative MRSA results to the Laboratory Information System, further validated by the Valab expert system before updating the electronic patient record.
raw.End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists (who read culture images and release results) and the infection control team.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Negative MRSA results are automatically sent to the LIS by PhenoMATRIX PLUS, validated by the Valab expert system and used to update the electronic patient record without delay; presumptively positive plates are sent to the reading folder for technologist review and confirmatory tests.
raw.Barriers_List: Time-consuming manual reading of negative plates and extended time to results; laboratory operating hours limiting the day shift; laboratory workload bottlenecks requiring priority criteria by specimen type; shortage of qualified personnel; availability of the WASPLab for plate discharge.
raw.Facilitators_List: Total laboratory automation (WASPLab) giving 24/7 image availability; automatic release of negative results to the LIS set as a high priority so results are sent around the clock; automatic discharge of negative plates when the WASPLab is available (low priority).
raw.Future_Directions: Broader application of the software to other culture-based analyses (urines, GBS screening, other infection-control screening) after thorough validation; studies of the precise impact on personnel load and productivity, patient outcomes, antimicrobial prescriptions and cost-savings.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (chromogenic culture-plate images / microbiological colony features; incubation time point)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Unmeasured workflow/personnel impact; unexplored downstream clinical effects; absence of patient-outcome, prescribing and cost analyses; single-centre routine setting.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: False positives driven by mixed growth of Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Bacillus sp. (about 85% of false positives) and by non-specific colours on chromogenic plates; two false negatives from small, pale colonies with poorly specific features.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear methods and full 2x2 tables (Tables 1-2) with 95% CIs; minor internal inconsistencies (abstract sensitivity 99.8% vs 99.9% in the results text; abstract positivity 866/17,223 vs 868/17,223 in the results text).
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-4 (objectives, methods, performance results and Tables 1-2); p. 5 and p. 8 (automatic release, PPV/NPV, workflow); pp. 9-10 (limitations, conclusions, funding, ethics).

raw.Title: Proof of concept study on early forecasting of antimicrobial resistance in hospitalized patients using machine learning and simple bacterial ecology data
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
raw.Funder_Names: Hôpital Européen Marseille; SESSTIM (Aix Marseille Univ, Inserm, IRD); PhD grant from ISSPAM, Aix Marseille Université
raw.Population_Description: Hospitalised patients: 30,975 antibiograms isolated from 13,166 patients in 6 ward types (emergency room 25%, critical care 24%, surgery 20%, medicine 19%) at the Hôpital Européen Marseille, 2014-2020; specimens mainly urine 41%, lower respiratory tract 23%, blood 14%, abscesses 12%
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP ranking for the NN models, by stage: (1) history of MDR bacterial carriage in the last 3 months, a strong predictor at all stages with high absolute SHAP values (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); (2) aspect on direct examination, significant at stage 2; (3) cultural feature, largest contribution at stage 3 'culture'; (4) at stage 4 'species', species then cultural features are the strongest contributors; specimen origin, ward type and date had a less significant effect at all stages
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Frequentist (FRQ), Bayesian (BAY), logistic regression (LR), AdaBoost (ADA), Gradient Boosting (GBS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Bagging (BAG), Random Forest (RF) and neural networks (NN), compared on mean AUROC at each stage of the bacteriological process on the 2020 validation dataset. Overall mean AUROC of all models rose from 0.594 (stage 1 'sampling') to 0.708 (stage 2 'direct'), 0.773 (stage 3 'culture') and 0.847 (stage 4 'species'). BAY, NN, FRQ and XGB performed much better than GBS, ADA, BAG, RF and LR. NN had the highest mean AUROC (0.823) and the highest AUROC at each stage except stage 4, where BAY reached 0.918. For the least frequent situations BAY held mean AUROCs of 0.824 (stage 3) and 0.917 (stage 4); NN dropped from 0.693 to 0.512 at stage 1 and from 0.811 to 0.658 at stage 2; FRQ fell from 0.893 to 0.662 at stage 4; LR was worst at all stages (mean AUROC 0.554)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: BAY (Bayesian inference) models and NN (neural network) models — named best on mean AUROC
raw.AUROC_Value: 0.918 (BAY model, stage 4 'species', all isolates); highest NN mean AUROC 0.823 across stages
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: 2020 validation dataset (all isolates); stage 4 'species' for the BAY model

raw.Reported_Limitations: Low performance at the early stage 1 'sampling' (mean AUROC 0.693) because only a few features were included; no demographics, comorbidities or history of antibiotic treatment; AUROCs vary widely between antibiotics; concept drift complicates use of the date; predictions and performance are specific to the Hôpital Européen Marseille ecology; rare situations are poorly predicted; intervention studies and implementation science are still needed
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Data-protection governance only: use of anonymised bacterial ecology data under the GDPR; the wider project received authorisation DR-2020-047 from the French national commission for data protection (CNIL); the authors note that patient-related sensitive data are strictly controlled in Europe
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the BAY and NN models named as best; AUROC taken from the 2020 validation dataset (all isolates) which the authors state is the dataset used for the reported results. Judgments: Breakpoint_Guideline = Other (French CA-SFM and European EUCAST guidelines); Infection_Type = Other (models cover a wide range of infected body sites, not one syndrome); Regulatory_Approval_Mentioned = No (the only regulatory mention is a CNIL data-protection authorisation, not a device/software clearance); Lifecycle_P5 left blank (deployment is aspirational, only a prototype is being tested at HEM); Study_Design ticked as development + retrospective cohort (the authors do not label the 2020 evaluation an external validation study)

raw.Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing of the 2014-2019 data (26,621 antibiograms, of which 4,915 in 2019 alone); validation on all 2020 data (4,354 antibiograms)
raw.External_Validation_Description: None performed; external evaluation is planned in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals including HEM
raw.Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers after each hidden dense layer and batch normalisation in the neural networks; XGB's higher regularisation mitigates overfitting; hyperparameters chosen by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation
raw.Explainability_Methods: SHAP; Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model; Other
raw.Clinical_Insights: History of MDR carriage in the last 3 months is a strong predictor at all stages (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); the cultural feature dominates at the culture stage and species then culture type at the species stage; in a worked scenario predicted susceptibility to CTX/CRO was 0.87 at the culture stage (good probability) and 0.40 at the species stage (bad probability, for Citrobacter koseri in critical care); NN SHAP values and BAY likelihood ratios were moderately consistent (Spearman 0.57, p = 0.0033)
raw.Data_Repository: No repository; anonymised data available from author S. Rebaudet upon reasonable request with a material transfer agreement
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors hypothesise that the overall architecture of the algorithms is generalisable and that similar models could be adapted to other hospitals trained with local bacteriological data; to be evaluated in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals and through an interoperable health data warehouse in eight hospitals, comparing federated learning with centralised and local approaches
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective monocentric design; hyperparameters tuned by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation on the training data; performance reported on the 2020 validation dataset (4,354 antibiograms) held out from the 2014-2019 training+testing data; no external, prospective or clinical-impact evaluation
raw.Integration_Point: Prototype web application (Gradio, private HuggingFace space) being tested at HEM; planned embedding in the laboratory information management system (LIMS) to provide preliminary probabilistic antibiograms, in EMR systems or health data warehouses, or as a stewardship dashboard
raw.End_User_Described: Hospital doctors/prescribers selecting empirical antimicrobial therapy; on-call infectiologists giving antimicrobial stewardship advice; antimicrobial stewardship teams (dashboard flagging prescriptions of low susceptibility probability)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Predictions at four stages matched to laboratory turnaround: stage 1 'sampling' (Day 0, specimen origin), stage 2 'direct' (Day 0-1, direct Gram stain aspect), stage 3 'culture' (Day 1-2, cultural feature) and stage 4 'species' (Day 2-3, species identification), used to refine empirical therapy until the antibiogram is available
raw.Stewardship_Details: Studies underway in six hospitals will retrospectively describe the susceptibility probability and spectrum width of prescribed empirical therapies to assess potential efficacy gains and safe de-escalations; a stewardship dashboard flagging prescriptions with low susceptibility probability is proposed
raw.Barriers_List: GDPR restrictions on patient-related sensitive data; EMR data stored in heterogeneous formats and not readily accessible in all hospital facilities; no demographics, comorbidities or antibiotic history, limiting stage 1 performance; concept drift makes the date difficult to model; BAY models are burdensome to program; rare situations are unmet in the training data; the system must not replace practice guidelines or prescriber decisions
raw.Facilitators_List: Only simple bacterial ecology data are needed, easily extracted from any laboratory information system without GDPR restrictions after on-site anonymisation; NN models can be implemented and tuned with open-source packages and scale to new input variables; FRQ/BAY models are intrinsically interpretable and SHAP explains the NN; the probability output is designed to enrich the prescriber's reasoning rather than replace it
raw.Future_Directions: Include demographic features (age, sex, residence), comorbidities and history of antibiotic consumption; impute subsequent-stage data; model month and year separately with temporal sliding windows, concept-drift detectors and continuous learning; assess model uncertainty; multi-centre and federated evaluations; intervention studies followed by implementation science
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for the NN models at population and individual level; feature-specific likelihood ratios for the BAY models
raw.Limitation_Categories: Model performance: low AUROC at stage 1 with a limited feature set; metric variability between antibiotics. Data: absence of demographics, comorbidities and antibiotic history (GDPR); concept drift. Setting: single-centre data specific to one hospital's ecology; rare situations unmet in training. Methods: label encoding choice; BAY models burdensome to program. Evidence base: no prospective or clinical-impact evaluation yet
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Removal of likely contaminants, duplicates and screening specimens before training; intermediate susceptibility recoded as resistant; missing susceptibility values filled by expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance; rare feature combinations absent from the training data cause prediction omissions; concept drift over time
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-16 (full PDF text layer); title, abstract and DOI p. 1; dataset description and model comparison pp. 2-3; AUROC results pp. 3-5; best models p. 6; SHAP interpretability pp. 6-7; discussion, limitations and barriers pp. 8-10; methods pp. 10-14; data availability p. 14; acknowledgements p. 15; competing interests, ethics and supplementary note p. 16

studies.title: Amikacin Concentrations Predictive of Ototoxicity in Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Patients
studies.journal: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 59:6337-6343)
studies.sample_size: 28 MDR-TB patients (patients, not isolates) with amikacin concentration measurements and audiometry assessments
studies.ai_purpose: To identify clinical factors, including amikacin concentration thresholds, that predict ototoxicity in MDR-TB patients using an agnostic machine learning method (classification and regression tree analysis), and to derive threshold decision-making values for clinicians.
studies.best_model: CART tree using cumulative days of therapy as the primary node with cumulative AUC second, test-set AUROC 0.97 - superior to the model forced to pick peak and trough (AUROC 0.46)

raw.Title: Amikacin Concentrations Predictive of Ototoxicity in Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Patients
raw.Journal_Source: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 59:6337-6343)
raw.Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health (grants R01AI097045 and R56AI111985-01)
raw.Population_Description: 28 multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (MDR-TB) patients in Botswana, aged 15 years or older, started on MDR-TB treatment and with serum amikacin concentration measurements
raw.Age_Range: 15 years of age or older (eligibility criterion); age ranges by group 28-70 years (Table 3)
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: CART variable ranking on the drug-dose/PK model: primary node cumulative days of therapy; cumulative AUC ranked second (improved on the primary node by another 87%); AUC0-24 score 34%; initial weight score 29%. Cumulative AUC thresholds from the concentration-only tree: 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: CART (classification and regression tree) models built in three steps with the Salford Predictive Miner System: (1) all potential predictors (AUROC 0.97 on the test sets); (2) pharmacokinetic/treatment factors only, primary node cumulative days of therapy, cumulative AUC second, AUC0-24 34%, initial weight 29% (AUROC 0.97); (3) drug concentrations only, identifying cumulative AUC thresholds of 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter; plus a CART model forced to pick peak and trough, AUROC 0.46 on the test set. Also a 2-compartment population PK model (ADAPT 5), probit models (TC50 87,323 days*mg*h/liter, TC80 120,238) and frequentist group comparisons in STATA 13.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: CART tree using cumulative days of therapy as the primary node with cumulative AUC second, test-set AUROC 0.97 - superior to the model forced to pick peak and trough (AUROC 0.46)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Test set (internal cross-validation; random repeated training/test splits) for the CART model using drug-dose and pharmacokinetic factors
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model built and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation of each tree and random repeated training/test splits only; no external validation, no prospective evaluation of the model and no deployment, so the highest evidence-supported level is internal validation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Amikacin has a long half-life in cochlear tissue so hearing loss may occur long after therapy stops; only amikacin concentrations were measured although MDR-TB patients receive other ototoxic drugs; insufficient data on prior streptomycin exposure to examine that relationship; defining ototoxicity remains imprecise because conventional audiometers test only up to 8 kHz while amikacin affects hearing up to 20 kHz.
raw.Sample_Size: 28 MDR-TB patients (patients, not isolates) with amikacin concentration measurements and audiometry assessments
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: T.G. has worked as a consultant for Astellas Pharma US, Inc., and LuminaCare Solutions and founded Jacaranda Biomed, Inc. All other authors have no conflicts to declare.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: All MDR-TB patients 15 years of age or older started on MDR-TB treatment between 1 January 2011 and 30 December 2012 with serum amikacin concentration measurements reported; at least one creatinine measurement within 1 month prior to or after the start of amikacin and one follow-up creatinine measurement (within the last 6 months prior to censoring).
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: Botswana national MDR-TB treatment programme (no named dataset)
raw.Dataset_Size: 28 patients; 2 amikacin concentration samples per patient (1 h and 23.5 h after dose)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: All 28 patients were treated within one national MDR-TB programme in Botswana (one country, one programme), so the sample does not represent other settings.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Serum (plasma) amikacin concentrations; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Ototoxicity (audiometry-confirmed hearing loss) attributable to amikacin treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis - not a drug-resistance outcome
raw.Drug_Classes: Aminoglycoside (amikacin); fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin); thioamide (ethionamide); cycloserine; pyrazinamide
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin; levofloxacin; ethionamide; cycloserine; pyrazinamide (prior streptomycin exposure in 10 patients)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Audiometry-determined neurosensory hearing loss defined as a shift or loss of 15 to 25 dB relative to baseline averaged at two or more contiguous frequencies in at least one ear, or loss of response at 3 consecutive frequencies where responses had previously been obtained; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss is synonymous with ototoxicity.
raw.AI_Purpose: To identify clinical factors, including amikacin concentration thresholds, that predict ototoxicity in MDR-TB patients using an agnostic machine learning method (classification and regression tree analysis), and to derive threshold decision-making values for clinicians.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 3 CART models (all predictors; pharmacokinetic and treatment factors only, Figure 3; peak and trough forced) plus probit models for comparison
raw.Feature_Engineering: Pharmacokinetic features derived from the population model (AUC0-24, cumulative AUC), cumulative dose and cumulative dose divided by weight, amikacin dose in mg/kg as daily and cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, peak and trough concentrations, plus clinical variables (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy). CART is used to break the collinearity of these highly correlated measures.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: CART classification and ranking subroutines (Gini splitting; predictors ranked in order of importance, with surrogate variables), tree pruning by AUROC and parsimony
raw.Num_Features_Total: 14 candidate predictors listed (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy, amikacin dose, cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, daily dose mg/kg, cumulative dose mg/kg, AUC0-24, cumulative AUC, peak, trough)
raw.Num_Features_Selected: not reported as a count; the final tree used cumulative days of therapy as the primary node and cumulative AUC second
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Priors set to equal (equal probability assignment for all categories), with no penalty sets for misclassification
raw.Software_Libraries: Salford Predictive Miner System; ADAPT 5 (including its SAMPLE subroutine); STATA version 13; COBAS INTEGRA assays
raw.Other_Metrics: AUROC (0.97 test set for the best model; 0.46 for the peak/trough-forced model); CART relative improvement scores (87% for cumulative AUC, 34% AUC0-24, 29% initial weight); probit r2 for cumulative AUC 0.97, weight 0.95 and duration 0.98; cumulative AUC TC50 87,323 (CI 81,248-93,216) and TC80 120,238 days*mg*h/liter; correlations r2 between exposure measures
raw.Baseline_Method: CART model forced to pick peak and trough concentrations as predictors - the parameters currently used for clinical dosing decisions
raw.Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.46 on the test set, inferior to the 0.97 of the duration-of-therapy and cumulative AUC model
raw.Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation of each tree, plus repeated random splitting of the data set into training and test data sets (predictive power assessed on the test set)
raw.Train_Test_Split: Random repeated splits of the data set into training and test data sets; reported performance is that of the training-set-derived tree on the test set (test-set AUROC 0.97)
raw.Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
raw.Clinical_Insights: Threshold cumulative AUC of ~87,232 days*mg*h/liter for a 10% probability of ototoxicity and ~120,000 for 20%; ototoxicity risk rises after ~6 months of therapy and approaches certainty at 9 months; peak and trough concentrations are not useful monitoring parameters; optimal blood-draw times for therapeutic drug monitoring were 0, 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the concentration-ototoxicity relationship is likely to hold as sample size increases because it was also identified by parametric probit models and is concordant with guinea pig animal experiments that give a biological basis for the findings.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: CART trees built with Gini splitting and 5-fold cross-validation, with repeated random training/test splits; no external validation data set, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment.
raw.Integration_Point: Therapeutic drug monitoring and amikacin dosing decisions for MDR-TB treatment, using cumulative AUC and duration of therapy thresholds in place of peak and trough concentrations.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians treating pulmonary tuberculosis / MDR-TB programmes
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Blood draws for amikacin therapeutic drug monitoring should be taken just before the dose and at 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h after the dose rather than at peak and trough; cumulative AUC and duration thresholds are then used to judge the risk of ototoxicity during treatment.
raw.Future_Directions: Measuring amikacin concentrations lets the optimal (safe) duration of therapy be calculated in the first week of therapy, and the identified sampling times (0, 15 min, 2.5 h, 18.7 h) should be used for therapeutic drug monitoring in tuberculosis programmes.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: CART importance ranking (relative improvement scores on the primary node)
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Cumulative amikacin AUC and duration of therapy - and not the peak and trough concentrations currently used for dosing - are the predictors of ototoxicity; the AUC relationship was sigmoidal and gave explicit decision thresholds.
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: CART recursive partitioning, a nonparametric method examining linear and nonlinear interactions simultaneously, including interactions among the predictors of ototoxicity
raw.Limitation_Categories: Toxicodynamic/outcome-measurement (long cochlear half-life, imprecise definition of ototoxicity, high-frequency hearing loss above audiometer range); unmeasured drug exposures (other ototoxic MDR-TB drugs, prior streptomycin); sample size
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Audiometry is imprecise for amikacin ototoxicity: conventional audiometers test up to 8 kHz while amikacin affects hearing up to 20 kHz, so high-tone deafness may be missed; data on prior streptomycin exposure were insufficient; one of four patients with subjective hearing loss may not have met the definition.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear methods (CART, model software, cross-validation) but performance reporting is limited to AUROC and CART improvement scores/thresholds; no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or calibration is reported; small sample (28 patients).
raw.Page_References: p. 1 title/abstract/citation; p. 2 study population, ototoxicity definitions and methods; p. 3 results and Tables 1-3; pp. 4-5 discussion and Figure 4; p. 6 funding, conflicts and references

studies.title: Machine learning-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolates from Uganda
studies.sample_size: 182 MTB isolates per drug (145 training / 37 testing); 226 MTB isolates in the Uganda dataset overall; 236 MTB isolates in the South Africa validation dataset
studies.ai_purpose: To evaluate machine learning algorithms for predicting drug resistance of MTB isolates to four anti-TB drugs from whole-genome SNP mutations and clinical data from Uganda, and to assess generalisability on an independent South African dataset
studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
studies.best_model: Logistic Regression (LR) for rifampicin (RIF) - the highest MCC (0.83, 95% CI 0.73-0.86) and AUC (0.96, 95% CI 0.95-0.98) of all best models on the Uganda dataset (the other per-drug bests were GBC for INH, XGBoost for EMB and LR for STM)

raw.Title: Machine learning-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolates from Uganda
raw.Funder_Names: Fogarty International Center of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Award Number U2RTW012116 (MakDARTA, Makerere University); National Science Foundation awards 2030508 and 1836650 (Open Science Grid); Wellcome Trust (CAMO-Net) Award No. 226692/Z/22/Z
raw.Population_Description: 182 MTB clinical isolates per drug (from a Uganda dataset of 226 isolates) with clinical data variables (age, sex, HIV status), SNP mutations across the entire genome as predictors, and phenotypic drug-susceptibility data for four anti-TB drugs as the outcome; an independent South Africa dataset of 236 isolates was used for generalisability assessment
raw.Data_Source_Other: Publicly available whole-genome sequence (WGS) data from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) with corresponding clinical data and drug-resistance phenotypes from previously published studies
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Ten algorithms, trained per drug and evaluated with recall/sensitivity, specificity, ROC_AUC and MCC (plus precision and F1 score for the best models): Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), CatBoost, Gradient Boosting (GBC), AdaBoost, XGBoost, Decision Trees (DT), Extra Trees Classifier (ETC). Best per drug on the Uganda dataset (Table 9): RIF LR (MCC 0.72, ROC-AUC 0.95); INH GBC (MCC 0.51, ROC-AUC 0.82); EMB XGBoost (MCC 0.69, ROC-AUC 0.89); STM LR (MCC 0.18, ROC-AUC 0.66)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Logistic Regression (LR) for rifampicin (RIF) - the highest MCC (0.83, 95% CI 0.73-0.86) and AUC (0.96, 95% CI 0.95-0.98) of all best models on the Uganda dataset (the other per-drug bests were GBC for INH, XGBoost for EMB and LR for STM)
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.F1_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset (Table 8), five-fold cross-validation on the training set
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Best models were developed and internally validated with five-fold cross-validation on the Uganda training set and then evaluated on the independent South Africa dataset (236 isolates) - external validation, not prospective evaluation or clinical deployment
raw.Reported_Limitations: Single reference genome (H37Rv) may exclude important genomic regions related to resistance; limited availability of patient clinical data constrained the models' ability to capture complex biological interactions; multicollinearity not extensively assessed (boosting classifiers robust to it); novel markers not yet shown to be causally involved in resistance
raw.Sample_Size: 182 MTB isolates per drug (145 training / 37 testing); 226 MTB isolates in the Uganda dataset overall; 236 MTB isolates in the South Africa validation dataset
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: MTB isolates with complete phenotypic drug-susceptibility information for the four drugs (RIF, INH, EMB, STM) and usable sequence data; for the SA dataset, only 236 of 399 MTB isolates had complete phenotypic information from the four drugs
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: 21 MTB isolates excluded - 19 with no antimicrobial resistance phenotype data for the four drugs and 2 with empty VCF files after filtering for low quality variants
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) - BioProjects PRJEB10533, PRJNA481638, PRJEB10577, PRJEB2424, PRJNA559528 and PRJNA74965
raw.Dataset_Size: 4994 variants across the entire MTB genome plus clinical variables; 182 MTB isolates per drug (145 training / 37 testing); 226 UG isolates in total; 236 SA isolates
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Missing clinical data imputed with the simple imputer module (mean strategy for numerical, most frequent strategy for categorical); missing SNP values recorded as N were encoded as '0'; 21 isolates with missing phenotype or empty VCF files excluded
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Uganda dataset drawn from five published studies/BioProjects across Uganda; validation dataset from patients in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; authors report a substantial drop in performance on the South African dataset
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phenotypic drug resistance (resistant vs susceptible) of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to four anti-TB drugs: rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB) and streptomycin (STM)
raw.Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol); aminoglycoside (streptomycin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB), streptomycin (STM)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary phenotype label: susceptible = 0, resistant = 1, from phenotypic drug-susceptibility data for each of the four drugs
raw.AI_Purpose: To evaluate machine learning algorithms for predicting drug resistance of MTB isolates to four anti-TB drugs from whole-genome SNP mutations and clinical data from Uganda, and to assess generalisability on an independent South African dataset
raw.Feature_Engineering: SNP matrix built from filtered VCFs (reference and alternate alleles by chromosome position, isolates merged); one-hot encoding of the SNP matrix (presence of allele = 1, absence = 0); missing SNP values (N) coded '0'; antibiotic phenotypes binary-coded (S = 0, R = 1); homogeneous variant set selected between training and validation datasets; clinical variables imputed; SMOTE up-sampling of the training set
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: No separate feature-selection step; the top ten features per drug were ranked using the feature importance attribute of the tree-based models (XGBoost, GBC) or the absolute values of the logistic regression coefficients
raw.Num_Features_Total: 4994 variants across the entire MTB genome plus clinical data variables
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 10 per drug (top ten most important features identified for each drug)
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE up-sampling applied to the training dataset; all models trained on both originally imbalanced and balanced datasets; severe class imbalance noted in the South Africa dataset
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: gridsearchCV with cross-validation on the training set; optimal parameters: LR C=10, max_iter=300 (RIF) and C=5, max_iter=500 (STM); XGBoost learning rate 0.3, max_depth 3, n_estimators 100, subsample 1.0 (EMB); GBC learning rate 0.5, max_depth 9, n_estimators 100, subsample 0.7 (INH); other models used default parameters
raw.Software_Libraries: Scikit-learn version 1.3.2
raw.Hardware_Details: Open Science Grid (OSG) High Throughput Computing infrastructure supported by National Science Foundation awards 2030508 and 1836650; no CPU/GPU/memory specification reported
raw.Other_Metrics: Recall (sensitivity), specificity, ROC_AUC and MCC reported for the best three models per drug (Tables 6-8) and for the best model per drug (Tables 9-10), each with 95% CI; precision and F1 score reported for the best models on the up-sampled UG dataset
raw.Baseline_Method: TB profiler (WHO catalogue-based tool)
raw.Baseline_Performance: On the UG dataset the best ML models had a higher ROC-AUC than TB profiler except LR for STM; LR mean sensitivity for RIF 0.75 vs TB profiler 0.5; XGBoost for EMB mean sensitivity 0.77 (same as TB profiler) with higher mean specificity 0.92 vs 0.88; TB profiler mean sensitivity for INH 0.82 vs GBC 0.76 with lower mean specificity 0.70 vs 0.75; on the SA dataset TB profiler outperformed all best models
raw.Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation on the training set with 95% CIs computed by bootstrap; performance also evaluated on a held-out Uganda test set of 37 isolates
raw.Train_Test_Split: 80% training (145 MTB isolates) / 20% testing (37 MTB isolates) per drug
raw.External_Validation_Description: South Africa (SA) dataset: WGS data from patients in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; 236 of 399 MTB isolates included with complete phenotypic information for the four drugs; WGS available under NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA559528
raw.Overfitting_Method: Ensemble tree models (ETC, RF) used to reduce overfitting; SMOTE balancing of the training set; regularisation strength tuned for LR via gridsearchCV; authors state a balance between dataset size, class distribution and model complexity is critical to avoiding overfitting
raw.Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
raw.Clinical_Insights: Known resistance genes confirmed (rpoB for RIF, katG for INH, rpsL for STM); novel SNPs detected in PE/PE-PGRS/PE-PPE genes (PE_PGRS18 with INH; PE_PGRS7, PPE34, PPE54 and PPE19 with RIF; PPE55 with STM); mutations in pykA (Rv1617), ureC (Rv1850) and cyp136 (Rv3059) associated with EMB resistance; conserved hypothetical proteins (Rv2059, Rv2082, Rv2828A, Rv2828c) and intergenic regions (oxyR-ahpC for INH; embC-embA for EMB) associated with resistance; HIV status a top feature for RIF and STM with a negative coefficient
raw.Generalisability_Details: Best models trained on the Uganda dataset were applied to the South Africa dataset; LR for RIF and STM did not generalise while the boosting classifiers (GBC for INH, XGBoost for EMB) generalised better; TB profiler outperformed all best models on the SA dataset; the authors attribute the differences to varying proportions of resistant/susceptible isolates and lineage-specific genomic variation
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Models trained and tuned on the Uganda dataset were evaluated on the independent South Africa dataset, which is external validation; no prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported
raw.Integration_Point: Not reported - no clinical system or workflow integration described; deployment across diverse populations is framed only as future work
raw.End_User_Described: Not reported - the paper names no specific end user for the models
raw.Barriers_List: Poor generalisability of models across datasets/populations with distinct characteristics; single reference genome may exclude resistance-related regions; limited patient clinical data; missing phenotype/VCF data excluded 21 isolates; severe class imbalance in the external dataset; multicollinearity not extensively assessed
raw.Future_Directions: Establish whether the novel resistance markers are causally involved in mediating resistance; investigate lineage-specific genomic variations and their impact on model performance; integrate multiple omics layers (transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) with comprehensive clinical information; expand datasets to additional drugs and clinical factors; balance dataset size, class distribution and model complexity; apply the approach to other areas such as drug repurposing and cancer resistance prediction
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 3 (microbiological/genomic - SNP mutations; sociodemographic - age and sex; clinical - HIV status)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance attribute for the tree-based models (XGBoost, GBC); absolute values of the logistic regression coefficients for LR
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Novel SNPs within PE, PE-PGRS and PE/PPE genes: PE_PGRS18 (INH), PE_PGRS7 / PPE34 / PPE54 / PPE19 (RIF), PPE55 (STM); pykA (Rv1617), ureC (Rv1850) and cyp136 (Rv3059) (EMB); conserved hypothetical proteins Rv2059, Rv2082, Rv2828A, Rv2828c; mutations in intergenic regions (oxyR-ahpC for INH, embC-embA for EMB); HIV status among the top ten features for RIF and STM
raw.Limitation_Categories: Model generalisability / cross-population performance; single reference genome; limited clinical data; multicollinearity not assessed; novel markers not yet causally established
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Read contamination screening (23 reads excluded with less than 95% proportion of MTB); low-quality variant filtering; 21 isolates excluded (19 without phenotype data, 2 with empty VCFs); missing clinical values imputed; severe class imbalance in the SA dataset
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model metrics and the best model per drug are reported in dedicated tables (Tables 6-10) with 95% confidence intervals

studies.title: Infection Inspection: using the power of citizen science for image-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli treated with ciprofloxacin
studies.sample_size: 49,074 single-cell images; 1,045,199 classifications by 5,273 volunteers (1,003,588 classifications by 4,927 users after removing training images)
studies.ai_purpose: Train volunteers to classify single-cell images and use their classifications and misclassifications to identify which image features drive accurate ciprofloxacin-sensitive/resistant classification, making the machine-learning classifier more robust to atypical phenotypes.
studies.resistance_type: Binary R/S for a single drug
studies.best_model: Deep learning model (highest accuracy: 75.3 ± 0.4% overall vs 66.8 ± 0.1% for volunteers)

raw.Title: Infection Inspection: using the power of citizen science for image-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli treated with ciprofloxacin
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
raw.Funder_Names: Oxford Martin School (Programme on Antimicrobial Resistance Testing); Wellcome Trust grant 110164/Z/15/Z; Clarendon Fund Scholarships; UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council grants BB/N018656/1 and BB/S008896/1; National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Healthcare Associated Infections and Antimicrobial Resistance (NIHR200915) with UKHSA; NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre
raw.Population_Description: 49,074 single-cell fluorescence microscopy images of ciprofloxacin-treated E. coli cells from five clinical bloodstream-infection strains (EC1, EC2, EC3, EC5, EC6); unit of analysis is the bacterial cell image, not patients.

Random Forest classifier (100 trees, min 3 samples/leaf): Mean Absolute Error 0.15 ± 0.01 on a holdout dataset. Citizen-scientist volunteers (comparator): 66.8 ± 0.1% overall, 66.4 ± 0.2% sensitive, 67.3 ± 0.2% resistant.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Deep learning model (highest accuracy: 75.3 ± 0.4% overall vs 66.8 ± 0.1% for volunteers)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Aggregated across all three dataset uploads (all images; Zooniverse users or the model)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The deep-learning classifier and the Random Forest were evaluated only on internal data (75–25 train-test split, cross-validation, holdout test set); no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported and the platform is described as in early stages of development.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Reliance on voluntary citizen-science contributions (variable data quality and quantity); no information on participating users; no quantitative feedback on the educational impact of tutorials; single antibiotic and small number of strains limiting generalisability; titration data only for EC1 and EC3.

raw.Sample_Size: 49,074 single-cell images; 1,045,199 classifications by 5,273 volunteers (1,003,588 classifications by 4,927 users after removing training images)

raw.Feature_Engineering: Seven CellProfiler features measured per cell (number of DNA regions, mean and SD of integrated DNA intensity, mean SD of DNA intensity, nucleoid area fraction, membrane form factor, membrane major axis length); all measurements normalised with StandardScaler; a normally distributed random-noise feature added as a control.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Seven features chosen a priori for potential biological relevance to the ciprofloxacin response (Fig. S2)
raw.Num_Features_Total: 8 (7 image features + 1 random-noise control feature)

raw.Other_Metrics: Mean Absolute Error 0.15 ± 0.01 (Random Forest, holdout); per-strain Zooniverse and model accuracies (Table 1); accuracies by treatment concentration (Fig. 2b); Gini coefficient of volunteer participation 0.81; median SHAP values per feature.
raw.Baseline_Method: Citizen-scientist (human) classification performance; normally distributed random-noise feature as a null baseline in the SHAP feature-importance analysis
raw.Baseline_Performance: Volunteers 66.8 ± 0.1% overall accuracy (sensitive 66.4 ± 0.2%; resistant 67.3 ± 0.2%)
raw.Internal_Validation: 75–25 train-test split with cross-validation (Mean Absolute Error) and a holdout test dataset
raw.Clinical_Insights: DNA compaction and heterogeneity, and the space the nucleoid occupies within the cell, are the key features determining whether an E. coli cell is responding to ciprofloxacin treatment.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Findings are limited to one antibiotic (ciprofloxacin) and a small number of E. coli strains, which limits generalisability to other antibiotics and pathogens.
raw.Integration_Point: Single-cell imaging-based antimicrobial susceptibility test on a microfluidic device, usable as a point-of-care test
raw.End_User_Described: Laboratory and clinical users of a rapid antibiotic susceptibility test (point-of-care healthcare settings)

raw.Barriers_List: Antibiotic response phenotypes of common pathogens and antibiotics must be characterised first; method requires a fluorescence microscope and microfluidic chips; platform still in early stages of development.
raw.Facilitators_List: Large, fast public participation through the Zooniverse citizen-science platform; a single-step, fast workflow and rich image features captured.
raw.Future_Directions: Explore other bacterial species and antibiotics; improve training materials and guidelines; raise public awareness; assess impact of tools on user education; capture more data on volunteer decision-making.

raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: It relied on voluntary contributions from citizen scientists, which introduced variability in data quality and quantity.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear: accuracy, 95% confidence intervals (Wald method with continuity correction), MAE, SHAP values and thresholds are reported explicitly.
raw.Page_References: p. 1 abstract; Table 1 p. 3; Methods pp. 2–5; Results pp. 5–8; Fig. 2 pp. 6–7; Fig. 6 caption p. 11; Data availability p. 12

studies.title: Automated detection of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with the MRSA CHROM imaging application on BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System
studies.sample_size: 1,593 evaluable specimens (1,775 enrolled, 166 excluded, 16 without a standard-of-care result removed)
studies.ai_purpose: To automate the reading of chromogenic MRSA screening plates: the MRSA App uses digital plate images and conventional image processing plus a four-stage machine-learning pipeline to interpret colorimetric information (mauve colonies), detect MRSA growth and sort cultures into categories for batch reading, replacing manual reading of agar plate images.
studies.pathogens_reported: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212 is named only as the negative quality-control organism.

raw.Title: Automated detection of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with the MRSA CHROM imaging application on BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System
raw.Funder_Names: Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD Life Sciences — Integrated Diagnostic Solutions)
raw.Population_Description: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one per patient) collected at three sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) between January and August 2019; a single 30 µl aliquot was inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II and imaged on the BD Kiestra TLA System. 1,775 specimens enrolled, 1,593 evaluable; deidentified patient age and gender recorded but no clinical characteristics reported.
raw.Age_Range: 3% of specimens from patients less than 20 years of age; 27% aged 20–59 years; 69% aged 60 years and over; no demographic information for 1%
raw.Data_Source_Other: Digital agar plate images of BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II captured by the BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System and managed in the Colony Information System (CIS)/Clindex; ground truth from laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images.
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
raw.Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Infection prevention and control team
raw.Delivery_Platform: Instrument / device embedded; Laboratory information system (LIS) integrated
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: MRSA App (BD Kiestra methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus Application) — the only model evaluated: sensitivity 98.15% (95% CI, 96.03, 99.32), specificity 96.69% (95% CI, 95.55, 97.60), concordance 96.98%, PPV 88.11%, NPV 99.52%. Internally it comprises four machine-learning models (zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification, plate positivity) for which no per-model metrics are reported.
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level the paper's own evidence supports is external validation: this is the first evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, a locked commercial algorithm, applied without retraining to independent anterior nares specimens collected at three sites in two countries (two US, one Canada) and read against a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard, with sensitivity (98.15%) and specificity (96.69%) reported. No model development or training on the study data is described, and there is no prospective clinical impact evaluation, CDS integration or routine-use assessment of this cohort.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Discrepant specimens were not available for repeat testing to confirm that discrepancies were not imaging artefacts, nor for confirmation of MRSA positivity by a different testing method; the study design allowed technologists at each site to choose one of two streaking patterns, so the higher false-positive count at Site 3 may reflect the pattern chosen, and de-identification prevented further analysis.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False-positive App results carry the potential for unwarranted patient management: about one in ten MRSA-App-positive results could trigger isolation, topical or systemic antibiotics or other clinical attention although the patient is negative; in this study technologists were blinded to App results, and in real-world use all suspected positives would be reviewed by a technologist.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Laboratory-automation diagnostic accuracy study of an AI imaging application (BD Kiestra MRSA App) on chromogenic MRSA screening plates; no patient-level clinical or sociodemographic data beyond age band and gender. Two conventions had to be judged. (1) Validation/maturity: the paper reports no development or training data, so the multi-site evaluation of the pre-existing commercial algorithm is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only', Clinical_Maturity_Level 3) rather than internal validation of the study's own dataset — flagged for team discussion. (2) Best_Performing_Model: a single index test is evaluated and no models are compared, so the NA checkbox is ticked. Reported artefact: the negative predictive value CI is printed in reverse order ('98.96, 98.78') in the results text. Sex was collected (gender stored in Clindex/CIS) but no sex distribution is reported.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Whether a locked, sponsor-developed commercial application evaluated for the first time on independent multi-site specimens is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only' / Clinical_Maturity_Level 3, as recorded here) or as internal validation of the study's own dataset (level 2); the MRSA App's training/development data are not reported anywhere in the paper.
raw.Sample_Size: 1,593 evaluable specimens (1,775 enrolled, 166 excluded, 16 without a standard-of-care result removed)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: S.M., J.L., D.M., C.O., J.-M.V. and K.B. are employees of the study sponsor (Becton, Dickinson and Company) and own BD shares; D.R. has received research support for this investigation and performed sponsored research with Abbott, Altona, BD, bioMerieux, Cepheid, Luminex, Hardy Diagnostics, HelixBind, Hologic, Qiagen, Q-Linea, Roche, Specific Diagnostics, Cleveland Diagnostics, Thermo Fisher and Vela Diagnostics, served as an advisor for Roche, Thermo Fisher, Luminex/DiaSorin and Seegene, received travel funds from Cepheid and owns equity in Next Gen Diagnostics; M.D. has received research support for this investigation; P.P. and C.E.G. have no conflicts; E.M. has received research support for this investigation and is a sponsored speaker for BD.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens collected at the three participating sites (standard of care at each facility); only one Eswab per patient was eligible for inclusion.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Plates removed from the incubator at any point before completion of the imaging process, or specimens meeting routine laboratory rejection criteria; after enrolment, 166 specimens were excluded (inoculation outside QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or failed image quality check, no truth collected) and 16 further cultures with no standard-of-care result were removed.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Imaging; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation (TLA) System with the BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II (CHROMagar); Colony Information System (CIS) and Clindex (BD Clinical Information system)
raw.Dataset_Size: 1,593 specimens evaluated (from 1,775 enrolled; 166 excluded; 16 without SOC result)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Three clinical laboratory sites: two in the United States (Illinois, Ohio) and one in Canada (Ontario) — a North American, high-income multi-site sample; representativeness of the wider population is not discussed.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one 30 µl aliquot inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA from anterior nares surveillance specimens: agreement between the MRSA App's automated colorimetric interpretation of CHROMagar MRSA II plate images (mauve colony growth) and the reference standard of laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images, reported as sensitivity, specificity, concordance, PPV and NPV.
raw.Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212 is named only as the negative quality-control organism.
raw.Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is presence/absence of MRSA (mauve colony growth) on chromogenic agar; no antimicrobial class outcome is modelled and no susceptibility testing was performed.
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Not tested: methicillin resistance is inferred from the chromogenic MRSA phenotype (mauve colonies); no susceptibility testing was performed.
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Mauve-pigmented (chromogenic) colony growth on BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II read from digital plate images = MRSA positive; plates are first assigned growth/no growth, and growing plates are assessed for chromogenic colony appearance signalling MRSA. The label is the laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images (standard of care / reference standard).
raw.AI_Purpose: To automate the reading of chromogenic MRSA screening plates: the MRSA App uses digital plate images and conventional image processing plus a four-stage machine-learning pipeline to interpret colorimetric information (mauve colonies), detect MRSA growth and sort cultures into categories for batch reading, replacing manual reading of agar plate images.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 (the MRSA App as a single index test, compared with the technologist reference standard; the App itself combines four machine-learning models — zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification and plate positivity — with no per-model comparison)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Areas of interest (pixel-value changes after incubation, i.e. CFUs or artefacts) are detected by conventional image processing; color, morphology, metrics and opacity are extracted from each zone and fed to an initial machine-learning model (CFU vs other), then plate-level metrics and descriptors of the detected CFU population feed a second model for growth status, with mauve/non-mauve classification and plate positivity in two further models.
raw.Software_Libraries: R (R Core Team, 2020) version 4.0.2; MedCalc Software (v.22.021)
raw.Other_Metrics: Concordance 96.98% (1,545/1,593); PPV 88.11% (95% CI, 84.62, 90.89); NPV 99.52% (95% CI, 98.96, 98.78 — as printed); 48 discrepant results (3.01%) with per-site discrepancy rates 0.8% (5/634), 2.7% (17/634) and 8% (26/325); 42 false positives and 6 false negatives; site-level sensitivities 99.56%, 91.30%, 98.00% and specificities 99.01%, 97.79%, 90.91%; chi-square tests across sites with P-values 0.0036, 0.0015, 0.0002, 0.0416, 0.9301NS and <0.0001.
raw.Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the same digital agar plate images by two trained, blinded laboratory technologists at each site (with a third arbiter reader if consensus was not reached), used as the reference standard / standard of care.
raw.Baseline_Performance: The technologist reading is the reference standard and is not scored separately; agreement with the MRSA App was 96.98% (1,545/1,593) with 42 App-only detections (false positives) and 6 technologist-only detections (false negatives).
raw.External_Validation_Description: First evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, applied without retraining to anterior nares specimens collected independently at three clinical sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) and compared with a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard; no training or development dataset is reported in the paper.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Authors argue that in real-world use, where technologists are not blinded to the App results, all suspected MRSA-positive plates would be reviewed by a technologist and the App's PPV would therefore likely be higher than the 88.11% measured here.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Multi-site diagnostic accuracy evaluation of the locked MRSA App against a blinded technologist reference standard on independent specimens (sensitivity 98.15%, specificity 96.69%); no model training on the study data, no prospective clinical impact evaluation, no CDS integration and no routine-use evidence reported for this cohort.
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory BD Kiestra TLA workflow: CHROMagar MRSA II plates imaged after 22-24 h of incubation, sorted by the MRSA App into batch-reading categories for technologist review and confirmation, with results then entered into the laboratory information system for viewing by physicians and clinical staff in the electronic medical record.
raw.End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists / medical laboratory technologists who read and interpret the plate images (with clinicians receiving the results); no other end user is specified.
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The App sorts MRSA screening cultures into growth/no growth categories so technologists can rapidly review and confirm pigmented colonies; cultures without growth can be batch-reviewed in up to 20 plates before final results, reducing data entry; in European laboratories mauve colonies are technologist-reviewed before reporting, no-growth cultures are automatically released and non-mauve growth is batch reported.
raw.Stewardship_Details: Not measured: the paper states only that faster reporting may support antimicrobial stewardship efforts, without assessing any stewardship outcome.
raw.Barriers_List: False-positive App results (42/1,593; PPV 88.11%) would need technologist review and confirmation to avoid unwarranted isolation and antibiotics; discrepant specimens were unavailable for repeat testing to exclude imaging artefacts; site-to-site variation in performance (lower sensitivity at Site 2, lower specificity at Site 3) and the two-option streaking pattern that could not be analysed further after de-identification; no visual explanation for 28 App-only detections.
raw.Facilitators_List: Laboratory staffing shortages and an ageing workforce; existing laboratory automation (Kiestra TLA, Copan WASPLab) already integrated in clinical microbiology laboratories; batch reading of no-growth cultures (up to 20 plates) and European auto-release of no-growth cultures reduce hands-on time, data entry and reporting delays.
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (digital agar plate images / microbiological colony features; laboratory plate-level metrics and CFU descriptors)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Discrepant specimens not available for repeat testing or confirmation by another method; study design allowed two streaking patterns, a possible explanation for the higher FP rate at Site 3 that could not be investigated further because specimens were de-identified; unexplained App-only detections (28 cultures); higher FP than FN balance driven by sensitivity-prioritising algorithm tuning.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: 166 enrolled specimens were excluded (inoculation outside the QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or a failed image quality check, plates with no truth collected) and 16 further cultures lacked a standard-of-care result; discrepant specimens were not retained for repeat testing; diffuse mauve pigment in the agar at the inoculation site and colony mixtures may explain some App-only detections.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Methods, index test, reference standard and per-site 2x2 data (Table 1) are reported with 95% CIs, but the NPV confidence interval is printed in reverse order as 98.96, 98.78 and the NPV/PPV are given only for the total, not per site.
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-2 (abstract, background, AI program overview); p. 3 (specimen collection, MRSA App algorithm, processing, plate reading); p. 4 (QC, statistics, results incl. PPV/NPV); pp. 5-6 (discussion, Table 1, workflow); p. 7 (limitations, conclusions, funding, contributions); p. 8 (affiliations, data availability, supplemental material, references).

raw.Clinical_Insights: The authors conclude that documented SSRI use is associated with a higher risk of antibiotic-resistant infection, framed as supporting prior in vitro findings and suggesting SSRI usage should be investigated as a possible driver of antimicrobial resistance

Comorbidity/medical-history-only comparison: deep learning AUROC 0.81 (95% CI, 0.81-0.81) and AUPRC 0.30 (95% CI, 0.29-0.31); gradient boosting AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76) and AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23)
