raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation: 80% of the data trained the models (70% training, 10% model selection) and 20% was held out for patient group-specific testing within the same 10 hospitals and period; no external or prospective validation, no CDS integration
raw.Reported_Limitations: Limitations inherent to retrospective analyses based on EHR data; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); a large study capturing difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured data format is nearly impossible
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Widespread overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics (the unintended consequence of previous risk stratification tools derived at centres with high resistance prevalence), which may have detrimental effects at the population and patient levels; national study reporting only 0.9% of samples retrieved ARO GNB while 76% of those patients were flagged as candidates for double GNB coverage
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: The 3 example hospitals differ socioeconomically: an academic quaternary centre serving a socioeconomically diverse population, a suburban community hospital serving an affluent population, and a community-based hospital serving a socioeconomically disadvantaged population; model performance varied with local resistance prevalence rather than patient casemix, so the same patient subgroup falls into different risk categories depending on the institution
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board approved the study and granted a waiver of consent due to the retrospective nature of the study; data sharing is via Supplement 2; no code or model sharing statement
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Record built from the pypdf text layer. Main judgements: the paper evaluates 2 models (a deep learning model named as 'the main tool' and a gradient-boosting model dedicated to SHAP variable importance) and reports no single primary dataset - results are given separately for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, so Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/Precision/F1 are answered No and AUROC/AUPRC are reported for the deep learning model with both onset settings named
raw.Unresolved_Items: No model-level AUROC is printed for the hospital-onset model (only AUPRC 0.25 for RS and 0.16 for RR); the AUROC 0.81 (0.81-0.81) figure appears only in the comorbidity-subset comparison and does not state which dataset; the paper names no single primary dataset for the review's unit of analysis
raw.Sample_Size: 39 893 patients with 85 238 sepsis episodes
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr Vazquez Guillamet reported selling stocks in Carsima Therapeutics, Bionano Genomics, and Ocugen Inc in September 2023 outside the submitted work; Dr Fraser reported that their spouse is a former senior vice president/chief medical officer and now consulting for Cigna/Express Scripts; no other disclosures were reported
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients meeting the US CDC adult sepsis event criteria admitted to any of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals between January 2016 to October 2021; inclusion combined presumed infection (blood cultures and 4 qualifying days of antibiotics) with concomitant organ dysfunction (any of vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, increased creatinine or bilirubin levels, and thrombocytopenia)
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: 148 patients excluded due to missing antimicrobial susceptibility results and 77 due to missing sex or race
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: Electronic health record of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals, greater St Louis region, Missouri and Illinois
raw.Dataset_Size: 49 726 admissions and 85 238 sepsis episodes in the final dataset
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Removed patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race); carried forward the last observation for missing laboratory results and vitals
raw.Ethnicity_Details: Race and ethnicity: Black 9112 (22.8%), White 23 982 (60.1%), Other 6799 (17.0%) in the entire cohort
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Large and diverse dataset of patients across urban and rural areas of the greater St Louis region in Missouri and Illinois; 3 hospitals illustrated as examples of different patient casemixes, including a socioeconomically disadvantaged population
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture specimen: Blood 1602 (13.7%), Urine 4575 (39.0%), Respiratory 2957 (25.2%), Other 2598 (22.1%)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: GNB antimicrobial resistance level in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis episodes, categorised as ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR)
raw.Pathogens: Escherichia coli (36.2% of RR isolates, community-onset), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (56.6% of RS isolates in community-onset; 58.3% in hospital-onset), Klebsiella spp; non-GNB organisms (eg, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, viruses) were labelled SS
raw.Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefepime)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: ceftriaxone; cefepime
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility results documented in the EHR; ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS; negative cultures and non-GNB cultures also labelled SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR); the most resistant GNB microbe determined the category for polymicrobial cultures; intermediate isolates labelled susceptible; CLSI breakpoints based on minimal inhibitory concentration
raw.AI_Purpose: To develop deep learning models based on artificial neural networks (separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis) that project levels of antimicrobial resistance in GNB, and to assess whether patient casemix and local prevalence rates of resistance explain the variable performance of a general risk stratification model across hospitals and patient subgroups
raw.Feature_Engineering: All vitals and laboratory data points within 5 days of the culture timestamp were resampled and the mean value of every 4-hour window was used by the deep learning model; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; shock defined as vasopressor or inotrope use within 24 hours of the culture timestamp; age, time since admission, vital signs and laboratory results treated as continuous; hospital, sex and race categorical; procedures, antibiotic administration, comorbidities and previous susceptible or resistant culture results binary; all input variables screened at the culture timestamp
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Laboratory value and vital sign features selected considering redundancy, collinearity, and availability in the EHR; gradient-boosting model with SHAP dedicated to variable importance for the first 10 features contributing to the model
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to oversample the RR and RS minority groups and focal loss to reweight the loss of the minority group
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Gradient boosting implemented with tuned tree depth and feature subsampling; deep learning implemented with tuned network width and depth and learning rate; a 10% random validation split of the training set used to monitor validation performance and terminate training before overfitting
raw.Software_Libraries: PyTorch version 2.1; XGBoost version 2.0.0; scikit-learn version 1.3.0
raw.Other_Metrics: AUPRC for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis; SHAP values for feature importance; correlation (R) between AUPRC and RS/RR prevalence rates
raw.Baseline_Method: Gradient-boosting model (XGBoost) compared with the deep learning model on the comorbidity and medical-history feature subset
raw.Baseline_Performance: Gradient boosting: AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76); AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23) (deep learning comparator: AUROC 0.81 [95% CI, 0.81-0.81]; AUPRC 0.30 [95% CI, 0.29-0.31])
raw.Internal_Validation: 80/20 split: 70% training, 10% model selection, 20% holdout for patient group-specific testing (infections from the same patient exist only in either the training or the testing set); 10% random validation split of the training set to terminate training before overfitting; models tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis
raw.Train_Test_Split: 80% train (70% for training and 10% for model selection); 20% holdout set for patient group-specific testing
raw.External_Validation_Description: None - the general model was tested on holdout data from the same hospitals and period
raw.Overfitting_Method: 10% random validation split of the training set used for both models to monitor validation performance during training and terminate training before overfitting; model brittleness (failure to generalise) addressed by developing a general model tested on same-hospital holdout data
raw.Clinical_Insights: In community-onset sepsis, history of P aeruginosa infections and history of antibiotic administration were the strongest factors discriminating RS and RR from SS; history of antibiotic-resistant organisms and previous episodes of severe sepsis or septic shock were associated with RR. In hospital-onset sepsis, age and history of P aeruginosa infections were the most impactful factors; time since admission was associated with lower risk of SS and higher risk of RR. Vasopressor use and longitudinal data added minimal contributions.
raw.Generalisability_Details: The results do not support widespread use of generalized models; model performance was associated with prevalence rates of resistant GNB and varied across hospitals and patient subgroups; future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates to accompany patient-level variables
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal holdout testing only: 80/20 patient group-specific split, models trained on the whole training set and tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, results reported without oversampling; performance varied widely across hospitals and subgroups and the authors conclude against widespread use of generalized models
raw.Integration_Point: Not described for this model (research model evaluated on holdout data); the Epic Sepsis Model is described as integrated into the clinical EHR system as prior work
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing between narrow- or broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics for patients with sepsis; risk stratification models that guide clinicians' empirical choices
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction of antimicrobial resistance must occur at suspicion of infection to initiate empirical antibiotics, so all input variables were screened at the culture timestamp
raw.Stewardship_Details: No stewardship outcome was measured; the authors state that future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates, and that the results argue against the use of generalized models for predicting resistant GNB etiologies in sepsis
raw.Barriers_List: Difficult-to-extract variables such as nursing home residence are not usually stored in a structured data format, making a large study that captures them nearly impossible; study limitations inherent to retrospective EHR-based analyses; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices)
raw.Facilitators_List: Model robustness against subgroup distribution heterogeneity may be improved using domain generalization approaches or group-fairness classification approaches, which the authors are considering for future work
raw.Future_Directions: Future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates (warranting availability of microbiology data) to accompany patient-level variables; institutions are encouraged to develop their own risk stratification models to identify patients at risk for resistant GNB, similar to maintaining local antibiograms; domain generalization and group-fairness approaches are being considered
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values from the gradient-boosting model, reported as mean impact on model output magnitude for the top 10 features
raw.Limitation_Categories: Retrospective EHR-based analysis; unmeasured confounders (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured format; no external or prospective validation; model performance not transferable across hospitals
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race) were removed; the last observation was carried forward for missing laboratory results and vitals; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; missing antimicrobial susceptibility results handled by general logic rules for intrinsic resistance
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear - STROBE reporting guideline and published recommendations for machine learning models followed; full feature list and preprocessing details in Supplement 1 (eTable, eFigures 1-2); all results reported with 95% CIs

raw.Title: Machine Learning-Led Optimization of Combination Therapy: Confronting the Public Health Threat of Extensively Drug Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria
raw.Country_Countries: United States of America (Buffalo and Troy, New York; Nutley, New Jersey; San Diego, California)
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
raw.Study_Design_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments providing the pharmacodynamic data for a mechanism-based mathematical model
raw.Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (R01AI165997; R01AI148560; L30AI164450)
raw.Population_Description: Four clinical, extensively drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada) studied in 7-day in vitro hollow fiber infection model experiments; regimens simulated in a critically ill patient population using published human population PK models (no human participants)
raw.Data_Source_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) data from previously performed studies (35 experiments, 1,056 samples) and previously published human population pharmacokinetic models for each agent
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
raw.Task_Type_Other: Genetic algorithm (GA)-led optimisation of multi-drug dosing regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) against PK/PD/toxicodynamic end points; mechanism-based pharmacodynamic model fitting and Monte Carlo simulation
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Four GA fitness functions (F1-F4) tested across 13 optimisation end points: PD-only end points (F1, 10 2 CFU/mL at the 90th/80th/70th/60th prediction interval), polymyxin B TD-only end points (F2), and joint polymyxin B + aztreonam TD end points with two weighting schemes (F3 0.990/0.005/0.005; F4 0.90/0.05/0.05). Reported output is target attainment and regimen parameters (Table 1) - no accuracy, AUROC or error metric is reported for any optimisation scheme.
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level supported: the mechanism-based PD model was internally qualified with visual predictive checks and the GA regimens were evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation only; no external validation, prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Only four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates / 35 HFIM experiments, so a larger, more representative panel of isolates is needed to match current XDR epidemiology; regimens were optimised on literature PK reports from monotherapy studies in critically ill patients, whereas co-administration augments exposure and optimal doses could therefore be lower.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The GA 1:1 PD:TD weighting scheme had to be abandoned: it terminated early after 200 iterations with no change in the fitness function and produced a regimen that attained the polymyxin B AUC24,ss target of 100 mg·h/L but failed to produce bacterial killing. Toxicity targets (polymyxin B nephrotoxicity, aztreonam hepatotoxicity) also constrained the optimised regimens.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Prospective regimen-optimisation study, not a diagnostic model: no classification/discrimination metrics exist, so every *_Reported accuracy field is answered No rather than left blank. AI_Application_Type and Task_Type have no vocabulary entry for GA-based regimen optimisation, so 'Other' was used (with AI Predictive and Prognostic Models / AI Clinical Decision Support Systems ticked for the modelling and regimen-guidance aspects) and Needs_Team_Discussion is Yes.
raw.Sample_Size: 4 clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); HFIM dataset of 35 experiments and 1,056 samples
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared no competing interests for this work.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Four clinical K. pneumoniae isolates from previously performed hollow fiber infection model studies (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); no patient-level eligibility criteria are reported
raw.Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
raw.Data_Source_Name: Not a named repository: hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments from previously performed studies plus published human population PK models for aztreonam, ceftazidime/avibactam and polymyxin B
raw.Dataset_Size: 35 7-day HFIM experiments (1,056 samples) across 4 isolates; 13 GA optimisation end points each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Four clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so the authors state that a larger panel of isolates should be explored to properly generalise the results to current XDR epidemiology
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Bacterial killing of XDR K. pneumoniae by GA-optimised combination regimens: attainment of a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection) in the HFIM, while keeping polymyxin B and aztreonam exposures within their toxicity limits
raw.Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (four clinical extensively drug-resistant isolates: ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada)
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (aztreonam, ceftazidime); beta-lactamase inhibitor (avibactam); polymyxins (polymyxin B)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Aztreonam; ceftazidime; avibactam; polymyxin B
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Threshold definition, not a metric: the bacterial PD end point was a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection, lower end of reported bacteraemia concentrations); the PK/TD end points were polymyxin B AUC24,ss = 100 mg/h/L and aztreonam AUCss = 1,336 mg/h/L, each evaluated at a prediction interval of simulated subjects
raw.Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
raw.AI_Purpose: Use a genetic algorithm, driven by a mechanism-based PD model with human population PK, to optimise aztreonam + ceftazidime/avibactam +/- polymyxin B combination regimens de novo against joint efficacy and toxicity end points for XDR K. pneumoniae
raw.Num_Models_Compared: No head-to-head comparison of predictive models: 4 GA fitness functions (F1-F4) across 13 optimisation end points, each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
raw.Feature_Engineering: Mechanism-based PD model translated to RxODE with HFIM PKs replaced by published human PopPK models; regimen inputs (dose, infusion time, doses per day, loading dose) rounded to the nearest milligram, 0.5 hours and integer value before GA evaluation
raw.Software_Libraries: GA package in R (genetic algorithm); RxODE solved with the Livermore Solver for Ordinary Differential Equations
raw.Other_Metrics: Regimen target attainment (10 2 CFU/mL at 168 h), median infusion duration 2 h (range 1.5-3 h), median dosing interval 9 h (range 6-12 h), mean aztreonam 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day, mean ceftazidime/avibactam 8.55 g/day (SD 1.45), mean polymyxin B 3.18 mg/kg/day (SD 1.05) producing AUC24,ss,avg 115 mg/h/L
raw.Baseline_Method: Comparator regimens derived empirically over years of clinical use, and current FDA package labelling for each agent
raw.Baseline_Performance: Optimised aztreonam daily dose 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day (with vs without an aztreonam TD end point) against FDA-labelled 6-8 g/day; optimised ceftazidime/avibactam dose exceeded the package label (mean 8.55 g/day); polymyxin B optimisation produced AUC24,ss,avg 93.5-115 mg/h/L against the 100 mg/h/L consensus target
raw.Internal_Validation: Visual predictive checks used to internally qualify the mechanism-based PD model
raw.Clinical_Insights: PD/TD weighting must be deferential to patient safety and clinical feasibility because missing an individual target carries consequences such as microbiological failure or drug toxicity; optimised regimens mirror empirically derived clinical dosing (prolonged beta-lactam infusion, higher avibactam exposure) and are proposed as a testing framework for new or special-population regimens
raw.Generalisability_Details: Four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so a larger and more representative panel of isolates is needed for the results to match current XDR epidemiology (strain types, virulence factors, resistance mechanisms); regimens rest on monotherapy PK data from critically ill patients
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal qualification of the mechanism-based PD model by visual predictive checks and Monte Carlo evaluation of GA-optimised regimens; no external validation cohort, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
raw.Integration_Point: Output of the optimised regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) is proposed for clinical trial simulation and preclinical regimen design; not integrated into any clinical, EHR or LIS system
raw.End_User_Described: Not named explicitly: the framework is aimed at preclinical drug development and at regimen design for special patient populations, i.e. researchers and prescribers in critically ill patients
raw.Barriers_List: Multiple PK end points must be met simultaneously for combination therapy and target attainment multiplies geometrically with each added drug, making optimisation experimentally intractable; choice of PD/TD weighting affects the search; PK variability between drugs; the 1:1 weighting scheme failed to explore the parameter space
raw.Facilitators_List: GA-led regimen design can be integrated into preclinical drug development to produce testable regimens, avoid pre-existing notions of a 'best' schedule, reduce the number of animal experiments, and hypothesise alternative regimens for special patient populations with altered PK
raw.Future_Directions: Expand the isolate panel to a representative sample of the most resistant isolates (by national prevalence of strain types, virulence factors and resistance mechanisms) so the results generalise to current XDR K. pneumoniae epidemiology; apply GA-led regimen design to new drugs and to special patient populations
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Mechanism-based model interaction terms: avibactam reduces the aztreonam KC50 by up to 99.3%, and polymyxin B kills aztreonam-induced persister cells
raw.Limitation_Categories: Limited isolate panel and generalisability; reliance on historical monotherapy PK data; modelling assumptions (persister cell subpopulation, two-subpopulation structure)
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Regimens were optimised on prior literature PK reports in critically ill patients all studied in monotherapy; co-administration of aztreonam and ceftazidime/avibactam augments exposure, so optimised doses could be lower than reported
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model, GA implementation (13 end points, population size 75, weightings) and optimised regimen parameters are reported in detail, but only PK/PD target attainment is reported - no accuracy-type performance statistics, no confidence intervals, no calibration

raw.Title: Development and validation of machine learning models to predict MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission by using electronic health record data
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
raw.Population_Description: ICU patients (adults, ICU stay ≥24 h) from PLAGH-ICU (n=3,536) and MIMIC-IV (n=34,923) who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; outcome is MDRO colonization or infection.
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: PLAGH-ICU (via SHAP values): C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), serum urea, duration of pre-ICU hospital stay, interleukin-6 (IL-6), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: LR, KNN, SVC, RF, XGBoost, MLP, and a stacking ensemble. In temporal validation the ensemble models performed best: PLAGH-ICU AUROC 0.786 [0.748, 0.825]; MIMIC-IV AUROC 0.744 [0.723, 0.766]. By AUROC, Random Forest, XGBoost and Ensemble outperformed the other algorithms.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Ensemble model
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Best-performing ensemble model on PLAGH-ICU temporal validation set
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation performed: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615); therefore maturity level 3 (external validation).
raw.Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design requiring prospective validation; low precision (positive predictive value) at thresholds ensuring higher recall, entailing potential high costs if applied clinically; models built from specific institutions may not be directly applicable elsewhere; feature importance indicates correlation, not causality.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Low positive predictive value at high-recall thresholds could entail high costs if applied clinically at this stage.
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Implementation challenges include data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, and regulatory compliance.
raw.Sample_Size: 3,536 patients (PLAGH-ICU)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
raw.Sex_Distribution: PLAGH-ICU Table 1: male n (%) — non-MDRO 1,980 (63.6), MDRO 301 (71.2)
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Patients who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; aged ≥18 years; ICU stay ≥24 h.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Age <18 years; ICU stay <24 h; MDRO detected within 14 days prior to ICU admission; positive MDRO within 1 day of ICU admission.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: PLAGH-ICU; MIMIC-IV version 2.2
raw.Dataset_Size: 3,536 patients (PLAGH-ICU); 34,923 patients (MIMIC-IV)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Variables with >30% missing excluded; cases with >20% missing lab values excluded; Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) for the remaining missing data.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Two centres: an ICU of the (Chinese) PLA General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (USA), the latter via the MIMIC-IV database.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Body fluid samples (not further specified)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission (binary outcome).

raw.Drug_Classes: three or more classes of antimicrobial agents (not enumerated)

raw.AI_Purpose: Early detection of patients at risk of MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission, to curb MDRO proliferation and support empirical pharmacotherapy.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 7 (6 base algorithms + stacking ensemble)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Min-max normalization before training LR, KNN, SVC and MLP models; Spearman correlation-based clustering to remove collinear features; MICE imputation; top-25 feature distillation.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Spearman's rank correlation for stratified clustering (collinearity removal), then Random Forest permutation feature importance ranking; top 25 features retained.
raw.Num_Features_Total: 25 (retained for the final prediction model)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Bayesian optimization with 5-fold cross-validation
raw.Software_Libraries: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, shap (Python); dplyr, ggplot2, pROC (R)
raw.Other_Metrics: Brier score, calibration curve intercept and slope, decision curve analysis (standardized net benefit).
raw.Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression (LR)
raw.Internal_Validation: Temporal validation within each dataset (data 2017-2019, after training on 2008-2016); 5-fold cross-validation used for hyperparameter tuning.
raw.External_Validation_Description: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (peak AUROC 0.638 [0.628, 0.648]); MIMIC-IV model assessed on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615 [0.585, 0.646]).
raw.Clinical_Insights: Interpretability allows clinicians to identify high-risk patients, understand individual risk profiles, and tailor treatment plans.
raw.Data_Repository: MIMIC-IV via PhysioNet (physionet.org/content/mimiciv/2.2/); other data from the corresponding author on request
raw.Generalisability_Details: Models show significant variance in feature selection and performance across institutions; collecting data from various hospitals/regions could enhance generalizability; unit-specific MDRO early-warning models may be preferable.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed in both directions: PLAGH-ICU model on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615) — sets maturity at level 3.
raw.Integration_Point: ICU-admission screening / risk stratification; future CDSS integration
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians (ICU)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Deployment with real-time data integration via EHR-compatible interfaces; models incorporated into a CDSS delivering alerts and recommendations.
raw.Barriers_List: Data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, regulatory compliance; limited feature-target correlations in early ICU EHR data; poor cross-institution transferability.
raw.Facilitators_List: Models are easily adaptable to hospital EHR systems and use routinely available EHR data.
raw.Future_Directions: Deployment in clinical settings with real-time data integration; integration into a CDSS; establishing a monitoring framework to continuously assess and enhance model performance.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP values
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Shorter pre-ICU hospital stays in PLAGH-ICU surprisingly correlated with increased MDRO risk (possibly reflecting resistant-bacteria carriage among patients transferred from other hospitals or community-acquired MDRO).
raw.Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design; need for prospective validation; low precision (PPV) / potential clinical cost; limited cross-institution generalizability; feature importance reflects correlation not causality.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data handled by excluding variables with >30% missing and cases with >20% missing lab values, then MICE imputation.

raw.Title: Machine learning algorithms to predict colistin-induced nephrotoxicity from electronic health records in patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection
raw.Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
raw.Funder_Names: Ministry of Education
raw.Population_Description: 1392 patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDRGN) infection receiving their first intravenous colistin at three Taipei Medical University hospitals (TMUH, SHH, WFH), Taiwan, 2011-2020; adults (>=18 y) with >=2 d of colistin, no chronic dialysis and available serum creatinine records
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP feature importance (CAT-SVM-SMOTE): days of colistin use, cumulative dose, daily dose, latest C-reactive protein, and baseline haemoglobin
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: 15 models (CatBoost, LGB, RF x SVM-SMOTE, SMOTE, SMOTETL, Tomek and original data) compared by sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC on the temporal validation set (heatmap, Supplementary Table S11). Best RFE-estimated F1: CatBoost 0.603 (48 features), LGB 0.610 (46 features), RF 0.585 (16 features). Best model CAT-SVM-SMOTE: AUROC 0.823, AUPRC 0.737, sensitivity 0.860, F1 0.740, MCC 0.533
raw.Best_Performing_Model: CAT-SVM-SMOTE (CatBoost with SVM-SMOTE resampling) - decided by the highest AUROC (0.823) and AUPRC (0.737), together with the highest sensitivity (0.860), F1 (0.740) and MCC (0.533) on the temporal validation set
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The reported performance of the best model comes from a temporally separate validation cohort (2018-2020, n=402) distinct from the derivation cohort (2011-2017), i.e. TRIPOD type 3 temporal/external validation; no prospective or independent multi-centre external test is reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design limits applicability; multiple healthcare datasets needed to generalise; newer AKI biomarkers (cystatin C, NGAL, IL-18) not assessed; features with >25% missing data discarded may have introduced bias; covariate shift between the two cohorts
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: High-sensitivity predictions may elevate false positives, but the authors argue the benefits outweigh misidentifying false negatives
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Vulnerable patients developing AKI despite low colistin doses are identified (14 of 17 patients with very low daily doses were AKI-positive), but no equity analysis by demographic group is reported
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Only ethics approval is described: Joint IRB approval with a waiver of patient consent for de-identified registry data; no data-sharing or model-governance plan, and no regulatory clearance
raw.Sample_Size: 1392 patients (989 in the derivation cohort and 402 in the temporal validation cohort)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: Declared none: "The authors bear all of the responsibility for the data in this article and have no conflicts of interest to declare."
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Admission to TMU Hospital (TMUH), Shuang Ho Hospital (SHH) or Wan Fang Hospital (WFH) with a first intravenous colistin course between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020; a patient needing more than two courses after a cured episode with an interval >90 d was treated as a new subject for the second course
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Pregnancy, age <18 y, colistin period <2 d, chronic dialysis, or no serum creatinine (SCr) records
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: Taipei Medical University Clinical Research Database (TMUCRD)
raw.Dataset_Size: 1392 patients (989 derivation / 402 temporal validation); 77 candidate features reduced by RFE to 48 (CatBoost), 46 (LGB) and 16 (RF)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Features with a missing rate above 25% were discarded; remaining missing values imputed by Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE)
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Three hospitals in one academic health system in Taiwan (single country, single health-system database); generalisability to other geographies and ethnic populations is stated as untested
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: No microbiological specimens analysed - blood/laboratory measurements from the EHR (serum creatinine and eGFR slope, creatinine clearance, WBC, CRP, haemoglobin, BUN, sodium, potassium)
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Colistin-induced nephrotoxicity (acute kidney injury) in patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection, defined by the KDIGO criteria
raw.Pathogens: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDRGN) organisms; individual species are not named in the text
raw.Drug_Classes: Polymyxins (colistin); concomitant nephrotoxic drugs including aminoglycosides and vancomycin
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Colistin (colistimethate sodium); aminoglycoside; vancomycin
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: KDIGO definition of colistin-induced AKI: serum creatinine increase of 0.3 mg/dL from the baseline value within 48 h, or a >=1.5-fold increase within 7 d
raw.AI_Purpose: To construct and compare 15 machine learning models (CatBoost, LGB, RF under four resampling strategies plus original data) that early predict colistin-induced AKI in MDRGN-infected patients, and to interpret the best model with SHAP
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 15 (three algorithms x four resampling strategies plus the original dataset)
raw.Feature_Engineering: New features engineered: creatinine clearance by the Cockcroft-Gault equation and eGFR by the MDRD formula; features with >25% missing rate discarded; remaining missing values imputed by MICE
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive feature elimination (RFE) with 5-fold cross-validation of the training set
raw.Num_Features_Total: 77 candidate features
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE, SVM-SMOTE, Tomek links and SMOTETL (SMOTE + Tomek link); the best model used SVM-SMOTE
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over 36 (CatBoost), 5940 (LGB) and 3520 (RF) combinations, combined with resampling in a pipeline to maximise the F1 score
raw.Software_Libraries: matplotlib.pyplot (AUROC and AUPRC curves); CatBoost, LightGBM and random forest implementations (library names not stated)
raw.Other_Metrics: AUPRC 0.737; MCC 0.533; hazard ratio for high- vs low-risk AKI group 24.79 (95% CI 14.32-42.92, P<0.005); multivariate logistic regression odds ratios (CBA dose/kg 2.113, CKD 1.614, longer course 0.733, other pathogens 0.583)
raw.Baseline_Method: Models built on the original data without resampling (and Tomek under-sampling), compared against SMOTE/SVM-SMOTE/SMOTETL models; multivariate logistic regression as a traditional comparator
raw.Baseline_Performance: Models without resampling had lower sensitivity, F1 and MCC than the resampling models; multivariate logistic regression: CBA dose per kg/day OR 2.113, CKD OR 1.614, longer course length OR 0.733, other pathogens OR 0.583

raw.AUROC_Population_Set: 150 RR-TB patients; test set of an 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random Forest developed and evaluated on internal data only: 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation (ROC-AUC) on 150 RR-TB isolates; no external, prospective or deployed evaluation.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Selection bias from excluding 75 of 225 RR-TB cases (33%); incomplete records in the national TB system so socioeconomic factors (income, education, housing), treatment adherence and prior anti-TB drug exposure were excluded; predominance of L2 strains limiting generalisability.
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Exclusion of socioeconomic factors (income, education, housing), treatment adherence and prior drug exposure because of incomplete records may bias the models toward microbiological and genetic predictors, particularly in retreatment or socially vulnerable patients.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Sex distribution differs between the narrative text (117, 78.0% male) and Table 1 (114, 76.0% male).
raw.Sample_Size: 150 RR-TB patients with successful WGS results (150 isolates)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Patients aged above 18 years with sputum culture-positive, pulmonary, RR-TB assessed for eligibility; those with consent to a standardized RR-TB regimen were included.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Pregnant, or infected with HIV, hepatitis B or C virus, or refused to participate.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: National TB information management system (China)
raw.Dataset_Size: 150 RR-TB patients/isolates with WGS; 133 mutations across 19 antibiotic resistance genes
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Mutations absent from a sample imputed with 0; mutation features restricted to those present in ≥5% of samples; samples with culture failure, contamination (<90% MTBC) or NTM excluded during WGS processing.
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single-region cohort: all patients diagnosed at local TB dispensaries in Ningbo, China; 90.0% of strains were lineage 2 (Beijing family), which the authors note may limit generalisability.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Sputum
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Treatment response in RR-TB measured as sputum culture conversion (SCC) at 2 and 6 months — SCC failure (culture positivity) is the predicted outcome, with phenotypic and genotypic resistance to INH, SM, EMB, AM, CM, LVX, PAS and PTO as determinants.
raw.Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, streptomycin) and second-line drugs (levofloxacin, amikacin, capreomycin, prothionamide, para-aminosalicylic acid), plus genotypic determinants for aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones.
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Phenotypic DST: isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), ethambutol (EMB), streptomycin (SM), levofloxacin (LVX), amikacin (AM), capreomycin (CM), prothionamide (PTO), para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS). Genotypic (TB-Profiler, 15 drugs): AM, BDQ, CM, CFZ, DLM, EMB, ETO, INH, kanamycin, LVX, LZD, MFX, PZA, RIF, SM.
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; Other
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotypic R/S per drug on solid media (Lowenstein-Jensen, WHO recommendations) and WGS-based DST by presence/absence of resistance-associated mutations in a WHO-recommended catalogue (Tier 1/Tier 2); strains were then categorised into RR-TB, MDR-TB and pre-XDR-TB (the 'Other' phenotype category).
raw.AI_Purpose: To identify clinical and genomic determinants of delayed sputum culture conversion and to predict SCC failure at 2 and 6 months in RR-TB patients, using a Random Forest model integrating WGS drug-resistance mutations with clinical and phenotypic DST features.
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 (Random Forest only; no comparator model was trained or benchmarked)
raw.Feature_Engineering: Clinical and phenotypic DST features encoded; mutations imputed with 0; mutation features restricted to those present in ≥5% of samples; RF trained with 100 trees on an 80/20 split with 5-fold CV; class imbalance handled with SMOTE.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Frequency filter — mutations present in ≥5% of samples were selected as features; importance then ranked by mean decrease in accuracy (MDA).
raw.Num_Features_Total: 133 mutations across 19 antibiotic resistance genes; total predictor count (mutations plus clinical/phenotypic features) not reported.
raw.Num_Features_Selected: Not reported numerically — mutations in ≥5% of samples retained as predictors.
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE (DMwR package)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: tuneLength = 3, optimising the number of variables sampled at each split (mtry) with caret's train function
raw.Software_Libraries: caret; randomForest; DMwR (SMOTE); ggplot2; gtsummary; TB-Profiler v6.5.0; fastp v0.20.1; Kraken v2; BWA v0.7.17; SAMtools/BCFtools; IQ-Tree v2
raw.Other_Metrics: ROC-AUC with SD estimated from 100 bootstrap iterations; mean decrease in accuracy (MDA) feature importance with SD from 100 bootstrap iterations; odds ratios and adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs from univariable/multivariable logistic regression.
raw.Internal_Validation: 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation (ROC-AUC); test-set AUC and SD estimated over 100 bootstrap iterations.
raw.Clinical_Insights: Smear positivity and LVX resistance were persistent independent predictors of SCC failure; ML feature importance showed time-dependent mutation effects (embB_p.Met306Ile at 2 months; katG_p.Ser315Thr and gyrA_p.Asp94Gly at 6 months), leading the authors to recommend rapid genotypic LVX testing to guide regimen selection and intensified monitoring of smear-positive patients.
raw.Data_Repository: Not named in the article — stated to be in online repositories / Supplementary Material.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Predominance of lineage 2 (Beijing family) strains may limit generalisability to settings where other lineages dominate; the model is not yet validated in other epidemiological settings; cohort drawn from one Chinese city.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: Random Forest trained on 150 RR-TB isolates with an 80/20 train-test split and 5-fold cross-validation; test-set AUC and SD from 100 bootstrap iterations. No external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians managing drug-resistant TB (use of genotypic LVX resistance testing to guide regimen selection and monitoring of smear-positive patients)
raw.Barriers_List: Incomplete records in the national TB information management system (socioeconomic factors, adherence, prior drug exposure excluded); selection bias from 75 excluded RR-TB cases (33%); predominance of L2 strains; need for standardised socioeconomic assessment and objective adherence monitoring.
raw.Future_Directions: Explore the functional mechanisms underlying the mutation-specific effects and validate the model in diverse epidemiological settings; integrate standardised socioeconomic assessments and objective adherence monitoring; studies with more balanced lineage representation to quantify lineage effects and their interaction with resistance mutations.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mean decrease in accuracy (MDA), with standard deviations from 100 bootstrap iterations
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: rrs_n.1401A>G (aminoglycoside resistance) was prioritised by the ML model although it is rarely assessed in phenotypic DST; mutation-specific temporal effects where katG_p.Ser315Thr and gyrA_p.Asp94Gly emerged as stronger predictors at 6 months.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Selection bias / excluded cases; data quality (incomplete records); omitted socioeconomic, adherence and prior drug exposure variables; single-region population and predominance of L2 lineage limiting generalisability.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Incomplete records in the national TB information management system; 48 enrolled patients lost (follow-up, refusal, death, transfer) and 27 excluded at WGS for culture failure, contamination (<90% MTBC) or NTM infection.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Detailed and clear: model type, features, tuning, validation and metrics are all stated, with bootstrap SDs reported. Minor internal inconsistencies — abstract AUC 0.76 ± 0.10 vs 0.763 ± 0.103 in text/results, and sex distribution 117 (78.0%) in the text vs 114 (76.0%) in Table 1.
raw.Page_References: Journal pages 1-12 (PDF pages 1-12); methods core pp. 2-3, results and model performance pp. 4-6, risk-factor tables pp. 7-9, limitations and funding pp. 10-11.

raw.Title: Development and validation of a hierarchical machine learning method using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for rapid SCCmec typing and PVL detection in MRSA: a multi-centre study

raw.Population_Description: Clinical specimens submitted for suspected bacterial infection at five healthcare institutions (345,748 specimens; 10,227 S. aureus isolates, of which 5,872 MRSA), retrospectively analysed; no patient-level data.

Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and F1-score are also given per row.
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest (named top performer for CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA and most balanced for PVL; XGBoost leads the first MRSA/MSSA step and LGBM the SCCmec II vs I+III step - the paper names no single overall best model)
raw.Accuracy_Population_Set: Validation (test) set, October-December, 10,227 S. aureus isolate spectra; CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA classification step, Random Forest (Table 2)
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validation (test) set, October-December, 10,227 S. aureus isolate spectra; CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA classification step, Random Forest (Table 2)
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Validation (test) set, October-December, 10,227 S. aureus isolate spectra; CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA classification step, Random Forest (Table 2)

raw.Reported_Limitations: AI-CDSS performance depends on MALDI-TOF MS spectra quality, which varies across institutions and instrumentation; consistency in data acquisition and preprocessing needed for reproducibility and generalisability; other virulence factors or resistance mechanisms not modelled; discriminative m/z features are not linked to specific proteins or biological pathways; direct impact on mortality unquantified; further clinical validation warranted.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Table 2 and the Results text disagree for the PVL stage: Table 2 gives Random Forest testing AUC 0.91, accuracy 0.90 and sensitivity 0.99, whereas the text states validating AUC 0.85, accuracy 0.92 and sensitivity 0.75. Performance values were coded from Table 2.
raw.Sample_Size: 345,748 bacterial specimens screened; 10,227 S. aureus isolates (5,872 MRSA; 4,355 MSSA); 2,848 SCCmec type IV isolates for the PVL model
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Clinical specimens submitted for suspected bacterial infection at the participating institutions; PVL testing (and hence the PVL model's labels) only for MRSA isolates typed as SCCmec type IV.
raw.Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype
raw.Data_Source_Name: Tri-Service General Hospital microbiology laboratory dataset (5 collaborating institutions, Taiwan)
raw.Dataset_Size: 345,748 bacterial specimens; 10,227 S. aureus isolates (5,872 MRSA, 4,355 MSSA); 2,848 SCCmec type IV isolates used for PVL prediction
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Five nationwide institutions: three northern urban centres specialising in chronic disease management and a fourth on an island serving a distinct population, selected to leverage geographic and demographic variation.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: urine, sputum, catheter-associated samples, blood samples, throat swabs, wound exudates, and body fluids
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: MRSA status (methicillin/oxacillin resistance) vs MSSA, SCCmec subtype (Types I-V, grouped HA-MRSA Types I-III and CA-MRSA Types IV-V) and PVL gene presence in SCCmec type IV MRSA isolates, all predicted from MALDI-TOF MS spectra.
raw.Drug_Classes: Penicillinase-resistant beta-lactams / methicillin (oxacillin)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (methicillin)
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary oxacillin R/S defines MRSA vs MSSA; SCCmec Types I-V assigned by DNA extraction, PCR amplification and capillary gel electrophoresis; PVL gene presence by PCR for SCCmec type IV isolates.
raw.AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a hierarchical machine-learning AI-clinical decision support system that predicts MRSA status, SCCmec subtype and PVL presence directly from MALDI-TOF MS spectra, replacing PCR-based workflows.
raw.Feature_Engineering: Raw spectra 2000-20,000 Da segmented into consecutive 5-Da intervals with the peak intensity of each interval as the representative value; log transformation of bin intensities; StandardScaler standardisation of every m/z bin.
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Random forest-based feature selection, retaining predictors with importance scores above 0.01
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: GridSearchCV (scikit-learn) with 5-fold cross-validation, optimising AUC
raw.Software_Libraries: PyOpenMS 3.1.0; Pandas; scikit-learn (StandardScaler, GridSearchCV); Random Forest; LGBM; XGBoost; joblib; Flask; HTML/CSS/JavaScript
raw.Other_Metrics: Training AUC (0.99 for every model and step); AUC-ROC curves; NPV (e.g. 0.99 for Random Forest CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA). No error metric (RMSE/MAE), kappa, MCC or AUPRC is reported.
raw.Internal_Validation: Chronological hold-out: January-September for training, October-December for validation; 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning.
raw.Train_Test_Split: Chronological split - January through September for training, October through December for validation
raw.Overfitting_Method: Ensemble algorithms (random forest, LGBM, XGBoost) selected for their capacity to mitigate overfitting on high-dimensional data; random forest feature selection; 5-fold cross-validated hyperparameter tuning.
raw.Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
raw.Clinical_Insights: The 4445-4450 segment, previously proposed as the PVL marker peak (4448 m/z), correlates only modestly with PVL presence (r = 0.28), whereas m/z 6405-6410 and 5865-5870 correlate most strongly; supports a multifeature rather than single-peak approach.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Generalisability depends on consistent spectral data acquisition and preprocessing across institutions and instruments; the five-institution sampling was intended to widen applicability, and further clinical validation is called for.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Temporal hold-out validation on the same five-institution dataset (train Jan-Sep, validate Oct-Dec); the paper reports validation (testing) AUC/accuracy rather than only training performance.
raw.Integration_Point: Microbiology laboratory workflow, immediately after MALDI-TOF MS species identification; results surfaced to clinicians through a web interface.
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians (and the microbiology laboratory) using the web AI-CDSS interface
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: MALDI-TOF MS species identification feeds a three-step hierarchical model (MRSA status, SCCmec genotype, then PVL presence in SCCmec type IV isolates); results and per-step confidence scores are displayed in the web interface for clinician interpretation.
raw.Barriers_List: PCR-based genotyping: complex primer design, non-specific amplification, variable reaction conditions, long processing times, specialised instruments and trained personnel; AI-CDSS: dependence on consistent MALDI-TOF spectra quality across institutions.
raw.Facilitators_List: Analysis of MALDI-TOF MS spectra already generated for species identification (no extra test); automated hierarchical workflow replacing PCR; web interface with per-step confidence; webinars, training and feedback collection for adoption.
raw.Future_Directions: Proteomic experiments to link discriminative m/z features to proteins and to integrate additional biomarkers; further clinical validation of the impact on mortality.
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest feature importance (importance score threshold > 0.01) plus correlation coefficients of each m/z segment with PVL+ status (Figure 2 heatmap); Table 1 counts how often each m/z segment appears in the top 10 per classification stage.
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: The 4445-4450 segment (the widely cited 4448 m/z peak) correlates only modestly with PVL (r = 0.28); m/z 6405-6410 and 5865-5870 are the strongest correlates, favouring a multifeature model over single-peak analysis.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Data quality / spectral variation across institutions; generalisability and reproducibility; scope of modelled outcome (only PVL, not other virulence factors or resistance mechanisms); lack of biological explanation of m/z features; unquantified clinical impact and need for further validation.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Consistency in spectral data acquisition and preprocessing is crucial for reproducibility and generalisability across diverse clinical environments.
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear on dataset, hierarchical design, split and metrics, and the code stack is named; however Table 2 and the Results text report different PVL-stage metrics, no patient-level data are described, and feature counts after selection are not given.
raw.Page_References: Abstract p.2; methods p.3-5; Table 1 and top-10 m/z features p.5-6; Table 2 p.6; Figure 3 web interface p.7; discussion and limitations p.8-9

raw.Title: Discovering multiple antibiotic resistance phenotypes using diverse top-k subgroup list discovery

raw.Task_Type_Other: Subgroup discovery / descriptive pattern mining (diverse top-k subgroup lists, i.e. phenotypes)

raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The only evaluation is an internal 70/30 train-test split with McNemar's test on the same mining view; no external validation, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment are reported
raw.Reported_Limitations: Performance cost (the algorithm repeatedly explores the collection of candidate subgroups) and the fact that it only accepts nominal attributes
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: None reported — the research uses a public database, so the ethics statement is not applicable
raw.Unresolved_Items: Accuracy / AUROC / other classifier metrics are reported only for the Random Forest and Logistic Regression models used to test the predictive capacity of the phenotypes (model 1 vs model 2), not for the review's unit of analysis (the best diverse top-k phenotypes, reported by quality and coverage); recorded here rather than in the *_Value fields
raw.Sample_Size: 3744 instances (strains) in the balanced mining view used in the experiments — 1872 positive (vancomycin-resistant) and 1872 negative; the mining view before subsampling contains 10,790 strains
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: All MIMIC-III patients who underwent culture tests using Vancomycin (strain-level instances from their cultures); only the first microorganism of a particular species per patient is kept
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Per CLSI M39-A4, only the first microorganism of a particular species from an individual patient is considered to avoid duplicate data that could introduce bias; preprocessing also deletes duplicated instances and attributes and removes empty or single-valued attributes
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: MIMIC-III (MIMIC-III database stored in a PostgreSQL database)
raw.Dataset_Size: Query dataset: 12,796 instances (strains) x 44 attributes; final mining view: 10,790 instances x 32 attributes; balanced experimental mining view: 3744 instances (1872 positive / 1872 negative)
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Missing values are treated as step (3) of the preprocessing pipeline ('treatment of missing values'); the imputation method itself is not specified in the paper
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single-database study (MIMIC-III ICU patients, admissions 2001–2012); geographic representativeness is not discussed, but the authors acknowledge the data are 'solely focused on ICUs', 'temporally displaced' and not all relevant data are available in tabular format
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture specimen description (culture_specimen_type_description): blood, sputum, urine, etc.; values appearing in the experiments include 'SWAB', 'URINE', 'SPUTUM', 'BRONCHOALVEOLAR_LAVAGE', 'CATHETER_TIP - IV' and 'BLOOD_CULTURE'
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Vancomycin resistance in Enterococcus (ERV): characterising groups of hospitalised patients whose culture grew an Enterococcus bacterium showing resistance to vancomycin; target of the phenotype mining is the susceptibility (sensitive/resistant) of the strain
raw.Pathogens: Enterococcus (ERV) is the target pathogen; Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia appear as prior-colonisation covariate organisms
raw.Num_Pathogens: 1 target pathogen (Enterococcus, ERV); 5 further organisms appear only as prior-colonisation covariates (Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia)
raw.Drug_Classes: Glycopeptides (Vancomycin, the target drug); prior-exposure variables for third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, B lactams and antifungal agents
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin (VANCOMYCIN, target drug of the MICROBIOLOGYEVENTS table); previous exposure to third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluorquinolones, aminoglycosides, b_lactam and antifungal agents
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; VRE
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptibility label: 'Susceptibility: sensitive or resistant' (attribute culture_susceptibility) for the VANCOMYCIN antibiotic, with the target phenomenon being an Enterococcus strain resistant to vancomycin (ERV)
raw.AI_Purpose: Mine diverse top-k antibiotic-resistance phenotypes (subgroup lists) from a real MIMIC-III use case, to give clinical experts multiple and diverse explanations of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus patterns and support decision-making
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 2 phenotyping algorithms compared (EDSLM vs SSD++); Random Forest and Logistic Regression were additionally fitted (with and without phenotype attributes) for the statistical validation
raw.Feature_Engineering: Two-stage pipeline: SQL query on MIMIC-III (PostgreSQL) creating previous-admission binary features, then preprocessing with (1) deletion of duplicated instances and attributes, (2) removal of empty or single-valued attributes, (3) treatment of missing values, (4) attribute discretization and (5) correlation analysis (Pearson coefficient, threshold 0.8)
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: No explicit feature-selection step: all 32 mining-view attributes are used; a Pearson correlation analysis with a threshold of 0.8 is applied during preprocessing, and the overlap strategy places correlated attributes in different subgroup lists
raw.Num_Features_Total: 44 attributes in the initial query dataset; 32 attributes in the final mining view
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 32 attributes (all mining-view attributes); subgroups are limited to a maximum depth of 4 selectors
raw.Class_Imbalance_Method: Subsampling of negative instances: from 8918 negatives to 1872 negatives to match the 1872 positive instances, giving a balanced mining view of 3744 instances
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Grid over 9 values of beta (0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0) and 8 values of max_positive_overlap / max_negative_overlap (0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.6), with k = 3 and sl_max_size = 10 fixed, giving 576 executions; model selection by quality (Eq. 4) and coverage (Eq. 5)
raw.Software_Libraries: pandas 2.0.3, scikit-learn 1.3.0, matplotlib 3.7.2, numpy 1.24.3 (pipeline); pingouin 0.5.5 (McNemar's test); subgroups Python library (EDSLM implementation); RuleList library (SSD++)
raw.Other_Metrics: Quality of the phenotypes (Eq. 3 and Eq. 4, based on the WRAcc quality measure of the subgroups) and coverage (Eq. 5) are the measures computed for every execution; overlap between phenotypes (Table 8) and McNemar's test p-values (Table 7) are additionally reported
raw.Baseline_Method: SSD++ algorithm (RuleList library) applied to the same dataset as an alternative phenotyping approach; Random Forest and Logistic Regression fitted without the phenotype attributes (model 1) as the baseline against which model 2 (with phenotype attributes) is compared
raw.Baseline_Performance: SSD++ phenotype: quality 0.061, covering 1030 of 1872 positive (55%), 1019 of 1872 negative (54%) and 2049 of the total instances (55%); Random Forest model 1 accuracy 0.73; Logistic Regression model 1 accuracy 0.66
raw.Internal_Validation: 70% of the mining-view instances for training and 30% for testing, with McNemar's test (pingouin 0.5.5) comparing classification models with and without phenotype attributes (Table 7)
raw.Clinical_Insights: The ERV phenotypes are dominated by general subgroups: patients with ERV in 'SWAB' cultures from surgical ICUs and in urine cultures with previous vancomycin exposure; a more specific subgroup has previous ERV colonisation and organ transplantation; further subgroups describe patients who are adults, largely women, and who do not die
raw.Data_Repository: GitHub (query of stage 1 and source code of stage 2): https://github.com/antoniolopezmc/Discovering-multiple-antibiotic-resistance-phenotypes-using-diverse-top-k-subgroup-list-discovery; source data: MIMIC-III database
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors note that MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, temporally displaced (admissions 2001–2012) and not all relevant data are available in tabular format, while the extracted phenotypes remain interpretable
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: 70/30 train-test split of the balanced mining view with McNemar's test on predictive capacity; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment
raw.Integration_Point: Not reported — the algorithm is delivered as the open-source subgroups Python library; no clinical system integration point is described
raw.End_User_Described: Clinical experts / clinicians interpreting the phenotypes (and researchers using the subgroups library)
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Phenotypes could be mined in different scenarios for decision-making, e.g. using patient data at hospital admission to carry out colonisation studies, or using microbiological diagnostic data to predict the growth of multiresistant bacteria
raw.Barriers_List: Performance (the algorithm must repeatedly explore the collection of candidate subgroups) and the fact that it only accepts nominal attributes; also limited availability of MIMIC-III data (ICU-focused, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
raw.Facilitators_List: Multiple and diverse explanations of the same dataset; an overlapping strategy improving diversity in terms of coverage; a deletion refinement strategy improving diversity in terms of descriptions; only subgroups covering at least one positive instance are added; the candidate subgroup collection can be filtered a-priori, improving legibility of results
raw.Future_Directions: Apply the proposal to other clinical problems and datasets (e.g. drug repurposing); design algorithms that mine diverse top-k subgroup lists without previously generating candidate subgroups; explore other measures to assess diverse top-k phenotypes; adapt the approach to other subgroup models (subgroup sets, truly unordered rule sets); add support for numerical attributes; extend to a multiclass setting
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 7 (clinical; microbiological; pharmacological; healthcare utilisation; laboratory; sociodemographic; temporal)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Minimum Description Length compression gain (Eq. 1) combined with the positive/negative overlap factor (Eq. 2) decides which subgroup is added to a phenotype; the WRAcc quality measure is used by VLSD when mining the candidate subgroups
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Subgroups are conjunctive patterns: a pattern is a set of selectors forming a conjunction of conditions (up to a maximum depth of 4 selectors); phenotypes chain subgroups as else-if rules
raw.Limitation_Categories: Performance / scalability (repeated exploration of the candidate subgroup collection); attribute type (only nominal attributes accepted); data limitations of MIMIC-III (ICU-only, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, are temporally displaced and not all relevant data are available in tabular format; duplicates handled per CLSI M39-A4 and missing values treated during preprocessing
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear reporting of dataset sizes, preprocessing steps, hyperparameter grid, quality/coverage values and statistical tests; the imputation method behind 'treatment of missing values' is not specified

raw.Reported_Limitations: Controlled-trial population may not be representative of larger ART populations; frequent virological monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; >12 months used as the referent therapy-duration category; all participants on efavirenz-based first-line regimens, so resistance patterns and predictors may not apply to other regimens; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other sub-Saharan African cohorts; possible misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Premature switching to second-line therapy (false positives) occurs even at specificities >98 % and has significant person- and system-wide consequences: for patients, lost potential life years from remaining on first-line therapy; for the health system, drug costs 6-10 times those of first-line therapy. Conversely, missing resistant patients risks accumulation and transmission of resistant viral strains
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Trade-offs may vary by population: providers may be more willing to risk false positives in HIV-infected pregnant women because viral suppression at delivery prevents vertical transmission; acceptable true positive:false positive ratios may also differ with anticipated time-to-referral
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Antiretroviral (HIV) drug resistance rather than bacterial AMR; the record codes it with the closest available vocabulary and flags the mapping choices in _notes. Model performance figures were read from the narrative text and Tables 2-3, which the text layer reproduces; the Additional file 1 supplementary tables (S1-S3) are not in the text layer
raw.Unresolved_Items: Whether Provider_Facing_Applications should include 'Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)' when the model predicts resistance from clinical and demographic variables rather than from genotype or spectra; whether a modelled switching estimate in a hypothetical 10,000-patient cohort counts as stewardship impact; whether the paper's population estimates are healthcare costs 'reported'
