raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The author(s) declare that they have no competing interests.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: Post-hoc analysis of de-identified PEARLS (A5175) data restricted to participants initiated on NNRTI-based regimens (lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz) with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml at any point after week 16 of enrolment
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded from PEARLS: CD4 count >300 cells/mm3, previous ART exposure (except women given ART for prevention of mother-to-child transmission), pregnancy, acute illness or clinical instability. In this analysis, participants with two sequential visits with VL >=1000 copies/ml but no resistance test, and those without available resistance results at the time of confirmed elevated VL (n = 15), were excluded
raw.Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: PEARLS trial (Prospective Evaluation of Antiretrovirals in Resource-Limited Settings), Adult AIDS Clinical Trials Group A5175, NCT00084136
raw.Dataset_Size: 1045 participants analysed; 305 with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml after week 16; 15 excluded for unavailable resistance results; final sample 290
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case/data-availability exclusion: participants with two sequential elevated VLs but no resistance test were excluded (15 participants dropped for unavailable resistance results); resistance testing was not done for participants who resuppressed and these were classified as not needing ART change; no imputation reported
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Participants from all PEARLS study sites with a sensitivity analysis restricted to those enrolled from resource-limited settings; the authors caution that trial participants may not be representative of larger ART populations
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Plasma HIV-1 RNA (Roche Amplicor Monitor assay [v1.5]) every eight weeks; stored specimens genotyped retrospectively for resistance
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: Need for ART change (i.e. antiretroviral resistance) among participants with the first VL >=1000 copies/ml, from an algorithm combining resuppression and genotypic resistance: resuppression - no ART change needed; no resuppression and no resistance - no ART change needed; no resuppression and resistance - ART change needed
raw.Drug_Classes: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI); protease inhibitors excluded (PI class reserved for second-line therapy)
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz (first-line NNRTI-based regimens; also abbreviated 3TC/ZDV BID + EFV QHS and FTC/TDF/EFV QHS)
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Participants with NRTI or NNRTI resistance mutations, defined by 2014 International AIDS Society guidelines (excluding mutation 101P), were classified as resistant; resistance to protease inhibitors was not included; baseline and acquired resistance were not distinguished
raw.AI_Purpose: Develop a risk score algorithm that predicts the need for ART change (resistance) among people with a single elevated viral load, so that providers in resource-limited settings can switch patients to second-line therapy without confirmatory VL testing
raw.Feature_Engineering: Predictors collapsed into discrete categorical variables for point-of-care use; four categorisations of time on treatment tested and the one with the lowest AIC selected as the reference model; full models included all variables with bivariate p-value <0.5; variables with low frequency, extreme collinearity or insufficient detail for clinical implementation excluded
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Backward elimination in multiple logistic regression: starting with the largest p-value, variables removed one at a time until <=5 remained regardless of p-value; full models contained all variables with bivariate p <0.5
raw.Num_Features_Total: 10 (full Model 1); 9 (full Model 2); 8 (full Model 3)
raw.Software_Libraries: Stata statistical software, Version 13.0 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX); no machine-learning libraries named
raw.Other_Metrics: AUROC for the models and for the derived weighted risk scores; sensitivity and specificity at each cutoff; Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration p-values; AIC for therapy-duration categorisation; likelihood-ratio tests between successive models; unadjusted prevalence odds ratios with 95 % CI; number of true and false positives in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients at varying resistance prevalence
raw.Baseline_Method: Reduced logistic-regression Models 1-3 compared against each other (Models 2 and 3 exclude treatment-initiation VL and/or CD4 as eligible predictors); AUROC equality tested by chi-squared test; AIC used to choose the therapy-duration categorisation
raw.Baseline_Performance: Reduced Model 2 AUROC 0.7981 and reduced Model 3 AUROC 0.7937 versus reduced Model 1 AUROC 0.8165; differences not statistically significant (p = 0.23 and p = 0.22)
raw.Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples with replacement, assessed over 1000 replications
raw.Clinical_Insights: In the best model, need for ART change was directly associated with higher treatment-initiation VL and higher VL at the first elevated measure, and inversely with treatment duration; age <30 and BMI >25.0 kg/m2 also predicted need for change; screening CD4 <100 cells/mm3 (Model 2) and ever missed medications (Model 3) were additionally retained
raw.Generalisability_Details: The authors argue PEARLS' broad inclusion criteria improve generalizability, that participants were recruited largely from resource-limited settings and the risk score performed well in that subgroup, but caution that trial participants may not represent larger ART populations and that findings may not apply to non-efavirenz-based regimens
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Development and internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples on 290 trial participants; performance at risk-score cutoffs >=9 with a high-specificity threshold; sensitivity analysis restricted to resource-limited settings; no external or prospective validation reported
raw.Integration_Point: Point-of-care use in ART clinics in resource-limited settings, based only on predictors available at the clinic, applied at the time of the first VL >=1000 copies/ml to decide immediate switch to second-line therapy instead of confirmatory testing
raw.End_User_Described: Providers (clinicians) in ART clinics in resource-limited settings
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: The risk score sits inside the WHO viral-load monitoring strategy: instead of the confirmatory test 3-6 months after an initial VL >1000 copies/ml, patients exceeding the algorithm threshold are switched immediately to second-line therapy; those below the threshold have confirmatory VL testing before any switch decision
raw.Stewardship_Details: No stewardship impact was measured: the paper only models, in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients, how many would be switched immediately (Model 1 correctly identifying 700 and misclassifying 248 at ~25 % resistance prevalence; 1540 true positives and 149 false positives at 55 % prevalence)
raw.Barriers_List: False positives cause premature second-line switching with significant person- and system-wide consequences (lost potential life years; drug costs 6-10 times first-line therapy); low sensitivity (~15-30 %) is accepted but means misses rely on confirmatory testing; resistance may be misclassified at low-level viraemia (<1000 copies/ml); frequent 8-weekly monitoring in the trial is unlikely in the intended settings; changing WHO CD4 eligibility could dampen efficiency gains
raw.Facilitators_List: Only readily available, point-of-care predictors used; a limited number of categorical variables (five) to keep the score manageable; high specificity minimises false positives; may avoid confirmatory VL tests and so save laboratory costs and reduce transmission of resistant virus
raw.Future_Directions: Prospective external validation and evaluation of the effect of the risk score on health outcomes and resource utilisation; modelling the consequences of delayed second-line initiation versus premature switching to understand threshold trade-offs; alternative cost-saving monitoring strategies such as pooled specimens and targeted VL testing
raw.Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 categories of potential predictors in the paper's own list (demographics; clinical diagnoses; immunological markers/CD4; self-reported and provider-assessed ART adherence; therapy duration); 7 coded predictor categories ticked above (clinical, microbiological, pharmacological, laboratory, behavioural, sociodemographic, temporal)
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Weighted risk score: predictor score = two times the beta coefficient rounded to the nearest integer
raw.Limitation_Categories: Trial population representativeness; frequent monitoring in the trial versus intended settings; referent category of therapy duration; efavirenz-based regimens only; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other cohorts; misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Resistance results unavailable for 15 participants with two sequential elevated VLs (excluded); resistance testing not performed for participants who resuppressed; frequent study-driven monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; adherence self-reported and provider-assessed; resistance may be present at low-level viraemia below the 1000 copies/ml threshold
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model development, candidate predictors, full and reduced model AUROCs, risk-score weights, sensitivity/specificity at defined cutoffs and calibration tests are all reported; no code or model repository link
raw.Page_References: pp. 1-13; methods pp. 3-4 (measures p. 3, statistical analyses p. 4); results pp. 5-6; Table 2 pp. 8-9; Table 3 and ROC/cohort figures p. 10; discussion and limitations pp. 10-11; funding, competing interests and author details p. 12; references pp. 12-13

raw.Title: Utilization of machine learning to predict antibiotic resistant event outcomes in acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing induction chemotherapy
raw.Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
raw.Country_Countries: United States of America (College Station, TX and Houston, TX)
raw.Funder_Names: K01AI143881 (NIAID)
raw.Population_Description: 95 adult patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) undergoing remission induction chemotherapy (IC) at MD Anderson Cancer Center, drawn from two longitudinal cohorts (PA13-0339, n=98; PA15-0780, n=56) with baseline stool metagenomics, baseline gut resistome data and complete antibiotic administration and clinical metadata.
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: Mean variable importance score (mean decrease in Gini impurity, averaged over 100 iterations): Methanobrevibacter smithii 0.717, Blautia producta 0.630, macrolide resistance genes 0.573, lincosamide/macrolide/streptogramin resistance genes 0.542, remaining 11 bacterial taxa 0.522-0.622. Top three by mean SHAP value: M. smithii, Clostridium leptum, Bacteroides dorei
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Four Random Forest model variations (100 iterations, 500 trees each): Model 1 - ARG class presence/absence + antibiotics >=72 h + species abundance (AUC=0.667, Youden's=0.879); Model 2 - unique ARG counts by class + antibiotics >=72 h (AUC=0.689, Youden's=0.835); Model 3 - ARG presence/absence + any antibiotic administration (AUC=0.666, Youden's=0.871); Model 4 - unique ARG counts + any administration (AUC=0.687, Youden's=0.855); optimized Model 2 with top 15 variables (aggregate AUC=0.730, Youden's=0.863, sensitivity 0.630, specificity 0.643)
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Model 2 - Random Forest using unique ARG counts by class, presence/absence of antibiotics administered >=72 hours and baseline species abundance, reduced to the top 15 variables; chosen on highest AUC, best sensitivity/specificity balance and balanced Youden's index
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables), aggregate of 100 iterations (80/20 stratified splits) in the 95-patient cohort with 14 AR events
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables), aggregate of 100 iterations (80/20 stratified splits) in the 95-patient cohort with 14 AR events
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables): aggregate AUC across 100 iterations (mean 0.742, median 0.745, range 0.505-0.969) in the 95-patient cohort
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was developed and internally validated only: 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits within the same 95-patient MDACC cohort, with no external or prospective validation
raw.Reported_Limitations: Genus-level 16S rRNA abundance threshold for selecting stools for culture may have led to missed ARC events; pooling colonization and infection events may obscure biologically distinct processes; SHAP ambiguity from extensive feature interactions and zero-inflated microbial data; small cohort size, few events and single-institution analyses; no external validation
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: IRB approval and written informed consent reported; no AI-specific ethical or governance risks discussed
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre US retrospective analysis of two MDACC AML cohorts; the AI component is a Random Forest classifier of AR event outcomes (ARC or ARI combined), with SHAP and importance-based interpretation, plus sCCA and network analysis as secondary analyses. Sex, chemotherapy type and intensity were only compared between AR-event groups as baseline characteristics (not a subgroup performance analysis), so subgroup fields are answered No. Amikacin administration was the only variable differing between groups (p=0.041).
raw.Unresolved_Items: Judgement calls: (1) Infection_Type left 'Not specified' because infection sites are never given, only the causative organisms; (2) Clinical_Outcomes coded No - AR infection/colonization is the prediction target, and no mortality, LOS, ICU or treatment-failure outcomes are reported; (3) Class_Imbalance_Addressed coded No although 80/20 splits were stratified - no resampling or class weighting is described; (4) Explanation_Level coded 'Both' because the SHAP beeswarm gives per-sample values aggregated to global mean absolute SHAP rankings; (5) Reporting_Guideline 'None reported' - no guideline is named anywhere in the text layer.

raw.Sex_Distribution: AR-event group: female 8 (57.1%), male 6 (42.9%); no-event group: female 40 (49.4%), male 41 (50.6)

raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Lack of baseline stool sample, lack of antibiotic administration data, lack of complete clinical metadata, and lack of resistome data.
raw.Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
raw.Data_Source_Name: MD Anderson Cancer Center AML cohorts PA13-0339 and PA15-0780; NCBI Sequence Read Archive BioProjects PRJNA352060, PRJNA526551, PRJNA1124986, PRJNA1129514, PRJNA1128111

raw.Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case analysis: patients lacking a baseline stool sample, antibiotic administration data, complete clinical metadata or resistome data were excluded

raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: AR event — a single combined outcome of confirmed AR colonization (ARC) or confirmed AR infection (ARI) with a CDC serious/urgent-threat pathogen (VRE, CRE, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA)
raw.Pathogens: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE), carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL; Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae), multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (MDRP; carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa), methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)

raw.Specific_Antibiotics: levofloxacin, metronidazole, linezolid, meropenem, cefepime, amikacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, daptomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefpodoxime, ciprofloxacin, tigecycline, minocycline, ertapenem
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; VRE
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Confirmed AR colonization (ARC) if any bacterial isolate from a stool sample was confirmed CRE, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, VRE, MDRP or MRSA; confirmed AR infection (ARI) if the clinical microbiology lab diagnosed a microbially defined infection with those organisms; both combined as an "AR event"
raw.AI_Purpose: To develop a Random Forest machine learning model that predicts antibiotic-resistant (AR) infection and colonization event outcomes in adult AML patients during induction chemotherapy by integrating baseline gut microbiome and resistome data with antibiotic administration and clinical data; secondary analyses were sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) and a correlation network of ARG classes and microbial taxa
raw.Feature_Engineering: ARG classes encoded as presence/absence or as counts of unique genes per class; antibiotic administration encoded as presence/absence or as exposure >=72 hours; variables retained only if received by >=10% of patients; baseline microbiome filtered to abundance 0.001 and 10% prevalence; CLR transformation with a pseudocount (min relative abundance/2) for sCCA
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Averaged variable importance scores (mean decrease in Gini impurity) over 100 iterations; top 20, 15 and 10 variables tested; top 15 retained per model
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Final model optimized by increasing the value of mtry (number of variables randomly sampled at each split) and increasing the node size to increase tree depth; sCCA hyperparameters optimized with CCA.permute (nperms = 100, niter = 5)
raw.Software_Libraries: PMA package (v. 1.2-2) in R; BugSeq (v4.0); minimap2; MetaPhlAn2 (v2.8.1); MEGAHIT (v1.2.8); metaSPAdes (v3.14.1); SPAdes (v3.14.1); VSEARCH; UNOISE3; Mothur; SILVA (version 138); QIIME 2; Seqtk (v1.3); Gephi
raw.Hardware_Details: Grace computing cluster at Texas A&M University; Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S4 flow cell (North Texas Genome Center)
raw.Other_Metrics: Youden's index (optimized Model 2: 0.863; models 1-4: 0.835-0.879); ROC curves with confidence intervals; variable importance (mean decrease in Gini impurity)
raw.Baseline_Method: Four Random Forest configurations compared against each other (ARG presence/absence vs unique ARG counts; antibiotics >=72 h vs any administration), plus comparison with previously published ARI prediction models
raw.Baseline_Performance: Model 1 AUC=0.667 (Youden's 0.879), Model 2 AUC=0.689 (0.835), Model 3 AUC=0.666 (0.871), Model 4 AUC=0.687 (0.855); published ARI models AUC 0.57-0.75
raw.Internal_Validation: 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits per model, 500 trees each, variable importance averaged over the 100 iterations; the optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables) re-run 100 times to produce the final AUC-ROC curve; no k-fold cross-validation used
raw.External_Validation_Description: None performed; the authors state they could not find a similar independent clinical cohort with the same sequencing and clinical metadata
raw.Overfitting_Method: Four model variants run across 100 independent 80/20 stratified splits, each with 500 trees; variables reduced to the top 15 most influential; final model optimized by increasing mtry and node size to limit overfitting
raw.Clinical_Insights: Methanobrevibacter smithii, Clostridium leptum and Bacteroides dorei were consistently associated with reduced AR event risk (protective commensals supporting gut microbial resilience); ARG classes for lincosamides, macrolides and streptogramins were negatively associated with AR events
raw.Data_Repository: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (BioProject IDs PRJNA352060, PRJNA526551, PRJNA1124986, PRJNA1129514, PRJNA1128111)
raw.Generalisability_Details: Model is developmental and single-institution; validation and refinement in larger multicentre cohorts and different high-risk populations is needed before clinical implementation
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only - 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits with 500 trees per model; the authors state they were unable to validate the model on an independent cohort
raw.Integration_Point: Not described; the model is developmental and is proposed for future implementation in infection risk stratification of AML patients on induction chemotherapy, with no system integration reported
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians - the authors state the findings offer valuable predictors for clinical decision-making and potential infection risk stratification
raw.Barriers_List: Small cohort size and few AR events; single-institution data; no independent validation cohort with comparable sequencing and clinical metadata; model still in development
raw.Facilitators_List: Model performance comparable to or exceeding other recent ARI prediction models (AUC 0.730 vs 0.57-0.75); integration of microbiome, resistome and clinical data; simultaneous assessment of AR infection and colonization risk
raw.Future_Directions: Validation and refinement in larger, multicentre cohorts and extension to different high-risk populations; functional validation via metatranscriptomics, metabolomics or gnotobiotic models to determine the role of the predicted protective taxa, their metabolic products and contributory ARGs
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Raw sum of decreases in Gini impurity across all trees in the Random Forest (mean variable importance score, not normalised); SHAP (Shapely Additive exPlanations) values for ranking by mean absolute SHAP value
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: ARG classes conferring resistance to lincosamides, macrolides and streptogramins were unexpectedly associated with REDUCED AR event risk (top predictors in the Random Forest, covariation with taxa in sCCA, and negative correlation with AR events in the network analysis), despite such genes usually being linked to broad-spectrum antibiotic use and worse outcomes
raw.Limitation_Categories: Ascertainment/label: 16S genus-level threshold may have missed ARC events; pooling of colonization and infection outcomes. Modelling: SHAP ambiguity from feature interactions and zero-inflated data. Sample: small cohort, few events, single institution, no external validation cohort.
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Microbial taxa data are inherently zero-inflated (most taxa absent/low), contributing to ambiguity in SHAP interpretation; no spike-in standards used; batch effects addressed only by consistent protocols, library preparation and sequencing conditions
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Model configurations, variable counts (89-92), validation scheme, AUC, Youden's index and sensitivity/specificity are reported in narrative form; further clinical metrics and confusion matrices are deferred to Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 (not in the provided text layer); dataset accession numbers and data availability statement are given

raw.Reported_Limitations: Small sample size; need for broader validation with additional strains; results reflect local (Quzhou) strain characteristics; inability to classify certain strains highlights limited accuracy of the software algorithm; discrepancies in protein peaks vs prior studies may follow from sample preparation and regional/temporal strain differences.
raw.Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre MALDI-TOF MS + machine learning (ClinProTools GA/SNN/QC) study on 267 K. pneumoniae isolates, developing (1) a CRKP vs CSKP typing model and (2) a model separating bloodstream-infection from intestinal-screening CRKP. Unit of analysis = SNN on the primary CRKP vs CSKP dataset. Peak-level AUCs (0.84-0.88) are reported for individual mass peaks, not for the model as a discriminator, so AUROC_Reported is No. Abstract labels the SNN cross-validation accuracy (90.08%) and recognition capacity (95.80%) as sensitivity and specificity, while the results call them CV accuracy and RC - both readings noted in the *_Value fields.
raw.Unresolved_Items: Whether the SNN's 90.08%/95.80% should be coded as sensitivity/specificity (abstract wording) or as cross-validation accuracy/recognition capacity (results wording); number of cross-validation folds is not stated; GA model performance figures are not reported; identities of the m/z 10,079 Da peak are unresolved by the authors.

raw.AI_Purpose: Apply MALDI-TOF MS with machine learning (ClinProTools GA, SNN and QC models) to identify CRKP from carbapenem-sensitive K. pneumoniae and to distinguish bloodstream-infection CRKP from intestinal-screening CRKP
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 3 (GA, SNN and QC)
raw.Feature_Engineering: No additional feature engineering beyond ClinProTools spectral processing: protein fingerprints analysed in Biotyper 3.0 and FlexAnalysis, peaks selected by ROC curve (p < 0.05, AUC > 0.8) and compared with gel plots
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: ClinProTools 3.0 statistical peak screening: ROC curve of each characteristic peak (p < 0.05) with AUC > 0.8; algorithms then perform their own automatic feature selection (GA, SNN) or statistical ranking (QC)
raw.Num_Features_Total: 25 characteristic peaks distinguished CRKP from CSKP (p < 0.000001); 6 peaks (m/z 4497.59, 4547.15, 5040.46, 8876.78, 8993.44, 9139.06 Da) distinguished the two CRKP sources
raw.Num_Features_Selected: 4 peaks for the CRKP vs CSKP model (m/z 2523.43, 3041.62, 4520.11 and 10,079.18 Da); 6 peaks for the different-sources model (m/z 4497.59, 4547.15, 5040.46, 8876.78, 8993.44, 9139.06 Da)
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: Automatic parameter tuning routines built into the ClinProTools algorithms; GA parameters (mutation rate, crossover rate, number of peaks in the model) described as adjustable to optimise performance
raw.Software_Libraries: ClinProTools 3.0, FlexAnalysis and Biotyper 3.0 (Bruker) with the MBT2969 reference database; SPAdes for whole-genome assembly
raw.Hardware_Details: Bruker Microflex LT/SH MALDI-TOF mass spectrometer; Siemens MicroScan WalkAway 96 PLUS automatic identification/susceptibility instrument; Illumina sequencing platform
raw.Other_Metrics: Cross-validation accuracy and recognition capacity (RC) for every model; positive and negative predictive values for SNN (96.30%/75%) and QC (94.74%/82.61%); peak-level AUCs (> 0.84 for m/z 2523.43, 3041.62, 4520.11, 10079.18; > 0.85 for m/z 8993 and 9139; > 0.88 for m/z 2523 and 4520); peak weights; classification accuracies for CSKP/CRKP and for bloodstream/intestinal CRKP
raw.Baseline_Method: Head-to-head comparison of the three ClinProTools algorithms (GA, SNN, QC) on the same spectral datasets
raw.Baseline_Performance: CRKP vs CSKP model: SNN CV accuracy 90.08% / RC 95.80% (superior to GA and QC); different-sources model: QC CV accuracy 86.85% / RC 88.46% versus SNN CV 83.57% / RC 94.82%
raw.Internal_Validation: Validation on held-out non-duplicate strains (20 CSKP, 58 CRKP for the SNN model; 22 bloodstream and 20 intestinal CRKP for the QC model) plus a 9-isolate clinical validation
raw.Train_Test_Split: Training: 79 CRKP and 50 CSKP blood isolates (typing model); validation: 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP non-duplicate strains - no percentage split stated
raw.CV_Folds: Cross-validation reported by ClinProTools but the number of folds is not stated
raw.Clinical_Insights: Peak-level biological interpretation: the m/z 4520-4529 range is linked to different Ambler classes of carbapenemases (A/KPC, B/NDM-VIM-IMP, D/OXA-48); the m/z 8876, 8993 and 9139 peaks enriched in bloodstream CRKP are proposed to reflect siderophore systems and capsule regulators associated with systemic virulence.
raw.Generalisability_Details: Single-hospital strain collection that predominantly represents Quzhou's resident population; authors call for broader validation with additional strains and note that protein-peak discrepancies between studies may reflect sample preparation and regional/temporal strain differences.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Validation of the SNN model on 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP non-duplicate strains from the same hospital (identification accuracy 90% and 89.66%) and a 9-isolate clinical validation (66.67%); no external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment.
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory MALDI-TOF MS workflow for rapid identification and typing of CRKP at the point of species identification, supporting early clinical diagnosis
raw.End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory staff and clinicians using MALDI-TOF MS identification results for early diagnosis of CRKP
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: ClinProTools models are built from routine MALDI-TOF protein fingerprints; the best model is saved and used to identify and validate incoming strains, with results expressed as statistics for rapid CRKP/CSKP and source typing in the laboratory workflow.
raw.Barriers_List: Software algorithm accuracy limits (ungrouped strains); poor mass-spectrometry scores of slime-type colonies; sample quality and preparation effects; small, single-centre, locally representative sample
raw.Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is rapid, cost-effective and easy to use and is already established in clinical laboratories; it is applied directly to routine protein fingerprints without additional assays
raw.Future_Directions: Larger sample sizes and more advanced machine learning techniques to improve algorithm sensitivity and specificity; broader validation with additional strains; further mass spectrometry and algorithm optimisation
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Characteristic peak weight calculated by ClinProTools 3.0 for each model (GA, SNN, QC)
raw.Novel_Predictors_Details: Peaks at m/z 8876, 8993 and 9139 Da are proposed as markers of source-specific virulence (siderophore/capsule factors) in bloodstream CRKP; the identity of the m/z 10,079 Da resistance-associated peak is explicitly unresolved and suggested to be fragments or expression products of resistance-associated proteins.
raw.Limitation_Categories: Sample size; single centre / local population representativeness; algorithm accuracy and ungrouped strains; sample quality (slime-type colonies); no external validation; peak differences versus prior studies
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Slime-type colonies gave poor mass spectrometry scores and were associated with misidentification/classification failure; sample preparation method and protein purity/concentration affect direct mass spectrometry accuracy
raw.Reporting_Clarity: Methods and results reported in detail with peak statistics tables (Tables 1-3) and figures; however the abstract's naming of the SNN cross-validation accuracy and recognition capacity as sensitivity and specificity is inconsistent with the results section

raw.Title: Screening swabs surpass traditional risk factors as predictors of MRSA bacteremia
raw.Population_Description: 376 adult patients with S. aureus bacteremia, 100 (26.6%) MRSA
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: MRSA screening swab (30-Day and Ever-Positive criteria) ranked highest by random-forest importance
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Random forests (variable importance by mean increase in accuracy and Gini index); Lasso logistic regression (ORs: 30-Day 10.6 [5.08-19.2], Ever-Positive 8.26 [5.23-15.8])
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Random forests
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Retrospective algorithm development validated only by internal 10-fold cross-validation; not externally or prospectively validated
raw.Reported_Limitations: Small numbers per comorbidity (mitigated with CCI); retrospective and therefore hypothesis-generating; institution screens nares only (loss of sensitivity for other body sites)
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Vancomycin overuse harms cited as the motivation: nephrotoxicity, longer hospitalisation, cost, increased mortality
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval obtained; patient consent waived as retrospective with no intervention; dataset release only on request with REB approval
raw.Sample_Size: 376 patients (100 MRSA)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: All consecutive adult S. aureus bacteremia (April 2010 - April 2015) at McGill University Health Center
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Only the first positive blood culture per patient included; repeat positive cultures excluded
raw.Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Dataset_Size: 376 patients
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single health centre spanning two hospitals in Montréal, Canada
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: Nares MRSA screening swabs; blood cultures for S. aureus bacteremia
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: MRSA vs MSSA bacteremia (methicillin resistance among S. aureus blood isolates)
raw.Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin); glycopeptides (vancomycin) and beta-lactams as therapy discussed
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin; vancomycin; beta-lactams
raw.Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary MRSA vs MSSA classification among S. aureus blood-culture isolates
raw.AI_Purpose: Predict MRSA bacteremia in S. aureus bloodstream infection to guide empiric anti-MRSA (vancomycin) therapy
raw.Feature_Engineering: Input variables: MRSA colonization status (30-Day and Ever-Positive), age, sex, previous admissions, and the Charlson Comorbidity Index
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: Random forests and Lasso with 10-fold cross validation and the 1SE rule
raw.Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross validation with the 1SE rule (Lasso lambda selection)
raw.Software_Libraries: glmnet, randomForest
raw.Other_Metrics: Lasso logistic regression odds ratios; random-forest variable importance (mean increase in accuracy, mean decrease in Gini); PPV and NPV as functions of prevalence
raw.Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross validation (Lasso, 1SE rule)
raw.Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
raw.Clinical_Insights: MRSA colonization swab is the only independent predictor of MRSA bacteremia among patient-level factors
raw.Generalisability_Details: Local prevalence of methicillin resistance and nosocomial MRSA outbreak status shape how colonization status factors into the vancomycin decision
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal 10-fold cross-validation only; retrospective derivation with no external or prospective validation
raw.Integration_Point: Clinical decision to initiate empiric anti-MRSA (vancomycin) therapy
raw.End_User_Described: Clinicians deciding on empiric vancomycin in patients with S. aureus bacteremia
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: MRSA colonization status informs the empiric vancomycin decision for stable patients with S. aureus bacteremia
raw.Future_Directions: Prospective studies to demonstrate reduced vancomycin overuse, increased early targeted beta-lactam therapy, and improved patient outcomes

raw.Train_Test_Split: Samples used in tool training were omitted from evaluation
raw.External_Validation_Description: Isolates from the PATRIC, ReSeqTB and LitRev databases
raw.Overfitting_Method: Recalibrated accuracy treated as upper bound; unadjusted accuracy as lower bound
raw.Generalisability_Details: WGS-based drug-resistance prediction faces infrastructural limitations to adoption in resource-poor settings
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Tools benchmarked on external isolates from three databases (PATRIC, ReSeqTB, LitRev) not used in tool training
raw.End_User_Described: Clinical microbiologists; physicians
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: WGS-based drug-resistance profiling guiding antibiotic prescription, in place of conventional DST

raw.Facilitators_List: Speed of WGS-based resistance profiling relative to conventional DST

raw.Limitation_Categories: Overfitting risk of recalibrated performance; low sensitivity for ETO, PAS, PTO and PZA; small sample sizes for several drugs; uncertainty in estimated misclassification rates; assumption of independent software outputs
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Conventional DST phenotypes assumed error-free but containing errors; discordant DST results across databases; samples with poor sequencing quality; samples with no-call or discordant predictions treated as missing

studies.ai_purpose: Develop a user-friendly clinical decision aid (decision tree) to predict the risk of resistance to commonly prescribed broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics in children with gram-negative bloodstream infections

raw.Title: A Decision Tree Using Patient Characteristics to Predict Resistance to Commonly Used Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics in Children With Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infections
raw.Journal_Source: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society
raw.AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
raw.Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (awards T32-A1052071, K23-AI127935, K24AI141580)
raw.Population_Description: Children with gram-negative bloodstream infections cared for at a tertiary care pediatric hospital (Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh); 689 episodes among 387 patients and 638 hospital admissions, June 2009 to June 2015
raw.Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
raw.Top_Predictive_Features: In order of discriminatory potential: (1) prior carbapenem treatment for >=7 days, (2) prior culture with CPT resistance within 6 months, (3) intestinal transplantation, (4) >=7 prior gram-negative bloodstream infection episodes, (5) age >=3 years; importance determined by recursive partitioning (Gini splitting index)
raw.Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
raw.All_Models_Evaluated: Decision tree (recursive partitioning, rpart in R): sensitivity 46%, specificity 91%, AUC 0.70 (leave-one-out cross-validated); PPV 69%, NPV 78%. Multivariable logistic regression model (generalized estimating equations): adjusted odds ratios only, eg prior carbapenem within 6 months OR 2.74 (95% CI 1.54-4.88).
raw.Best_Performing_Model: Decision tree (recursive partitioning; rpart in R) - the only predictive model developed and evaluated, with its discrimination (AUC 0.70) and classification metrics reported
raw.Sensitivity_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated classification of patients as high risk of BSA-resistant infection
raw.Specificity_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated classification of patients as high risk of BSA-resistant infection
raw.Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Whole cohort; prevalence of BSA-resistant bloodstream infection 31%
raw.AUROC_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated model (pre-cross-validation value 0.68)
raw.Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only (leave-one-out cross-validation); the tree was developed and validated on the same data set and the authors state it needs wider validation before clinical practice.
raw.Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design and no outpatient data, with possible misclassification or missing data; infections may have been missed if cultures were obtained elsewhere; single tertiary pediatric centre; additional risk factors not captured; too few carbapenem-resistant infections to model CPT and carbapenem resistance separately; the same data set was used to develop and validate the tree; limited generalisability to other infection types or colonization.
raw.Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Misclassification may lead to undertreatment (close to 50% of high-risk BSA-resistant episodes classified as low risk) or overtreatment (9% classified as high risk).
raw.Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; the cohort is described only by race, sex and age.
raw.Ethical_Governance_Risks: Institutional Review Board approved the study with a waiver of informed consent; no further ethical or governance risks are discussed.
raw.Sample_Size: 689 episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infection (387 patients; 638 hospital admissions)
raw.Conflicts_of_Interest: P. D. T. received an investigator-initiated research grant from Merck, unrelated to the present work; A. M. M. reports consulting for Becton Dickinson for work unrelated to this project; all other authors report no potential conflicts.
raw.Inclusion_Criteria: All patients admitted to CHP from June 2009 through June 2015 with at least 1 blood culture, from a peripheral or a central catheter source, in which gram-negative bacteria grew.
raw.Exclusion_Criteria: Not admitted to hospital or insufficient antibiotic susceptibility information available; uniformly susceptible respiratory pathogens (eg, Haemophilus influenzae); pathogens primarily associated with gastroenteritis (eg, Salmonella and Shigella species); organisms intrinsically resistant to cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam (eg, Burkholderia cepacia complex and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia).
raw.Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
raw.Data_Source_Name: CHP microbiology database; CHP data warehouse
raw.Dataset_Size: 689 episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infection; 387 patients; 638 hospital admissions
raw.Missing_Data_Method: Manual chart review
raw.Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary care pediatric hospital serving Western Pennsylvania; the authors note most complex cases in the region are managed at this hospital.
raw.Specimen_Type_Detail: blood culture from a peripheral or a central catheter source
raw.Primary_AMR_Outcome: BSA resistance: bloodstream infection with a gram-negative organism nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin, or meeting criteria for ESBL production
raw.Pathogens: Klebsiella species, Escherichia species, Enterobacter species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia species, Acinetobacter species, Citrobacter species, Proteus mirabilis, Morganella morganii, Achromobacter species, other gram-negative organisms (Chryseobacterium meningosepticum/Flavobacterium, Pantoea agglomerans, Aeromonas hydrophila)
raw.Num_Pathogens: 11 categories in Table 1 (13+ species named, including the 'other gram-negative organisms' footnote)
raw.Drug_Classes: Broad-spectrum antibiotics: cefepime and piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin); ESBL production
raw.Specific_Antibiotics: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin
raw.AMR_Outcome_Definition: BSA resistance defined as a culture that (1) was nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin or (2) met criteria for ESBL production; chosen a priori over conventional MDRGN definitions.
raw.AI_Purpose: Develop a user-friendly clinical decision aid (decision tree) to predict the risk of resistance to commonly prescribed broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics in children with gram-negative bloodstream infections
raw.Num_Models_Compared: 1 predictive model developed (decision tree); a multivariable logistic regression model was also fitted and its results compared with the tree
raw.Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables retained with cutoffs generated by the tree; number of prior admissions converted into ordinal categories; days of antibiotic exposure within 6 months dichotomized at >=7 days
raw.Feature_Selection_Method: All predictor variables assessed for contribution to discrimination; splits chosen by the Gini splitting index in recursive partitioning
raw.Software_Libraries: rpart (Recursive Partitioning and Regression Trees); Stata 14.0 for the descriptive and regression analyses
raw.Other_Metrics: Positive predictive value 69%; negative predictive value 78%; prevalence of BSA-resistant bloodstream infection 31%
raw.Baseline_Method: Multivariable logistic regression fitted with generalized estimating equations (exchangeable correlation structure within patient, robust variance estimate)
raw.Baseline_Performance: Adjusted odds ratios: intestinal transplantation 2.73 (95% CI 1.62-4.59); prior culture with a CPT-resistant organism within 6 months 1.94 (1.18-3.19); number of prior gram-negative bloodstream infections 1.07 (1.01-1.13); prior carbapenem within 6 months 2.74 (1.54-4.88)
raw.Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation
raw.Train_Test_Split: None reported; the same data set was used to develop and validate the tree
raw.Overfitting_Method: Leave-one-out cross-validation; the authors acknowledge the tree may perform differently in a different cohort of patients
raw.Clinical_Insights: Recent carbapenem therapy, a prior resistant culture, intestinal transplantation, >=7 prior gram-negative bloodstream infection episodes and age >=3 years raise the risk of a resistant infection; findings are congruent with clinical intuition and with the regression model
raw.Generalisability_Details: The findings may not be generalizable to other types of infections or colonization status, and the tree needs validation in diverse patient populations; in a lower-prevalence setting (eg, community hospitals) the positive predictive value would decrease.
raw.Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation by leave-one-out cross-validation only; the data set was used to both develop and validate the tree; no external validation performed
raw.Integration_Point: At the time Gram stains from positive blood cultures indicate gram-negative organisms, before organism or susceptibility data are available
raw.End_User_Described: clinicians
raw.Clinical_Workflow_Details: Two hypothetical scenarios illustrate use: patient A (10-year-old with prior cefepime-resistant E. coli urinary infection and piperacillin-tazobactam treatment) categorized as high risk, warranting broader empiric therapy; patient B (2-year-old on chemotherapy, no prior carbapenem, 2 prior susceptible episodes) considered lower risk, with empiric cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam reasonable.
raw.Barriers_List: Suboptimal sensitivity (46%): clinical judgment and deviations from tree predictions are needed when misclassification could be detrimental; a proportion of resistant infections classified as low risk are not foreseeable
raw.Facilitators_List: Decision trees incorporate complex interactions, account for collinearity, generate easy-to-use cutoff values for continuous variables, and avoid requiring computation of a composite score at the time of use
raw.Future_Directions: Refine prediction algorithms for individual patients' risk of antibiotic resistance and assess the potential impact on patient management
raw.Top_Features_Importance_Method: Recursive partitioning: the variable that best minimized misclassification by the Gini splitting index was used to split the data
raw.Feature_Interactions_Method: Recursive partitioning tree splits (incorporating complex interactions and collinearity)
raw.Limitation_Categories: Design and data: retrospective, no outpatient data, possible misclassification/missing data, infections may have been missed; Setting: single tertiary center; Modelling: same data set used for development and validation, too few carbapenem-resistant isolates for a staged model, need for wider validation; Generalisability: other infection types or colonization
raw.Data_Quality_Concerns: Possible misclassification or missing data from the retrospective design without outpatient data; bloodstream infections may not have been captured if cultures were obtained at an outside facility
